title: 2  Preparing and exploring longitudinal data in R
text:
2.3 Cleaning a raw visit export
Real exports rarely look like walk_long.csv. The file walk_visits_raw.csv is a deliberately untidy version of the same visits, with the problems that a trial database or a clinic spreadsheet typically produces. This section works through it step by step and records every decision.

2.3.1 The research question and estimand
The target is an analysis file in which each row is one attended visit of one randomised participant, with a unique key \((i, j)\), a correctly parsed date, the actual time since randomisation, numeric outcome and covariate values, and flags for every value that was changed or questioned. The cleaning must not change the estimand. Rules that depend on outcomes or on arm can do exactly that, so they are fixed before anyone looks at results by arm.


2.3.2 Data structure and outcome types

raw <- read_csv(here("data", "walk_visits_raw.csv"),
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
raw

#> # A tibble: 1,906 × 5
#>    participant visit_label visit_date sbp_mmhg steps_k
#>    <chr>       <chr>       <chr>      <chr>    <chr>  
#>  1 W233        M0          2024-01-31 156      5      
#>  2 W146        M3          2024-06-16 151      4.5    
#>  3 W353        M6          2024-12-26 140      7.5    
#>  4 W102        M3          2024-07-09 144      5.6    
#>  5 W255        M0          2024-03-26 131      8.5    
#>  6 W060        M12         2025-06-17 119      6.4    
#>  7 W030        M3          2024-11-13 142      7.3    
#>  8 W175        M12         2025-08-30 129      10.5   
#>  9 W295        M3          2024-12-24 135      11.7   
#> 10 W147        M9          2024-11-22 149      9.6    
#> # ℹ 1,896 more rows


Every column is read as text. That is deliberate: if read_csv() guessed the types, a single stray character in sbp_mmhg would turn the whole column into text, or a parsing problem would turn a value into NA with only a warning. Reading as text and converting explicitly lets you see and count each problem. The file has 1906 rows. walk_long.csv has 1897, so there are 9 more rows than attended visits.


2.3.3 Intuition
Cleaning is a sequence of small, checkable transformations, each followed by a test. The order matters. Identifiers must be standardised before looking for duplicates, because w004 and W004 are the same participant. Exact duplicates must be removed before conflicting duplicates are counted, otherwise a pair of identical rows looks like a conflict. Dates must be parsed before actual time can be derived. Every change is recorded in a log so that another analyst could repeat it.


2.3.4 The model
Let \(D_{ij}\) be the visit date of participant \(i\) at scheduled visit \(j\), \(D^{\text{rand}}_i\) the randomisation date and \(s_j\) the scheduled month. WALK defines a month as 30.44 days (\(365.25/12\) rounded to two decimals). The actual time is
\[
t_{ij} = \frac{D_{ij} - D^{\text{rand}}_i}{30.44},
\]
in months. The visit was due on the target date \(D^{\text{rand}}_i + \operatorname{round}(30.44\, s_j)\), and the deviation in days is
\[
d_{ij} = D_{ij} - \bigl(D^{\text{rand}}_i + \operatorname{round}(30.44\, s_j)\bigr).
\]
A visit is out of window if \(|d_{ij}| > w_j\), where \(w_j\) is the half-width of the protocol window for visit \(j\). A value \(y_{ij}\) is implausible if it lies outside a range fixed in advance, here \([70, 250]\) mmHg for SBP. These quantities are what the code below computes.


2.3.5 Assumptions and limitations
Each rule rests on an assumption that should be written down. Converting IDs to upper case assumes that w004 and W004 are the same person, which is safe only because the protocol format is W followed by three digits. Treating rows identical in every column as copies assumes that two genuine measurements cannot agree exactly on date, SBP and steps. The rule for conflicting duplicates is a convention. Without the source documents nobody knows which record is right. Plausibility limits catch gross errors only. A value of 160 entered instead of 150 is plausible and will never be detected by a range check.


2.3.6 Fitting the model in R
Step 1. Standardise identifiers and visit labels. toupper(trimws()) removes case and spacing differences. The visit label M12 becomes the scheduled month 12 and visit number 6. The stopifnot() lines stop the code if any ID does not match the protocol format or any label is unknown.

raw |> filter(participant != toupper(participant)) |> distinct(participant)

#> # A tibble: 4 × 1
#>   participant
#>   <chr>      
#> 1 w256       
#> 2 w004       
#> 3 w051       
#> 4 w123

step1 <- raw |>
  mutate(id          = toupper(trimws(participant)),
         month_sched = as.numeric(sub("^M", "", visit_label)),
         visit       = match(month_sched, sched_months))
stopifnot(all(grepl("^W[0-9]{3}$", step1$id)), !anyNA(step1$visit))

Step 2. Parse dates and convert text to numbers. as.Date() with an explicit format returns NA for anything that does not match. readr::parse_double() converts text to numbers and reports problems.

step2 <- step1 |>
  mutate(visit_date = as.Date(visit_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
         sbp        = parse_double(sbp_mmhg),
         steps      = parse_double(steps_k)) |>
  select(id, visit, month_sched, visit_date, sbp, steps)
c(bad_dates = sum(is.na(step2$visit_date)), missing_sbp = sum(is.na(step2$sbp)),
  missing_steps = sum(is.na(step2$steps)))

#>     bad_dates   missing_sbp missing_steps 
#>             0             1             0



step2 |> filter(is.na(sbp))

#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   id    visit month_sched visit_date   sbp steps
#>   <chr> <int>       <dbl> <date>     <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 W345      1           0 2024-08-26    NA   9.9


One SBP value is missing. In the raw file the cell is empty, and read_csv() turns empty strings into NA by default. This is a missing value at an attended visit: the participant came, steps were recorded, but SBP was not entered. It is different from a missed visit and should be queried with the clinic.
Step 3. Remove exact duplicates. Rows that agree in every column are copies of one record.

n_exact_dup <- sum(duplicated(step2))
step2[duplicated(step2) | duplicated(step2, fromLast = TRUE), ] |>
  arrange(id, visit)

#> # A tibble: 12 × 6
#>    id    visit month_sched visit_date   sbp steps
#>    <chr> <int>       <dbl> <date>     <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 W062      6          12 2025-01-26   160   9.2
#>  2 W062      6          12 2025-01-26   160   9.2
#>  3 W064      2           1 2024-03-20   125   6.7
#>  4 W064      2           1 2024-03-20   125   6.7
#>  5 W135      3           3 2024-09-21   144   5.6
#>  6 W135      3           3 2024-09-21   144   5.6
#>  7 W266      6          12 2025-10-11   113   4.9
#>  8 W266      6          12 2025-10-11   113   4.9
#>  9 W272      3           3 2025-02-11   149   6.7
#> 10 W272      3           3 2025-02-11   149   6.7
#> 11 W329      2           1 2024-07-03   142  10.7
#> 12 W329      2           1 2024-07-03   142  10.7

step3 <- distinct(step2)

There are 6 exact duplicate rows. Removing them leaves 1900 rows.
Step 4. Find and resolve conflicting duplicates. After removing exact copies, any remaining repeat of the key \((i, j)\) is a conflict: two different records for the same visit.

conflicts <- step3 |>
  add_count(id, visit, name = "n_records") |>
  filter(n_records > 1) |>
  arrange(id, visit, visit_date)
conflicts

#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   id    visit month_sched visit_date   sbp steps n_records
#>   <chr> <int>       <dbl> <date>     <dbl> <dbl>     <int>
#> 1 W216      2           1 2024-07-20   143   7.7         2
#> 2 W216      2           1 2024-07-22   137   7.7         2
#> 3 W255      5           9 2024-12-12   129   7.7         2
#> 4 W255      5           9 2024-12-14   139   7.7         2
#> 5 W290      2           1 2024-11-21   136   5.9         2
#> 6 W290      2           1 2024-11-23   140   5.9         2


There are 3 visits with two records each. Within each pair the dates differ by 2 days and SBP differs by between 4 and 10 mmHg. Some rule is needed to keep one record per visit. The best option is to query the clinic and use the source document. When that is impossible, common conventions are to keep the earliest record (the first measurement taken in the visit window), to keep the record closest to the target date, or to average the two values. WALK’s data management plan specifies the first: keep the earliest-dated record and flag the visit.
The rule must be set without looking at outcomes by arm. Suppose an analyst looked at the three pairs, saw which version made the enhanced programme look better, and chose a rule accordingly. With three pairs the effect would be tiny, but the principle scales: a rule chosen after seeing its consequences is part of the analysis, and it can bias the estimated treatment effect in a direction the analyst prefers. The same applies to outlier removal and window definitions. This is why trial guidelines expect data-handling rules to be written into the statistical analysis plan before unblinding (Gamble et al. 2017).

step4 <- step3 |>
  group_by(id, visit) |>
  mutate(conflict_flag = n() > 1) |>
  arrange(visit_date, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup()
stopifnot(nrow(count(step4, id, visit) |> filter(n > 1)) == 0)
nrow(step4)

#> [1] 1897


Step 5. Derive actual time. Join the randomisation date and apply the formulas above. unmatched = "error" stops the code if any visit has no baseline row.

days_per_month <- 30.44
step5 <- step4 |>
  left_join(baseline |> select(id, rand_date),
            by = "id", relationship = "many-to-one", unmatched = "error") |>
  mutate(days        = as.numeric(visit_date - rand_date),
         month       = round(days / days_per_month, 2),
         target_date = rand_date + round(month_sched * days_per_month),
         dev_days    = as.numeric(visit_date - target_date))
stopifnot(all(step5$days >= 0), all(step5$month[step5$visit == 1] == 0))

The checks confirm that no visit is dated before randomisation and that every baseline visit took place on the randomisation date.
Step 6. Check plausibility. The range 70–250 mmHg was fixed in advance as plausible for adults with raised blood pressure.

step5 |> filter(sbp < 70 | sbp > 250)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 12
#>   id    visit month_sched visit_date   sbp steps conflict_flag rand_date 
#>   <chr> <int>       <dbl> <date>     <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>         <date>    
#> 1 W088      6          12 2025-02-20  1190   4.2 FALSE         2024-02-09
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: days <dbl>, month <dbl>, target_date <date>,
#> #   dev_days <dbl>


One value, 1190 mmHg for W088 at month 12, is impossible. It looks like 119 with an extra zero (a typing error multiplying the value by 10). It is tempting to correct it, and some data management plans allow obvious transcription errors to be corrected. WALK’s plan does not, so the value is set to missing, the raw value is kept in a separate column, and a query is logged. If the clinic confirms 119, the correction is made in the database and the cleaning code is rerun.

step6 <- step5 |>
  mutate(sbp_flag = case_when(is.na(sbp) ~ "blank",
                              sbp < 70 | sbp > 250 ~ "implausible",
                              TRUE ~ "ok"),
         sbp_raw = sbp,
         sbp     = if_else(sbp_flag == "implausible", NA_real_, sbp))
count(step6, sbp_flag)

#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   sbp_flag        n
#>   <chr>       <int>
#> 1 blank           1
#> 2 implausible     1
#> 3 ok           1895


Step 7. Compare scheduled and actual times. The (hypothetical) WALK protocol allows ±7 days around month 1, ±14 days around month 3 and ±28 days around months 6, 9 and 12.

window_days <- c(`0` = 0, `1` = 7, `3` = 14, `6` = 28, `9` = 28, `12` = 28)
walk_clean <- step6 |>
  mutate(window = window_days[as.character(month_sched)],
         out_of_window = abs(dev_days) > window) |>
  select(id, visit, month_sched, visit_date, rand_date, month, dev_days,
         out_of_window, sbp, sbp_raw, sbp_flag, steps, conflict_flag) |>
  arrange(id, visit)

window_table <- walk_clean |>
  filter(visit > 1) |>
  group_by(month_sched) |>
  summarise(window = first(window_days[as.character(month_sched)]),
            n = n(), min_dev = min(dev_days), max_dev = max(dev_days),
            sd_dev = round(sd(dev_days), 1), n_out = sum(out_of_window))
window_table

#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   month_sched window     n min_dev max_dev sd_dev n_out
#>         <dbl>  <dbl> <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl> <int>
#> 1           1      7   324      -9      12    3.7    10
#> 2           3     14   319     -23      21    7.7    15
#> 3           6     28   309     -26      26   10.2     0
#> 4           9     28   297     -37      31   12.4     3
#> 5          12     28   288     -36      40   13.6     6




2.3.7 Interpreting the output
The window table shows that timing becomes more variable as follow-up goes on. The standard deviation of the deviation from the target date grows from 3.7 days at month 1 to 13.6 days at month 12, and the most extreme visit is 40 days from its target. In total 34 visits (2.2% of follow-up visits) fall outside the window. The decision is to keep them and flag them. Excluding them would throw away valid measurements and create extra missing data. Because the course models use actual time (month) for the random slope, a visit at 13.2 months is placed at 13.2 months, not at 12. Analyses that use the scheduled visit as a factor treat it as a month-12 measurement. A sensitivity analysis that excludes out-of-window visits can show whether that matters.

cleaning_log <- tibble(
  step = c("Rows read", "Exact duplicate rows removed",
           "Rows after removing exact duplicates",
           "Visits with conflicting records", "Rows after resolving conflicts",
           "Blank SBP values", "Implausible SBP values set to missing",
           "Out-of-window visits (kept, flagged)"),
  n = c(nrow(raw), n_exact_dup, nrow(step3),
        n_distinct(paste(conflicts$id, conflicts$visit)), nrow(walk_clean),
        sum(walk_clean$sbp_flag == "blank"),
        sum(walk_clean$sbp_flag == "implausible"),
        sum(walk_clean$out_of_window)))
knitr::kable(cleaning_log, caption = "Cleaning log for walk_visits_raw.csv")

The cleaning log is the main output of this section. Together with a query log (one line per questioned value, with the action taken), it lets anyone reproduce the analysis file and see every decision.


2.3.8 Checking the model
Because WALK is simulated, the checked analysis file walk_long.csv exists and the cleaned data can be compared with it. In a real study the equivalent check is double data entry, source-document verification of a sample, or comparison with a previous data freeze.

agreement <- walk_clean |>
  full_join(walk |> select(id, visit, month_ref = month, sbp_ref = sbp,
                           steps_ref = steps), by = c("id", "visit"))
sbp_differs <- agreement |>
  filter(is.na(sbp) | is.na(sbp_ref) | sbp != sbp_ref)
month_diff <- agreement$month - agreement$month_ref
c(only_clean = sum(is.na(agreement$month_ref)),
  only_walk_long = sum(is.na(agreement$month)),
  sbp_differs = nrow(sbp_differs),
  steps_differs = sum(agreement$steps != agreement$steps_ref))

#>     only_clean only_walk_long    sbp_differs  steps_differs 
#>              0              0              2              0

sbp_differs |> select(id, visit, sbp, sbp_raw, sbp_ref, sbp_flag)

#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   id    visit   sbp sbp_raw sbp_ref sbp_flag   
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>      
#> 1 W088      6    NA    1190     119 implausible
#> 2 W345      1    NA      NA     152 blank

table(round(month_diff, 2))

#> 
#> -0.02 -0.01     0  0.01  0.02 
#>    72   471   829   454    71


The cleaned file has 1897 rows, the same keys as walk_long.csv, and identical steps values. SBP differs in exactly 2 rows: the blank value and the implausible value, both of which we set to missing while walk_long.csv holds the true values. Actual time differs in 1068 of 1897 rows, but never by more than 0.02 months (well under one day). The difference is a rounding artefact that we can explain exactly. The raw file was built by adding round(month * 30.44) days to the randomisation date, so the visit date was rounded to a whole day and the original two-decimal month cannot be recovered from it. Our month is the correct time of the recorded date. These small differences are honest and harmless, and the report should say so rather than force the two files to agree.


2.3.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



The raw visit export contained 1906 records. After identifiers were converted to upper case, 6 exact duplicate records were removed. 3 visits had two conflicting records; following the prespecified rule, the earliest-dated record was retained and the visit flagged. One SBP value was blank and one (1190 mmHg) was implausible; both were treated as missing and queried. Actual time since randomisation was calculated from visit and randomisation dates. 34 follow-up visits (2.2%) were outside the protocol window and were retained, with time modelled as actual time. The analysis file contained 1897 visits from 360 participants.








ImportantCommon mistakes




Looking for duplicates before standardising IDs. Copies that differ only in case are missed.
Letting read_csv() guess types on a messy file. Problems turn into silent NA values. Read as text, convert explicitly and count the failures.
Choosing the duplicate or outlier rule after looking at results by arm. Fix the rule in the analysis plan, before unblinding.
Deleting out-of-window visits. They are valid measurements at a different time. Use actual time and flag them.
“Correcting” values without a documented rule. Keep the raw value, set the cleaned value to missing and raise a query, unless the plan allows the correction.
Overwriting the raw file. Cleaning code reads the raw export and writes a new file. The raw file is never edited by hand.

section: 2.4 Missing visits, summaries and participant flow
text:
2.4 Missing visits, summaries and participant flow
From here on the module uses the checked analysis file walk_long.csv (loaded as walk), so that the numbers agree with the rest of the course.

2.4.1 The research question and estimand
Before modelling we need to know who was randomised, who was seen at each visit, how the groups compared at baseline and what the outcome looked like at each visit. These are descriptive targets: counts, proportions, means and standard deviations, computed for the right denominators.


2.4.2 Data structure and outcome types
A long file holds attended visits only, so missed visits are invisible in it. To count them, build the complete grid of every randomised participant crossed with every scheduled visit, from the design: 360 participants × 6 visits. Do not build the grid from the data (a participant never seen would be lost) and do not use walk_complete.csv, which no real study has.


2.4.3 Intuition
Two kinds of missing visit behave differently. Intermittent missingness means a participant missed a visit and came back later. Dropout means a participant was never seen again after some visit. Dropout gives a monotone pattern: once missing, always missing. The distinction matters because dropout usually has stronger links to the outcome and accumulates over time.


2.4.4 The model
Let \(R_{ij} = 1\) if \(y_{ij}\) is observed and \(0\) otherwise. For participant \(i\) let \(L_i = \max\{j : R_{ij} = 1\}\) be the last attended visit. A missing visit \(j\) is intermittent if \(j < L_i\) and follows dropout if \(j > L_i\). The observed mean SBP in arm \(g\) at visit \(j\) is
\[
\bar{y}_{gj} = \frac{\sum_{i \in g} R_{ij}\, y_{ij}}{\sum_{i \in g} R_{ij}},
\]
the average over those seen. Its denominator changes from visit to visit.


2.4.5 Assumptions and limitations
The grid assumes that the schedule in the protocol applies to everyone. Descriptive tables of observed data are exactly that: they describe the people who were measured, not the people randomised. Baseline tables in randomised trials describe the groups. Significance tests of baseline differences between randomised arms are not meaningful, because any difference is due to chance by construction.


2.4.6 Fitting the model in R

grid <- baseline |>
  select(id, arm) |>
  crossing(visit = seq_along(sched_months)) |>
  mutate(month_sched = sched_months[visit]) |>
  left_join(walk |> select(id, visit, sbp), by = c("id", "visit")) |>
  mutate(observed = !is.na(sbp)) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(last_seen = max(visit[observed]),
         miss_type = case_when(observed ~ "observed",
                               visit < last_seen ~ "intermittent",
                               TRUE ~ "after dropout")) |>
  ungroup()
grid |> count(arm, miss_type) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = miss_type, values_from = n)

#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   arm   `after dropout` intermittent observed
#>   <fct>           <int>        <int>    <int>
#> 1 UC                 71           21      628
#> 2 SP                 58           20      642
#> 3 EP                 74           19      627


A baseline table by arm, with a small helper for mean (SD):

mean_sd <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f (%.", digits, "f)"),
          mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}
baseline_table <- baseline |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = as.character(n()),
            `Age, years` = mean_sd(age),
            `Female, n (%)` = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", sum(sex == "Female"),
                                      100 * mean(sex == "Female")),
            `BMI, kg/m2` = mean_sd(bmi),
            `SBP, mmHg` = mean_sd(sbp0),
            `Steps, 1000/day` = mean_sd(steps0)) |>
  pivot_longer(-arm, names_to = "Characteristic") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = value)

Visit-specific summaries, and a participant-flow table built with the course helper visit_flow():

  group_by(arm, month_sched) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp), sd = sd(sbp), mean_month = mean(month))
visit_summary |> filter(arm == "EP")

#> 6 EP             12    93 136.6 12.66    12.00

flow <- visit_flow(walk, id, month_sched, arm) |>
  left_join(count(baseline, arm, name = "randomised"), by = "arm") |>
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", n_seen, 100 * n_seen / randomised)) |>
  select(arm, month_sched, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = cell)

2.4.7 Interpreting the output
The grid has 2160 scheduled visits, of which 263 (12.2%) are missing: 60 intermittent and 203 after dropout. Dropout (last attended visit before month 12) occurred in 25 UC, 20 SP and 27 EP participants. The flow table shows attendance falling steadily, to between 78% and 83% at month 12.
The baseline table shows groups that are similar, as randomisation should produce. Mean baseline SBP is 146.2, 147.2 and 147.5 mmHg in the three arms. The proportion of women differs by several percentage points between arms. That is chance variation, not a reason for a test. It is a reason to consider adjusting for sex if it is prognostic, as the course’s covariate-adjusted model does.
The visit summary for the enhanced programme shows mean SBP falling from 147.5 mmHg at baseline to 136.6 mmHg at month 12, with the number of observations falling from 120 to 93. The column mean_month shows that the average actual time at each visit is close to the scheduled time, so the irregular timing does not shift the visits systematically.


2.4.8 Checking the model
The grid must have exactly \(N \times 6\) rows, the number of observed cells must equal the number of rows in the long file (1897 and 1897), and the flow table at month 0 must equal the number randomised. Checks like these catch a filter applied in the wrong place.


2.4.9 Reporting
“Of 360 randomised participants, 288 (80%) attended the month-12 visit. Of the 2160 scheduled visits, 263 were missed: 60 intermittently and 203 after dropout.” The flow table itself belongs in the CONSORT-style participant-flow section of a trial report.






ImportantCommon mistakes




Building the grid from the observed data. Participants or visits never seen disappear. Build it from the randomisation list and the protocol schedule.
Reporting percentages of those seen instead of those randomised. State the denominator.
Testing baseline differences between randomised arms. Describe them; do not test them.
Confusing a missing value at an attended visit with a missed visit. They have different causes and are counted separately.

title: 2  Preparing and exploring longitudinal data in R
text:
2.5 Exploratory plots

walk_lab <- walk |>
  mutate(arm_lab = factor(walk_arm_labels[as.character(arm)],
                          levels = walk_arm_labels))


2.5.1 The research question and estimand
Plots answer questions that tables cannot: How variable are individual trajectories? Do participants differ more in level or in rate of change? Is change linear? Who is missing, and when? Do people who leave look different before they leave? These are the questions that guide the choice of model in later modules (Singer and Willett 2003; Fitzmaurice et al. 2011).


2.5.2 Data structure and outcome types
Individual-level plots use the long file with actual time on the horizontal axis. Group summaries use scheduled time, because means are computed per visit. The missingness map uses the complete grid built in the previous section.


2.5.3 Intuition
A spaghetti plot draws one line per participant. With hundreds of participants the lines merge into a cloud, so a random subset (selected with a fixed seed, never chosen by hand) shows individual shapes. Individual trajectory panels give each participant their own small plot. A group mean plot summarises each arm at each visit. A missingness map shows each participant as a row and each visit as a column. Pattern plots show mean profiles separately for groups defined by when participants dropped out.


2.5.4 The model
The observed group mean plot shows \(\bar y_{gj}\) with a 95% confidence interval \(\bar y_{gj} \pm t_{0.975,\, n_{gj}-1}\, s_{gj}/\sqrt{n_{gj}}\), where \(s_{gj}\) is the standard deviation and \(n_{gj}\) the number observed. This interval treats the participants seen at visit \(j\) as a simple random sample. It says nothing about correlation between visits, or about who is missing.


2.5.5 Assumptions and limitations
Plots of observed data show the observed data. A spaghetti plot gives more visual weight to participants who stay longer. Group means are computed on a different set of people at each visit. The pattern plot splits the data into small groups whose means are noisy.


2.5.6 Fitting the model in R

plot_spaghetti(walk_lab, month, sbp, id, group = arm_lab, alpha = 0.15) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "SBP (mmHg)")







Figure 2.1: Spaghetti plot of SBP for all 360 participants, by arm. Each line is one participant. Time is actual months since randomisation.






plot_spaghetti(walk_lab, month, sbp, id, group = arm_lab, n_show = 30,
               seed = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "SBP (mmHg)")







Figure 2.2: Spaghetti plot of a random subset of 30 participants (seed 2).






set.seed(4)
panel_ids <- baseline |> group_by(arm) |> slice_sample(n = 4) |> pull(id)
walk_lab |>
  filter(id %in% panel_ids) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, sbp, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ id, ncol = 4) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "SBP (mmHg)")







Figure 2.3: Individual trajectories for four randomly chosen participants per arm.






plot_observed_means(walk_lab, month_sched, sbp, arm_lab) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Observed mean SBP (mmHg), 95% CI")







Figure 2.4: Observed mean SBP by arm and scheduled visit, with 95% confidence intervals. Each mean uses only the participants seen at that visit.






plot_missing_map(grid, id, visit, observed, order_by = last_seen) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, scales = "free_y", labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month")







Figure 2.5: Missingness map. Each row is a participant, sorted by last attended visit; dark cells are observed visits.






retention <- grid |>
  group_by(arm, month_sched) |>
  summarise(pct_still_in = 100 * mean(last_seen >= visit))
ggplot(retention, aes(month_sched, pct_still_in, colour = arm)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Participants not yet dropped out (%)")







Figure 2.6: Percentage of randomised participants who have not yet dropped out, by arm.






pattern_means <- walk |>
  left_join(baseline |> select(id, last_month_sched), by = "id",
            relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  mutate(pattern = factor(last_month_sched, levels = sched_months,
                          labels = paste("Last seen month", sched_months))) |>
  group_by(arm, pattern, month_sched) |>
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp), n = n())
pattern_means |>
  ggplot(aes(month_sched, mean_sbp, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73",
                                 "#CC79A7", "#222222"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Mean observed SBP (mmHg)")







Figure 2.7: Mean observed SBP by dropout pattern (scheduled month of the last attended visit). Point size shows the number of participants. Participants seen only at baseline appear as single points. Every pattern other than ‘last seen month 12’ contains between 2 and 9 participants per arm.





The pattern plot is noisy because most dropout patterns contain only a handful of people. A simple numerical summary answers the key question more directly: just before they left, was SBP in those who dropped out higher than in those who stayed? For each visit before month 12, compare each participant’s SBP with the mean of their arm at that visit.

dropout_last_sbp <- walk |>
  left_join(baseline |> select(id, last_month_sched), by = "id",
            relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  filter(month_sched < 12) |>
  group_by(arm, month_sched) |>
  mutate(dev_from_mean = sbp - mean(sbp)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(status = if_else(month_sched == last_month_sched,
                          "Last visit before dropout", "Seen again later")) |>
  group_by(status) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_dev = mean(dev_from_mean))
dropout_last_sbp

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   status                        n mean_dev
#>   <chr>                     <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 Last visit before dropout    72   5.127 
#> 2 Seen again later           1537  -0.2402




2.5.7 Interpreting the output
The full spaghetti plot shows that differences between participants dominate. At every visit the middle 90% of SBP values span roughly 42 to 45 mmHg, while the arm averages change by a few mmHg. The subset makes individual lines visible. Each participant fluctuates from visit to visit around their own level, which is the within-person variation described in Module 1, and in the programme arms many lines drop during the first months. The individual panels confirm this and show that participants have different numbers of visits, at slightly different times. Mixed models handle both features naturally.
The observed mean plot suggests a fall in SBP in all arms during the first three months, largest in the enhanced programme and smallest in usual care, followed by a plateau. The change is clearly not linear in time, an early sign that the linear-time model of later modules is a simplification and a reason why the primary model uses scheduled visit as a factor.
The missingness map shows the monotone staircase of dropout at the bottom of each panel and scattered intermittent gaps above it. The retention curves are similar in the three arms. By month 12, 79% (UC), 83% (SP) and 78% (EP) of participants had not dropped out. The simulation does include slightly higher dropout in the enhanced programme, but with 120 participants per arm a difference of this size could easily arise by chance, and the curves cross during follow-up.
The dropout summary is the most important result of this section. At their last visit before dropping out, the 72 participants who later left had SBP on average 5.1 mmHg above the mean of their arm at that visit. Their mean baseline SBP was 150.4 mmHg, against 146.1 mmHg in participants who did not drop out. Dropout is related to the observed outcome. The pattern plot shows the same thing less cleanly. Participants seen only at baseline, and most early-dropout patterns, start above the completers in their arm, although with groups this small some patterns go the other way (for example the few usual-care participants last seen at month 9).


2.5.8 Checking the model
Use a fixed seed for subsets so the figure can be reproduced, and draw several subsets to make sure the one shown is typical. Check that the number of lines equals the number of participants. Check axis units, and whether the horizontal axis is actual or scheduled time.


2.5.9 Reporting
“Individual SBP trajectories varied mainly in level, with substantial visit-to-visit fluctuation. Mean SBP fell during the first three months in all arms, most in the enhanced programme. Participants who dropped out had higher SBP at their last attended visit than those who continued (on average 5.1 mmHg above the arm-specific visit mean).”






ImportantCommon mistakes




Choosing “interesting” participants by hand for a subset plot. Use a random sample with a seed.
Plotting scheduled time for individual trajectories. Use actual time; the scheduled visit is for group summaries.
Reading the observed mean plot as the treatment effect. It mixes treatment effects with changes in who is still measured (next section).
Ignoring the missingness plots. They are the first evidence about the missing-data mechanism.

title: 2  Preparing and exploring longitudinal data in R
text:
2.6 Observed means versus model-estimated trajectories

2.6.1 The research question and estimand
The trial asks how mean SBP would change in each arm if everyone randomised were followed to month 12. The target is \(E(Y_{ij})\) for each arm and visit, and the difference in mean change from baseline between arms. The observed mean \(\bar{y}_{gj}\) estimates something else: the mean among those still measured at visit \(j\), \(E(Y_{ij} \mid R_{ij} = 1)\).


2.6.2 Data structure and outcome types
The long file walk_long.csv, with dropout. For teaching only, walk_complete.csv contains all 2160 scheduled values, including the ones that went missing. This comparison is possible only because the data are simulated. No real study can compute the complete-data mean.


2.6.3 Intuition
If participants with higher SBP are more likely to leave, the people still measured at month 12 have, on average, lower SBP than the full randomised group would have had. The observed mean is pulled down. A mixed model fitted to all observed data handles this differently. Each participant’s early measurements tell the model about that participant’s level, and the correlation between visits lets the model use those early values for the later visits that are missing. When dropout depends only on observed values, this is the right thing to do, and the model’s estimated means move back towards the complete-data means.


2.6.4 The model
Under missing at random (MAR), the probability that \(y_{ij}\) is missing depends on the observed data (here the last observed SBP and arm) but not on the unobserved value itself, given the observed data (Rubin 1976; Little and Rubin 2019). Even under MAR, in general
\[
E(Y_{ij} \mid R_{ij} = 1) \neq E(Y_{ij}),
\]
because \(R_{ij}\) depends on earlier outcomes that are correlated with \(Y_{ij}\). The primary WALK model,
\[
y_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol\beta + b_{0i} + b_{1i} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
with scheduled visit as a factor interacting with arm in \(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol\beta\), is fitted by likelihood to all observed \(y_{ij}\). Under MAR the likelihood-based estimates of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) are valid without modelling the dropout process, provided the model is correctly specified. Modules 4 and 10 explain the model and this result.


2.6.5 Assumptions and limitations
The comparison relies on MAR, which holds in this simulation by design but can never be verified from observed data. If dropout depended on the unobserved SBP itself (missing not at random), the mixed model would also be biased. Module 10 covers sensitivity analyses for that case. Here we use the model only as a preview.


2.6.6 Fitting the model in R

complete <- load_walk("complete")
m_primary <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk,
                  control = lmer_ctrl)
em_visits <- as.data.frame(emmeans(m_primary, ~ visit_f | arm))
means_compare <- complete |>
  group_by(arm, visit_f) |>
  summarise(complete_mean = mean(sbp),
            observed_mean = mean(sbp[observed]),
            n_observed    = sum(observed)) |>
  left_join(em_visits |> select(arm, visit_f, model_mean = emmean),
            by = c("arm", "visit_f")) |>
  mutate(obs_bias   = observed_mean - complete_mean,
         model_bias = model_mean - complete_mean) |>
  ungroup()
means_compare |> filter(visit_f != "0") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

#> # A tibble: 15 × 8
#>    arm   visit_f complete_mean observed_mean n_observed model_mean obs_bias
#>    <fct> <fct>           <dbl>         <dbl>      <int>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 UC    1               144.5         143.4        107      144.6    -1.06
#>  2 UC    3               143.9         142.7        106      143.6    -1.21
#>  3 UC    6               144.4         142.9        101      144.6    -1.44
#>  4 UC    9               144.6         143.6         99      144.9    -1.02
#>  5 UC    12              144.7         144.3         95      144.9    -0.39
#>  6 SP    1               145.3         144.2        107      144.8    -1.13
#>  7 SP    3               142.0         141.4        110      142.0    -0.55
#>  8 SP    6               140.5         140.0        103      140.8    -0.59
#>  9 SP    9               139.8         139.0        102      140.0    -0.81
#> 10 SP    12              140.2         139.6        100      140.5    -0.6 
#> 11 EP    1               142.7         142.6        110      142.6    -0.18
#> 12 EP    3               139.9         139.0        103      139.7    -0.89
#> 13 EP    6               137.2         136.1        105      136.9    -1.03
#> 14 EP    9               137.4         136.8         96      137.4    -0.59
#> 15 EP    12              137.7         136.6         93      137.2    -1.09
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: model_bias <dbl>



means_compare |>
  select(arm, visit_f, `All scheduled visits (teaching only)` = complete_mean,
         `Observed visits only` = observed_mean,
         `Mixed model, observed data` = model_mean) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(arm, visit_f), names_to = "source", values_to = "mean") |>
  mutate(month = as.numeric(as.character(visit_f))) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, mean, linetype = source, shape = source)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sched_months) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)", linetype = NULL, shape = NULL)







Figure 2.8: Mean SBP by arm and scheduled visit from three sources: all scheduled visits (available only because the data are simulated), observed visits only, and the primary mixed model fitted to the observed data.







2.6.7 Interpreting the output
The observed mean is below the complete-data mean at 15 of the 15 follow-up visits, by between 0.2 and 1.4 mmHg. The direction is what the dropout analysis predicted: those who left had higher SBP, so those who remain look healthier. The mixed-model estimates lie much closer to the complete-data means. Their average absolute error over follow-up visits is 0.23 mmHg, against 0.84 mmHg for the observed means, and their errors go in both directions instead of all one way.
The bias in observed means affects the estimated change from baseline too. In usual care the complete-data change at month 12 is -1.5 mmHg. The observed means give -1.8 mmHg and the model gives -1.3 mmHg. In the enhanced programme the corresponding values are -9.9, -11.0 and -10.3 mmHg. The observed means exaggerate the fall in SBP in all three arms. The size of the bias is modest here because dropout was moderate (20% of participants), but it grows with the amount of dropout and with the strength of its dependence on the outcome.
The complete-data means are themselves estimates from 120 participants per arm. They are not the true values in walk_truth.rds. The comparison here isolates the effect of missingness. How close each method comes to the truth is a question for later modules.


2.6.8 Checking the model
Outside a simulation, the comparison of observed and model-estimated means is still informative. If they differ noticeably, and the missingness plots show dropout related to earlier outcomes, the observed means should not be presented as estimates of the arm means. Plot both, and label the observed means as “observed among those seen”.


2.6.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Observed mean SBP at each visit is reported descriptively with the number of participants contributing. Because participants with higher SBP were more likely to drop out, treatment effects were estimated from a linear mixed model fitted to all observed data, which gives valid estimates when dropout depends on observed values (missing at random). In this simulated example, the observed month-12 mean in the enhanced programme (136.6 mmHg) was lower than the model estimate (137.2 mmHg).








ImportantCommon mistakes




Presenting observed visit means as the estimated treatment trajectory. They describe a shrinking and selected group.
Analysing completers only. This discards information and, under MAR dropout, is biased in the same direction as the observed means.
Believing that a mixed model solves every missing-data problem. It is valid under MAR and correct model specification. Module 10 covers MNAR and sensitivity analyses.
Using walk_complete.csv in an analysis. It exists only to show what missingness does. Real studies never have it.

title: 2  Preparing and exploring longitudinal data in R
text:
Summary
A longitudinal analysis is only as good as the file it starts from. Reshaping, joining and cleaning are routine operations, but each has a characteristic failure (a time-varying column left in a reshape, a duplicated key in a join, duplicates sought before IDs are standardised), and each can be checked by counting rows and keys before and after. The cleaning decisions that affect outcomes, such as which of two conflicting records to keep, are made by rules fixed in advance and recorded in a log. Once the data are clean, a complete grid built from the design reveals the missing visits, and plots of individual trajectories, group means, missingness and dropout patterns show what the models will have to handle. In WALK they show large differences between people, a nonlinear early fall in SBP, and dropout among participants with higher SBP. That last finding is why observed means at each visit drift below the means of everyone randomised, and why the course estimates trajectories from models fitted to all observed data.

Further reading

Wickham (2014) sets out the principles of tidy data that underlie the long format and the tidyr functions.
Singer and Willett (2003) (chapter 2) and Fitzmaurice et al. (2011) describe exploratory analysis of longitudinal data, including individual trajectory plots.
Diggle et al. (2002), chapter 3, covers graphical exploration of longitudinal data and of the mean and covariance structure.
Little and Rubin (2019) defines MCAR, MAR and MNAR and explains when likelihood-based analysis of the observed data is valid.
Gamble et al. (2017) lists what a statistical analysis plan should prespecify, including the handling of data and missing values.

title: 3  Statistical foundations and traditional approaches
text:
Learning outcomes
Before mixed models existed in standard software, analysts of repeated measurements had a toolbox of simpler methods: a regression that treats every observation as independent, a paired t-test of baseline against follow-up, a repeated-measures analysis of variance, an analysis of the last visit adjusted for baseline, or a separate test at every visit. These methods are still everywhere in published papers, in reviewers’ requests and in statistical analysis plans. Some of them remain the best tool for a narrow question. Others give answers that look plausible but rest on assumptions that longitudinal data rarely meet. This module reviews the regression ideas the rest of the course builds on, works through each traditional method with the WALK trial, and shows exactly where each one stops being adequate. By the end you should be able to read an analysis that uses these methods, judge whether it answers the stated question, and explain why the course moves on to linear mixed-effects models in Module 4.
By the end of this module participants will be able to:

title: 3  Statistical foundations and traditional approaches
section: 3.1 Part 1. Regression foundations in a longitudinal context
text:
3.1 Part 1. Regression foundations in a longitudinal context

3.1.1 Regression with time and an arm-by-time interaction
This section revisits ordinary linear regression with the WALK data. The model is not a good final analysis, because it treats every observation as independent, but every later model in the course shares its mean structure and the way its coefficients are read. Getting the interpretation right here pays off in every later module.

The research question and estimand
“Does the rate of change in SBP over the first year differ between each walking programme and usual care?” If we assume that mean SBP changes linearly with time in each arm, the estimand is the difference in mean slope (mmHg per month) between SP and UC, and between EP and UC. Multiplying by 12 gives the implied difference in mean change over a year.


Data structure and outcome types
The outcome SBP is continuous. The data are in long format with one row per observation; each participant contributes between one and six rows. Time is the actual visit time month, a continuous variable. Arm is a three-level factor with UC as the reference level.


Intuition
Fit a straight line through the SBP measurements of each arm. The intercept of each line is the mean SBP at month 0 and the slope is the mean change per month. An interaction between arm and month lets the slopes differ between arms; without it the lines would be forced to be parallel, and the model could only say that one arm is higher than another by the same amount at every time. In a randomised trial the question is precisely whether the lines diverge, so the interaction terms carry the treatment effect.


The model
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{SP}_i + \beta_3 \text{EP}_i + \beta_4\, t_{ij}\text{SP}_i + \beta_5\, t_{ij}\text{EP}_i + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ independent}.
\]
Here \(y_{ij}\) is the SBP of participant \(i\) at occasion \(j\) and \(t_{ij}\) is the actual time of that occasion in months. \(\text{SP}_i\) and \(\text{EP}_i\) are indicators (1 if participant \(i\) is in that arm, 0 otherwise), so UC is the reference. \(\beta_0\) is the mean SBP in UC at month 0; \(\beta_1\) is the mean change per month in UC; \(\beta_2\) and \(\beta_3\) are the differences in mean SBP from UC at month 0; \(\beta_4\) and \(\beta_5\) are the differences in slope from UC, so the SP slope is \(\beta_1 + \beta_4\) and the EP slope is \(\beta_1 + \beta_5\). The residual error \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) has variance \(\sigma^2\), and ordinary least squares assumes that residuals are independent of one another, including those from the same participant.


Assumptions and limitations
The assumptions are linearity of the mean in time within each arm, constant residual variance, approximately normal residuals (important for small samples) and, crucially, independence of the residuals. The last assumption is false for repeated measurements. Participants who start high tend to stay high, so two residuals from the same participant are positively correlated. Module 1 showed by simulation what this does: the standard error of a between-subject comparison (such as the arm difference at month 0) is too small, and the standard error of a within-subject comparison (such as a slope) is usually too large, because the model does not know that each participant acts as their own control. A linear mean is also only an approximation for WALK, where most of the fall in SBP occurs in the first six months.


Fitting the model in R

m_ols <- lm(sbp ~ month * arm, data = walk)
summary(m_ols)

#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = sbp ~ month * arm, data = walk)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
#> -39.59  -9.40   0.70   9.14  45.71 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept) 144.3304     0.8028  179.79   <2e-16 ***
#> month        -0.0828     0.1237   -0.67   0.5032    
#> armSP         0.6448     1.1329    0.57   0.5694    
#> armEP        -0.3659     1.1331   -0.32   0.7468    
#> month:armSP  -0.5114     0.1739   -2.94   0.0033 ** 
#> month:armEP  -0.7217     0.1752   -4.12    4e-05 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 13.3 on 1891 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.0465, Adjusted R-squared:  0.044 
#> F-statistic: 18.5 on 5 and 1891 DF,  p-value: <2e-16



ols_tab <- fixef_table(m_ols)
ols_tab

#>          term  estimate     se    lower    upper         p
#> 1 (Intercept) 144.33038 0.8028 142.7569 145.9038 0.000e+00
#> 2       month  -0.08284 0.1237  -0.3253   0.1596 5.032e-01
#> 3       armSP   0.64476 1.1329  -1.5757   2.8653 5.694e-01
#> 4       armEP  -0.36587 1.1331  -2.5867   1.8550 7.468e-01
#> 5 month:armSP  -0.51145 0.1739  -0.8524  -0.1705 3.317e-03
#> 6 month:armEP  -0.72174 0.1752  -1.0652  -0.3783 3.976e-05

b <- coef(m_ols)



Interpreting the output
The formula month * arm expands to the main effects of month and arm plus their interaction month:arm. The table below reads the key lines.








Output line
What it means
Value here




(Intercept)
Mean SBP in UC at month 0
144.3 mmHg


month
Mean change per month in UC
-0.08 mmHg/month


armSP, armEP
Difference from UC at month 0
0.64, -0.37 mmHg


month:armSP
Extra change per month in SP compared with UC
-0.51 mmHg/month


month:armEP
Extra change per month in EP compared with UC
-0.72 mmHg/month


Residual standard error
Estimate of \(\sigma\)
13.3 mmHg



The main effect of arm is the arm difference at month 0 only, because that is where the interaction terms are zero. It is close to zero, as randomisation should make it. A common error is to call armEP “the effect of the enhanced programme”. The programme effect is in the interaction: SBP in the EP arm falls by an extra 0.72 mmHg per month compared with UC (95% confidence interval -1.07 to -0.38). Over 12 months that is an extra fall of 8.7 mmHg. The slope in UC itself is -0.08 mmHg per month, close to zero. The 95% confidence interval is the range of slope differences compatible with the data under the model: if we repeated the trial many times, intervals built in this way would contain the true value 95% of the time, provided the model’s assumptions hold. That proviso is the problem here, as the next subsection shows.
Predictions follow from the coefficients. For an EP participant at month 12 the model predicts \(\hat\beta_0 + 12\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3 + 12\hat\beta_5\) = 134.3 mmHg; for UC it predicts 143.3 mmHg. The predict() function does the same arithmetic with standard errors.


Checking the model
The usual residual-versus-fitted plot (Figure 3.2) looks unremarkable: no curvature, no funnel. It cannot reveal the main problem, because that problem is about pairs of residuals from the same person. To see it, reshape the residuals to wide format and correlate them across scheduled visits.

walk$res_ols <- resid(m_ols)
ggplot(walk, aes(fitted(m_ols), res_ols)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#888888") +
  labs(x = "Fitted SBP (mmHg)", y = "Residual (mmHg)")







Figure 3.2: Residuals against fitted values from the ordinary least squares model. The plot shows no obvious curvature or change in spread, but it cannot show correlation between residuals of the same participant.






res_cor <- visit_correlation(walk, id, month_sched, res_ols)
round(res_cor, 2)

#>       0    1    3    6    9   12
#> 0  1.00 0.87 0.79 0.73 0.75 0.72
#> 1  0.87 1.00 0.83 0.79 0.76 0.74
#> 3  0.79 0.83 1.00 0.78 0.75 0.74
#> 6  0.73 0.79 0.78 1.00 0.78 0.75
#> 9  0.75 0.76 0.75 0.78 1.00 0.83
#> 12 0.72 0.74 0.74 0.75 0.83 1.00


The correlations between residuals of the same participant at different visits range from 0.72 to 0.87. Independence would require them to be near zero. This single table is the reason ordinary regression is not an acceptable final analysis of longitudinal data: its standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values are based on a variance formula that does not apply. Notice also that the correlation is highest between neighbouring visits (0.87 between months 0 and 1) and lower for visits further apart (0.72 between months 0 and 12). We will meet this pattern again when we discuss sphericity.


Reporting






TipReporting example



We would not report this model as a primary analysis. If it were shown for illustration, an honest description would be: “An ordinary least squares regression of SBP on month, arm and their interaction, ignoring within-participant correlation, gave a difference in slope between the enhanced programme and usual care of -0.72 mmHg per month (95% CI -1.07 to -0.38). Residuals from the same participant were strongly correlated (0.72 to 0.87), so these intervals are not valid; the primary analysis uses a linear mixed model.”




Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Reading the arm main effect as the treatment effect. With an interaction in the model, armEP is the arm difference at month 0. The treatment effect on change is in month:armEP.
Dropping the interaction to “simplify” the model. Without it the arm lines are parallel and the model cannot detect a treatment effect on change.
Trusting lm() standard errors for repeated measurements. They assume independent observations. Check the within-participant residual correlation; it is almost never zero.
Using scheduled time when actual time is available. The regression above uses month; using month_sched would ignore the real timing of visits.

title: 3  Statistical foundations and traditional approaches
text:
3.2 Part 2. Comparing two occasions

3.2.1 The paired t-test: baseline versus month 12 within an arm

The research question and estimand
“By how much does mean SBP change from baseline to month 12 among participants in the enhanced programme?” The estimand is the mean within-person change \(\mu_d = E(Y_{i,12} - Y_{i,0})\) in one arm. This is a within-group question. It says nothing about whether the programme caused the change, because the change in a single arm mixes the programme effect with everything else that happens over a year: regression to the mean (participants were recruited because their blood pressure was raised), seasonal effects, the attention of being in a trial, and changes in medication.


Data structure and outcome types
A continuous outcome measured on the same participants at two occasions. Each participant contributes a pair \((y_{i,0}, y_{i,12})\); only participants with both values can be used. In WALK the pairs come from the wide file.


Intuition
Measuring the same person twice removes the large differences between people from the comparison. Instead of comparing two groups of measurements, we compute each person’s difference \(d_i = y_{i,12} - y_{i,0}\) and ask whether the mean difference is zero. Because baseline and month-12 SBP are strongly positively correlated, the differences vary much less than the raw values, and the comparison is precise.


The model
\[
d_i = y_{i,12} - y_{i,0}, \qquad d_i \sim N(\mu_d, \sigma_d^2) \text{ independently}, \qquad
t = \frac{\bar d}{s_d / \sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1} \text{ under } H_0: \mu_d = 0 .
\]
\(\bar d\) is the mean of the \(n\) differences and \(s_d\) their standard deviation. The variance of a difference is \(\sigma_d^2 = \sigma_0^2 + \sigma_{12}^2 - 2\rho\,\sigma_0\sigma_{12}\), where \(\rho\) is the correlation between baseline and month-12 SBP. The larger \(\rho\) is, the smaller \(\sigma_d^2\), which is why pairing helps.


Assumptions and limitations
The differences must be independent across participants and approximately normal (or \(n\) large enough for the central limit theorem, which with about 90 pairs it comfortably is). Only complete pairs are used, which is a complete-case analysis: if dropout before month 12 depends on SBP, as it does in WALK, the participants who remain are not a random sample of those randomised. The test uses only two of the six visits. Most importantly, it answers a within-group question; a between-arm comparison of change needs a two-sample analysis (Part 4).


Fitting the model in R

ep <- wide |> filter(arm == "EP", !is.na(sbp_m0), !is.na(sbp_m12))
tt_ep <- t.test(ep$sbp_m12, ep$sbp_m0, paired = TRUE)
tt_ep

#> 
#>  Paired t-test
#> 
#> data:  ep$sbp_m12 and ep$sbp_m0
#> t = -11, df = 92, p-value <2e-16
#> alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  -12.089  -8.298
#> sample estimates:
#> mean difference 
#>          -10.19




Interpreting the output
Among the 93 EP participants with both measurements, SBP fell by a mean of 10.2 mmHg (95% CI for the mean change -12.1 to -8.3; t = -10.7 on 92 degrees of freedom, p < 0.001). The sign convention matters: the first argument minus the second, so a negative difference is a fall.
It is tempting to stop here and declare the programme effective. Run the same test in usual care:

uc <- wide |> filter(arm == "UC", !is.na(sbp_m0), !is.na(sbp_m12))
tt_uc <- t.test(uc$sbp_m12, uc$sbp_m0, paired = TRUE)
c(mean_change = unname(tt_uc$estimate), lower = tt_uc$conf.int[1],
  upper = tt_uc$conf.int[2], p = tt_uc$p.value)

#> mean_change       lower       upper           p 
#>     -1.0105     -3.1455      1.1245      0.3497


In UC the mean change is -1.0 mmHg (95% CI -3.1 to 1.1). The programme effect is the difference between these changes, and a pair of within-group tests does not estimate it or test it. A significant change in one arm and a non-significant change in another does not show that the arms differ; the difference between “significant” and “not significant” is not itself statistically significant (Vickers and Altman 2001). Part 4 estimates the between-arm difference directly.
Because the data are simulated we can compare with the truth, which is possible only for simulated data: the true mean change to month 12 is -10.2 mmHg in EP and -2.1 mmHg in UC.


Checking the model
Check the distribution of the differences, not of the raw values.

p1 <- ggplot(ep, aes(sbp_m12 - sbp_m0)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#D55E00", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Change in SBP, month 12 minus baseline (mmHg)", y = "Participants")
p2 <- ggplot(ep, aes(sample = sbp_m12 - sbp_m0)) +
  stat_qq(size = 1) + stat_qq_line(colour = "#888888") +
  labs(x = "Normal quantiles", y = "Observed change (mmHg)")
p1 + p2







Figure 3.3: Distribution of within-person change from baseline to month 12 in the enhanced programme (left) and a normal Q-Q plot of the same differences (right).





The differences are roughly symmetric with no extreme values, so the normality assumption is reasonable. Independence between participants follows from the design. The assumption that cannot be checked from these data alone is that the 93 completers represent all 120 EP participants.


Reporting






TipReporting example



“Among participants in the enhanced programme with SBP recorded at baseline and month 12 (n = 93), mean SBP fell by 10.2 mmHg (95% CI 8.3 to 12.1) between baseline and month 12. This within-arm change does not estimate the effect of the programme, which is reported as the difference in mean change against usual care.”




Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Using a within-arm paired test to claim a treatment effect. It measures change, not the effect of the intervention. Compare arms.
Comparing p-values between arms (“significant in EP, not in UC”) instead of estimating the difference between arms.
Running an unpaired two-sample t-test on paired data. It ignores the correlation and is far less precise.
Forgetting which way the difference is taken. State “month 12 minus baseline” explicitly.

title: 3  Statistical foundations and traditional approaches
text:
3.3 Part 3. Repeated-measures ANOVA

3.3.1 Repeated-measures ANOVA on completers

The research question and estimand
Repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) answers three omnibus questions about mean SBP at the six scheduled visits: does the mean differ between arms when averaged over visits (the between-subject effect of arm), does the mean change across visits when averaged over arms (the within-subject effect of visit), and does the pattern of change differ between arms (the arm-by-visit interaction)? In a randomised trial the interaction is the question of interest. Note that these are F-tests of “no difference anywhere”, not estimates of a clinically interpretable quantity with a confidence interval. RM-ANOVA does not directly deliver the difference in mean change at month 12; that has to come from follow-up contrasts.


Data structure and outcome types
A continuous outcome measured at the same fixed set of occasions on every participant, with one or more between-subject factors (here arm). The method requires a balanced, complete design: every participant must have all six measurements. The univariate version uses long data; the multivariate version uses wide data with one column per visit.


Intuition
RM-ANOVA splits the total variation in SBP into a between-participant part and a within-participant part. The between-participant part tests arm, using the variation between participant averages as its error term. The within-participant part tests visit and arm-by-visit, using the variation of each participant’s measurements around their own average as its error term. Taking out each participant’s average removes the large stable differences between people, so the within-participant tests are sensitive. The price is an assumption about how the within-participant errors are correlated, called sphericity.


The model
For participant \(i\) in arm \(g\) at scheduled visit \(j\) (\(j = 1, \dots, 6\)):
\[
y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_g + \gamma_j + (\alpha\gamma)_{gj} + b_{0i} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad b_{0i} \sim N(0, \tau_0^2), \quad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
\]
with \(b_{0i}\) and \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) independent. \(\mu\) is the overall mean, \(\alpha_g\) the effect of arm \(g\), \(\gamma_j\) the effect of visit \(j\) and \((\alpha\gamma)_{gj}\) the interaction (each set constrained, for example to sum to zero). \(b_{0i}\) is a participant effect that makes all of participant \(i\)’s measurements share a common shift, and \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) is the residual error. This is a random-intercept model, the simplest mixed model of Module 4, written with visit as a categorical factor. It implies compound symmetry: every measurement has variance \(\tau_0^2 + \sigma^2\) and every pair of measurements from the same participant has covariance \(\tau_0^2\), whatever the gap between them. The F-tests remain valid under the slightly weaker condition of sphericity, discussed below.


Assumptions and limitations
RM-ANOVA assumes independent participants, normal errors, equal covariance matrices across arms and sphericity. Its limitations for longitudinal data are serious:

Complete cases only. Any participant with a missed visit is deleted entirely (listwise deletion). In WALK this removes 122 of 360 participants (34%). When dropout depends on observed SBP (MAR), completers are a selected group and the estimates can be biased; Module 10 returns to this.
Fixed occasions. Visits are treated as identical categories for everyone. The actual visit times, which in WALK vary around the schedule, are discarded.
No time-varying covariates. Daily steps, measured at each visit, cannot enter the model.
No individual trajectories. There are no participant-specific slopes; the only participant effect is a shift in level. The heterogeneity in rates of change, which Module 4 models with random slopes, is pushed into the error.
Omnibus tests rather than estimates. The interaction F-test says that the arms differ somewhere, not by how much at month 12.



Fitting the model in R
First, build the complete-case data. The long version is needed for aov().

cc <- wide[complete.cases(wide[, yv]), ]
table(cc$arm)

#> 
#> UC SP EP 
#> 76 84 78

lc <- cc |>
  select(id, arm, all_of(yv)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(yv), names_to = "visit", values_to = "sbp") |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = yv), id = factor(id))

The univariate approach uses aov() with an Error() term. Error(id/visit) tells R that participants are the experimental units for arm and that visit varies within participants, so two error strata are formed.

rm_aov <- aov(sbp ~ arm * visit + Error(id / visit), data = lc)
summary(rm_aov)

#> 
#> Error: id
#>            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
#> arm         2   2792    1396     1.7   0.19
#> Residuals 235 193510     823               
#> 
#> Error: id:visit
#>             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)    
#> visit        5   6876    1375   36.97 < 2e-16 ***
#> arm:visit   10   2783     278    7.48 1.3e-11 ***
#> Residuals 1175  43711      37                    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

s_aov <- summary(rm_aov)
btw <- s_aov[["Error: id"]][[1]]
wth <- s_aov[["Error: id:visit"]][[1]]

The multivariate approach fits a multivariate linear model to the wide data: the response is a matrix of six columns, one per visit. anova() with X = ~1 and test = "Spherical" then tests the within-subject effects using contrasts orthogonal to the constant, which is exactly the RM-ANOVA, and adds the Greenhouse–Geisser and Huynh–Feldt corrections. mauchly.test() tests sphericity.

Y <- as.matrix(cc[, yv])
rm_mlm <- lm(Y ~ arm, data = cc)
idata <- data.frame(visit = factor(yv, levels = yv))
rm_sph <- anova(rm_mlm, X = ~1, idata = idata, test = "Spherical")
rm_sph

#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> 
#> Contrasts orthogonal to
#> ~1
#> 
#> Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon: 0.8490
#> Huynh-Feldt epsilon:        0.8665
#> 
#>              Df     F num Df den Df   Pr(>F)   G-G Pr   H-F Pr
#> (Intercept)   1 36.97      5   1175 0.00e+00 0.00e+00 0.00e+00
#> arm           2  7.48     10   1175 1.29e-11 3.57e-10 2.42e-10
#> Residuals   235

mau <- mauchly.test(rm_mlm, X = ~1, idata = idata)
mau

#> 
#>  Mauchly's test of sphericity
#>  Contrasts orthogonal to
#>  ~1
#> 
#> 
#> data:  SSD matrix from lm(formula = Y ~ arm, data = cc)
#> W = 0.65, p-value = 4e-15




Interpreting the output
In the multivariate table, the row labelled (Intercept) tests the effect of visit (the within-subject contrasts averaged over arms) and the row labelled arm tests the arm-by-visit interaction. The labels look odd because the model is fitted to the visit contrasts: the intercept of the contrasts is the average pattern over visits, and the arm terms are differences in that pattern. The F statistics agree with aov().








Output line
What it means
Value here




Error: id, arm
Arms differ in SBP averaged over all six visits?
F = 1.70 on 2 and 235 df, p = 0.186


Error: id:visit, visit
Mean SBP changes across visits?
F = 36.97 on 5 and 1175 df, p < 0.001


Error: id:visit, arm:visit
Pattern over visits differs between arms?
F = 7.48 on 10 and 1175 df, p < 0.001


Greenhouse–Geisser epsilon
Estimated departure from sphericity (1 = none)
0.849


Huynh–Feldt epsilon
Less conservative estimate of the same
0.867


G-G Pr, H-F Pr
p-values with degrees of freedom multiplied by epsilon
interaction: p < 0.001 (GG)


Mauchly’s W
Test of sphericity
W = 0.65, p < 0.001



The arm-by-visit interaction is strong: the arms follow different patterns over the year. The between-subject test of arm is not significant, which may seem surprising given Figure 3.1. It is not a contradiction. That test averages SBP over all six visits, including baseline and month 1 when the arms hardly differ, and its error term is the large between-participant variation. The arm main effect is therefore the wrong test for a treatment effect on change, exactly as the arm main effect in Part 1 was the wrong coefficient.
Mauchly’s test rejects sphericity firmly, so the uncorrected p-values for the within-subject effects are too small. After correction the interaction remains highly significant. With 238 participants the conclusion here is not in doubt; with smaller samples the correction can change it.


Checking the model
The key check for RM-ANOVA is sphericity, followed by the usual checks of normality and of equal covariance matrices across arms.

Sphericity and the corrections
Sphericity is the condition that the variance of the difference between any two visits is the same for every pair of visits:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(y_{ij} - y_{ik}) = \text{constant for all } j \neq k .
\]
The within-subject F-tests compare variation in these differences, so they need the differences to be equally variable. Compound symmetry (equal variances, equal correlations) is sufficient for sphericity; sphericity is slightly more general but in practice rarely holds when compound symmetry fails. Longitudinal data typically violate it, because measurements close in time are more alike than measurements far apart.
We can see this in the observed covariance matrix of the completers.

S_cc <- cov(Y)
round(S_cc, 1)

#>         sbp_m0 sbp_m1 sbp_m3 sbp_m6 sbp_m9 sbp_m12
#> sbp_m0   156.6  141.7  123.9  119.8  120.3   115.2
#> sbp_m1   141.7  168.3  136.8  134.8  126.5   126.6
#> sbp_m3   123.9  136.8  163.8  137.3  128.8   127.4
#> sbp_m6   119.8  134.8  137.3  183.5  143.7   143.0
#> sbp_m9   120.3  126.5  128.8  143.7  174.2   146.9
#> sbp_m12  115.2  126.6  127.4  143.0  146.9   178.0



cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(round(cov2cor(S_cc), 2)))
levels(cor_long$Var1) <- levels(cor_long$Var2) <- c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)
ggplot(cor_long, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F2F2F2", high = "#0072B2", name = "Correlation") +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Scheduled month") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())







Figure 3.4: Observed correlation of SBP between scheduled visits among the completers. Correlations are highest next to the diagonal and decline as visits get further apart, a pattern that compound symmetry does not allow.





The variances on the diagonal range from 156.6 to 183.5 mmHg\(^2\), and the correlations from 0.69 to 0.87. Sphericity is about the differences, so compute the variance of every pairwise difference, \(s_{jj} + s_{kk} - 2 s_{jk}\):

pairs <- t(combn(6, 2))
dv <- data.frame(
  pair = paste0("m", c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)[pairs[, 1]], " vs m",
                c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)[pairs[, 2]]),
  var_diff = S_cc[cbind(pairs[, 1], pairs[, 1])] +
    S_cc[cbind(pairs[, 2], pairs[, 2])] - 2 * S_cc[pairs])
dv$var_diff <- round(dv$var_diff, 1)
dv[order(dv$var_diff), ]

#>         pair var_diff
#> 1   m0 vs m1     41.6
#> 6   m1 vs m3     58.5
#> 15 m9 vs m12     58.5
#> 13  m6 vs m9     70.4
#> 2   m0 vs m3     72.6
#> 10  m3 vs m6     72.7
#> 14 m6 vs m12     75.5
#> 11  m3 vs m9     80.5
#> 7   m1 vs m6     82.3
#> 12 m3 vs m12     87.0
#> 8   m1 vs m9     89.6
#> 4   m0 vs m9     90.2
#> 9  m1 vs m12     93.1
#> 3   m0 vs m6    100.4
#> 5  m0 vs m12    104.2


If sphericity held, these 15 variances would be roughly equal. They range from 41.6 (m0 vs m1) to 104.2 (m0 vs m12), a ratio of about 2.5. Differences between adjacent visits vary least; differences between distant visits vary most.
When sphericity fails, the F statistic does not follow the F distribution with the nominal degrees of freedom, and the test rejects too often. Greenhouse and Geisser (1959) showed that a good approximation is obtained by multiplying both degrees of freedom by a factor \(\epsilon\) between \(1/(k-1)\) and 1, where \(k\) is the number of occasions. Let \(C\) be a \(k \times (k-1)\) matrix of orthonormal contrasts (for example polynomial contrasts) and \(S\) the pooled within-arm covariance matrix. With \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{k-1}\) the eigenvalues of \(C^\top S C\),
\[
\hat\epsilon_{\text{GG}} = \frac{\left(\sum_r \lambda_r\right)^2}{(k-1)\sum_r \lambda_r^2} .
\]
If all eigenvalues are equal (perfect sphericity) \(\hat\epsilon_{\text{GG}} = 1\). We can reproduce the value R printed:

S_pool <- estVar(rm_mlm)          # pooled within-arm covariance matrix
C <- contr.poly(6)                # orthonormal contrasts
lam <- eigen(t(C) %*% S_pool %*% C)$values
sum(lam)^2 / (5 * sum(lam^2))

#> [1] 0.849


\(\hat\epsilon_{\text{GG}}\) is known to be conservative (biased downwards) when the true \(\epsilon\) is near 1. Huynh and Feldt (1976) proposed a less conservative estimator, \(\hat\epsilon_{\text{HF}}\), which is never smaller than \(\hat\epsilon_{\text{GG}}\) and is truncated at 1. Here \(\hat\epsilon_{\text{GG}}\) = 0.849 and \(\hat\epsilon_{\text{HF}}\) = 0.867, so the corrected interaction test uses about 8.5 and 998 degrees of freedom (Greenhouse–Geisser) instead of 10 and 1175. A common rule of thumb is to report Greenhouse–Geisser when \(\hat\epsilon\) is below about 0.75 and Huynh–Feldt otherwise; many analysts simply report Greenhouse–Geisser always. Mauchly’s test is not a good guide on its own: it has low power in small samples and rejects trivially in large ones, so look at \(\hat\epsilon\) instead.
The corrections fix the p-values. They do not fix the other limitations, and they do not turn the omnibus tests into estimates of a treatment effect.


Normality and equal covariance matrices
Beyond sphericity, check normality of the within-participant residuals and the equality of covariance matrices across arms.

r_long <- data.frame(res = as.vector(resid(rm_mlm)))
q1 <- ggplot(r_long, aes(sample = res)) + stat_qq(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#888888") +
  labs(x = "Normal quantiles", y = "Residual (mmHg)")
q2 <- lc |> group_by(arm, visit) |> summarise(v = var(sbp)) |>
  mutate(month = as.numeric(sub("sbp_m", "", visit))) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, v, colour = arm)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Variance of SBP (mmHg²)")
q1 + q2







Figure 3.5: Normal Q-Q plot of residuals from the multivariate linear model (all six visits pooled, left) and the variance of SBP by visit and arm among completers (right).





The residuals are close to normal. Variances are broadly similar across arms and tend to increase over time, consistent with participants changing at different rates, which is exactly what a random-slope model captures.



Reporting






TipReporting example



“Among the 238 participants with SBP at all six scheduled visits (66% of those randomised), a repeated-measures ANOVA showed that the pattern of SBP over time differed between arms (arm-by-visit interaction F = 7.48, Greenhouse–Geisser \(\hat\epsilon\) = 0.85, corrected p < 0.001). Mauchly’s test indicated departure from sphericity (W = 0.65, p < 0.001). Because this analysis excludes 122 participants with incomplete data and ignores actual visit times, it is presented for comparison only; the primary analysis is a linear mixed model using all available data.”




Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Reporting uncorrected within-subject p-values when sphericity fails. Use the Greenhouse–Geisser or Huynh–Feldt p-values and report \(\hat\epsilon\).
Interpreting the between-subject arm test as the treatment effect. It averages over visits, including baseline. The interaction is the relevant test.
Not stating how many participants were excluded. Listwise deletion is easy to miss; report the number analysed and the number randomised.
Using RM-ANOVA when visit times vary or covariates change over time. Use a mixed model (Module 4).
Stopping at the omnibus F-test. Report an estimate with a confidence interval for the contrast that answers the question.









NoteWhy this matters



RM-ANOVA is a special case of the linear mixed model with a random intercept, categorical time and complete data. Module 4 relaxes each restriction: it uses every available observation, uses actual times, allows random slopes so that variances and correlations can change over time, and delivers estimates of the difference in mean change with confidence intervals.





3.3.2 Multivariate tests as an alternative to sphericity Advanced
This extension is needed only if you must analyse complete balanced data without assuming sphericity at all and without a mixed model. The multivariate approach (profile analysis, MANOVA) treats the six visits as a vector with an unstructured covariance matrix, so sphericity is not required. The same anova() call gives it with a different test:

anova(rm_mlm, X = ~1, idata = idata, test = "Pillai")

#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> 
#> Contrasts orthogonal to
#> ~1
#> 
#>              Df Pillai approx F num Df den Df  Pr(>F)    
#> (Intercept)   1  0.388    29.35      5    231 < 2e-16 ***
#> arm           2  0.187     4.79     10    464 1.5e-06 ***
#> Residuals   235                                          
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The multivariate test spends degrees of freedom estimating every variance and covariance, so it loses power when the number of participants is not large relative to the number of occasions, and it still requires complete data. The unstructured covariance model of Module 5, fitted by REML to all available data, is the modern equivalent.
