text:
3.4 Part 4. Baseline and one follow-up: three analyses

3.4.1 Follow-up only, change score and ANCOVA at month 12
Many trials name a single primary time point. For WALK suppose it is month 12. There are three common ways to compare arms using baseline and month-12 SBP, and they do not give the same answer.

The research question and estimand
“What is the effect of each walking programme, compared with usual care, on SBP at month 12?” In a randomised trial this estimand can be written in two equivalent ways: the difference in mean SBP at month 12 between arms, or the difference in mean change from baseline to month 12. They are equal because randomisation makes the expected baseline means equal in all arms. The true values for WALK (known only because the data are simulated) are -4.6 mmHg for SP and -8.1 mmHg for EP. Because the estimand is the same, the choice between the three analyses is about precision and assumptions, not about the question (Senn 2006; Vickers and Altman 2001).


Data structure and outcome types
One row per participant with baseline SBP (\(y_{i0}\)), month-12 SBP (\(y_{i,12}\)) and arm. Only participants with a month-12 value can be used.

d12 <- wide |>
  filter(!is.na(sbp_m0), !is.na(sbp_m12)) |>
  mutate(chg = sbp_m12 - sbp_m0)
table(d12$arm)

#> 
#>  UC  SP  EP 
#>  95 100  93

r0_12 <- cor(d12$sbp_m0, d12$sbp_m12)

288 participants have month-12 data. The correlation between baseline and month-12 SBP is 0.69.


Intuition
The follow-up-only analysis compares month-12 means and ignores baseline. The change-score analysis subtracts each participant’s baseline, which removes stable differences between people but also adds the baseline measurement error. ANCOVA (analysis of covariance) lets the data decide how much of the baseline to subtract: it regresses month-12 SBP on baseline and arm, and the coefficient of baseline is estimated, not fixed. Follow-up-only subtracts none of baseline, change subtracts all of it, and ANCOVA subtracts the optimal fraction.


The model
All three are linear regressions with one row per participant:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Follow-up only:}\quad & y_{i,12} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{SP}_i + \beta_2 \text{EP}_i + \varepsilon_i \\
\text{Change score:}\quad & y_{i,12} - y_{i0} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{SP}_i + \beta_2 \text{EP}_i + \varepsilon_i \\
\text{ANCOVA:}\quad & y_{i,12} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{SP}_i + \beta_2 \text{EP}_i + \gamma\, y_{i0} + \varepsilon_i
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) independent (a different \(\sigma^2\) in each model). \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) are the treatment effects of SP and EP against UC, and \(\gamma\) is the regression coefficient of month-12 on baseline SBP. Rearranging the ANCOVA model as \(y_{i,12} - \gamma y_{i0} = \dots\) shows that follow-up-only is ANCOVA with \(\gamma = 0\) and change is ANCOVA with \(\gamma = 1\).
Suppose baseline and follow-up have the same variance \(\sigma_y^2\) and correlation \(\rho\). Then, for a given sample size, the variance of the estimated treatment effect is proportional to
\[
\text{follow-up: } \sigma_y^2, \qquad \text{change: } 2\sigma_y^2(1-\rho), \qquad \text{ANCOVA: } \sigma_y^2(1-\rho^2).
\]
ANCOVA is never worse than either alternative (in large samples), because \(1 - \rho^2 \le 1\) and \(1 - \rho^2 \le 2(1-\rho)\) for every \(\rho\). The change score beats follow-up-only only when \(\rho > 0.5\).


Assumptions and limitations
All three assume independent participants and approximately normal residuals with constant variance. ANCOVA also assumes a linear relationship between baseline and follow-up with the same slope in every arm (no baseline-by-arm interaction); a mild violation does not bias the treatment effect in a randomised trial. The unbiasedness of all three for the treatment effect rests on randomisation, which balances baseline in expectation. All three use only the participants seen at month 12 (288 of 360), so they are complete-case analyses with the same vulnerability to dropout that depends on SBP; they also discard the four intermediate visits that carry information about the participants who dropped out.


Fitting the model in R

m_fu  <- lm(sbp_m12 ~ arm, data = d12)
m_chg <- lm(chg ~ arm, data = d12)
m_anc <- lm(sbp_m12 ~ arm + sbp_m0, data = d12)
summary(m_anc)

#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = sbp_m12 ~ arm + sbp_m0, data = d12)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#> -24.340  -6.015   0.319   5.741  24.044 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  36.8230     6.2389    5.90  1.0e-08 ***
#> armSP        -5.4519     1.3021   -4.19  3.8e-05 ***
#> armEP        -8.8116     1.3266   -6.64  1.6e-10 ***
#> sbp_m0        0.7397     0.0424   17.43  < 2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 9.08 on 284 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.544,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.539 
#> F-statistic:  113 on 3 and 284 DF,  p-value: <2e-16



tab12 <- bind_rows(
  fixef_table(m_fu)  |> mutate(analysis = "Follow-up only"),
  fixef_table(m_chg) |> mutate(analysis = "Change score"),
  fixef_table(m_anc) |> mutate(analysis = "ANCOVA")
) |> filter(term %in% c("armSP", "armEP")) |>
  select(analysis, term, estimate, se, lower, upper, p)
tab12

#>         analysis  term estimate    se   lower  upper         p
#> 1 Follow-up only armSP   -4.777 1.869  -8.440 -1.113 1.112e-02
#> 2 Follow-up only armEP   -7.756 1.903 -11.486 -4.026 5.956e-05
#> 3   Change score armSP   -5.689 1.383  -8.399 -2.980 5.074e-05
#> 4   Change score armEP   -9.183 1.408 -11.942 -6.424 3.130e-10
#> 5         ANCOVA armSP   -5.452 1.302  -8.004 -2.900 3.776e-05
#> 6         ANCOVA armEP   -8.812 1.327 -11.412 -6.212 1.569e-10

g <- function(a, t, col) tab12[tab12$analysis == a & tab12$term == t, col]



Interpreting the output
In the ANCOVA output, armEP = -8.81 is the difference in mean month-12 SBP between EP and UC for participants with the same baseline SBP, and the sbp_m0 coefficient \(\hat\gamma\) = 0.74 says that a participant 10 mmHg higher at baseline is on average 7.4 mmHg higher at month 12. Because \(\hat\gamma\) lies between 0 and 1, the ANCOVA estimate lies between the other two, as Figure 3.6 shows.

tc <- truth$true_change
tv <- data.frame(term = c("armSP", "armEP"),
                 truth = c(tc$change[tc$arm == "SP" & tc$month == 12],
                           tc$change[tc$arm == "EP" & tc$month == 12]) -
                   tc$change[tc$arm == "UC" & tc$month == 12])
tab12 |>
  mutate(analysis = factor(analysis, levels = c("Follow-up only", "Change score", "ANCOVA")),
         term = factor(term, levels = c("armSP", "armEP"),
                       labels = c("SP vs UC", "EP vs UC"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, analysis)) +
  geom_vline(data = tv |> mutate(term = factor(term, levels = c("armSP", "armEP"),
                                               labels = c("SP vs UC", "EP vs UC"))),
             aes(xintercept = truth), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#888888") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), height = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ term) +
  labs(x = "Difference in month-12 SBP vs usual care (mmHg)", y = NULL)

#> Warning: `geom_errorbarh()` was deprecated in ggplot2 4.0.0.
#> ℹ Please use the `orientation` argument of `geom_errorbar()` instead.


#> `height` was translated to `width`.








Figure 3.6: Estimated effect on SBP at month 12 (95% CI) of each programme compared with usual care, using three analyses of the same participants. The dashed lines mark the true values, known only because the data are simulated.








Analysis
SP vs UC (95% CI)
EP vs UC (95% CI)
SE for EP




Follow-up only
-4.8 (-8.4 to -1.1)
-7.8 (-11.5 to -4.0)
1.90


Change score
-5.7 (-8.4 to -3.0)
-9.2 (-11.9 to -6.4)
1.41


ANCOVA
-5.5 (-8.0 to -2.9)
-8.8 (-11.4 to -6.2)
1.33



All three analyses agree that both programmes lower SBP, but the standard errors differ: the ANCOVA standard error for EP is 30% smaller than the follow-up-only one and 6% smaller than the change-score one. With \(\rho\) = 0.69 the formulas above predict variance ratios of 1, 0.63 and 0.53, that is standard error ratios of 1, 0.79 and 0.73; the observed ratios relative to follow-up only are 0.74 and 0.70. A smaller standard error for the same estimand is equivalent to a larger trial for free.
The three point estimates differ from one another by chance baseline imbalance among the 288 participants analysed. If the SP arm happened to start slightly higher, the change score credits SP with the extra regression to the mean while follow-up-only does not; ANCOVA adjusts for the imbalance by the right amount. The estimates also differ from the true values. Part of this is sampling error, and part may be bias from analysing only participants who stayed to month 12. Module 4’s primary mixed model uses all 360 participants and gives month-12 differences in mean change of -5.38 (SP) and -8.97 (EP) mmHg.

A simulation of precision
The variance formulas are easy to check by simulation. We generate many randomised two-arm trials with 100 participants per arm, a true effect of −5 mmHg and different baseline–follow-up correlations, and record the spread of each estimator across trials.

sim_three <- function(rho, n = 100, effect = -5, sd = 13, reps = 1000) {
  S <- sd^2 * matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2)
  est <- replicate(reps, {
    y <- MASS::mvrnorm(2 * n, c(145, 145), S)
    trt <- rep(0:1, each = n)
    y[, 2] <- y[, 2] + effect * trt
    c(fu  = coef(lm(y[, 2] ~ trt))[2],
      chg = coef(lm(I(y[, 2] - y[, 1]) ~ trt))[2],
      anc = coef(lm(y[, 2] ~ trt + y[, 1]))[2])
  })
  data.frame(rho = rho, analysis = c("Follow-up only", "Change score", "ANCOVA"),
             mean_est = unname(rowMeans(est)), emp_se = unname(apply(est, 1, sd)))
}
set.seed(303)
sim_res <- bind_rows(lapply(c(0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9), sim_three))
sim_res

#>    rho       analysis mean_est emp_se
#> 1  0.2 Follow-up only   -5.157 1.8309
#> 2  0.2   Change score   -5.146 2.3470
#> 3  0.2         ANCOVA   -5.153 1.8060
#> 4  0.5 Follow-up only   -5.035 1.7789
#> 5  0.5   Change score   -5.001 1.7909
#> 6  0.5         ANCOVA   -5.026 1.5464
#> 7  0.7 Follow-up only   -4.970 1.7517
#> 8  0.7   Change score   -5.007 1.4139
#> 9  0.7         ANCOVA   -5.000 1.2709
#> 10 0.9 Follow-up only   -4.975 1.8016
#> 11 0.9   Change score   -4.964 0.8365
#> 12 0.9         ANCOVA   -4.964 0.8110

se_at <- function(r, a) sim_res$emp_se[sim_res$rho == r & sim_res$analysis == a]


ggplot(sim_res, aes(rho, emp_se, colour = analysis)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Follow-up only" = "#6B6B6B",
                                 "Change score" = "#0072B2",
                                 "ANCOVA" = "#D55E00"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Correlation between baseline and follow-up",
       y = "Empirical SE of the treatment effect (mmHg)")







Figure 3.7: Empirical standard error of three estimators of the same treatment effect over 1,000 simulated randomised trials (100 per arm) at each baseline-follow-up correlation. ANCOVA is the most precise at every correlation.





All three estimators are unbiased: their means across simulated trials are all close to −5 (column mean_est). Their precision differs. At \(\rho = 0.2\) the change score is the least precise (empirical SE 2.35 against 1.83 for follow-up only), because subtracting a weakly related baseline adds noise. At \(\rho = 0.9\) the change score is almost as good as ANCOVA (0.84 vs 0.81) and follow-up only is poor. ANCOVA is the most precise at every correlation. This is the main reason why baseline-adjusted ANCOVA is the recommended primary analysis for a randomised trial with a single follow-up (Senn 2006; Vickers and Altman 2001; Twisk et al. 2018).


Lord’s paradox: when groups are not randomised
In a randomised trial the three analyses estimate the same quantity. In an observational comparison of pre-existing groups that differ at baseline, they do not, and change-score analysis and ANCOVA can give opposite conclusions from the same data. This is known as Lord’s paradox. The simulation below creates two groups whose true SBP levels differ by 15 mmHg and do not change at all; each measurement adds independent measurement error.

set.seed(17)
n_l <- 500
grp <- rep(c("A", "B"), each = n_l)
true_level <- rnorm(2 * n_l, ifelse(grp == "A", 135, 150), 10)
lord <- data.frame(grp = grp,
                   y0 = true_level + rnorm(2 * n_l, 0, 7),
                   y1 = true_level + rnorm(2 * n_l, 0, 7))
lord_chg <- coef(summary(lm(I(y1 - y0) ~ grp, data = lord)))["grpB", ]
lord_anc <- coef(summary(lm(y1 ~ grp + y0, data = lord)))["grpB", ]
rbind(change = lord_chg, ancova = lord_anc)

#>        Estimate Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)
#> change  -0.8266     0.6321  -1.308 1.913e-01
#> ancova   4.8106     0.6832   7.041 3.543e-12


The change score finds no group difference (estimate -0.83 mmHg, p = 0.191), which is correct for the question “did the groups change differently?”. ANCOVA finds that group B is 4.8 mmHg higher at follow-up than group A among people with the same baseline value (p < 0.001). That is also a correct answer to a different question. Among people with the same observed baseline of, say, 142 mmHg, those in group B are likely to have a true level above 142 (their baseline reading was low by chance), so at follow-up they move up towards their group’s higher mean; those in group A tend to have a true level below 142 and move down. Neither analysis is wrong arithmetically; they answer different questions, and without randomisation there is no reason for those answers to coincide. In observational data the choice must follow from a clearly stated causal question, and often neither simple analysis is adequate (see Hernán and Robins (2020)). In a randomised trial the paradox disappears because the groups do not differ at baseline in expectation.



Checking the model
For ANCOVA check, as for any regression, the residual-versus-fitted plot and a Q-Q plot, plus the assumption of a common baseline slope in each arm.

m_anc_int <- lm(sbp_m12 ~ arm * sbp_m0, data = d12)
anova(m_anc, m_anc_int)

#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: sbp_m12 ~ arm + sbp_m0
#> Model 2: sbp_m12 ~ arm * sbp_m0
#>   Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq    F Pr(>F)
#> 1    284 23438                         
#> 2    282 23436  2      2.33 0.01   0.99



a1 <- ggplot(d12, aes(sbp_m0, sbp_m12, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", y = "Month-12 SBP (mmHg)")
a2 <- ggplot(data.frame(f = fitted(m_anc), r = resid(m_anc)), aes(f, r)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#888888") +
  labs(x = "Fitted month-12 SBP (mmHg)", y = "Residual (mmHg)")
a1 + a2







Figure 3.8: Month-12 SBP against baseline SBP by arm with least-squares lines (left), and residuals against fitted values from the ANCOVA model (right).





The lines are close to parallel and the test of the arm-by-baseline interaction is p = 0.986, so a common slope is reasonable. The residuals show no pattern.


Reporting






TipReporting example



“The effect of each programme on SBP at month 12 was estimated by analysis of covariance, regressing month-12 SBP on arm and baseline SBP, in the 288 participants with a month-12 measurement. Compared with usual care, mean SBP at month 12 was 5.5 mmHg lower in the standard programme (95% CI 2.9 to 8.0) and 8.8 mmHg lower in the enhanced programme (95% CI 6.2 to 11.4). This complete-case analysis excludes 72 participants without month-12 data.”




Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Analysing change scores by default. In a randomised trial ANCOVA is at least as precise, and much more so when the baseline–follow-up correlation is moderate.
Testing for baseline imbalance and adjusting only if “significant”. In a randomised trial any baseline difference is due to chance by definition; pre-specify the baseline adjustment instead.
Using change as the outcome and also adjusting for baseline, then calling it different from ANCOVA. Regressing change on arm and baseline gives exactly the same arm coefficient as ANCOVA.
Applying ANCOVA to non-randomised groups without thinking about the causal question (Lord’s paradox).
Forgetting that only participants with the follow-up value are analysed. State the number and consider the dropout mechanism.

section: 3.5 Part 5. Separate tests at each visit
text:
3.5 Part 5. Separate tests at each visit

3.5.1 Why separate tests at each visit are inadequate

The research question and estimand
A common shortcut is to compare arms at each visit with a separate t-test or one-way ANOVA. The implied research question is vague (“when do the arms differ?”), and there is no single estimand: there are as many estimates as visits, each using a different subset of participants.


Data structure and outcome types
A continuous outcome at each scheduled visit, analysed one visit at a time from the wide file. At each visit only participants seen at that visit are included.


Intuition
Each test is a valid cross-sectional comparison of the people seen at that visit. Taken together, the tests are a poor analysis for three reasons. First, multiplicity: with many tests the chance of at least one false positive grows. Second, inefficiency: each test ignores the information in the participant’s other measurements, including baseline, so the standard errors are those of a follow-up-only analysis. Third, inconsistency with missing data: each visit uses a different group of people, so a change in the estimates over time mixes the treatment effect with changes in who is still in the study.


The model
At each visit \(j\) separately,
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\text{SP}_i + \beta_{2j}\text{EP}_i + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma_j^2),
\]
fitted only to participants observed at visit \(j\). The symbols are as before, with a subscript \(j\) because each visit has its own coefficients and residual variance. Nothing connects the models across visits.


Assumptions and limitations
Each test assumes independent observations and normality at that visit, which is reasonable. The limitations are the three listed above. With \(m\) independent tests at level 0.05 the probability of at least one false positive when no effect exists is \(1 - 0.95^m\); for 6 visits and 2 comparisons (\(m = 12\)) that is 0.46. The tests in a longitudinal study are positively correlated, which reduces this figure but does not remove the problem.


Fitting the model in R

per_visit <- bind_rows(lapply(yv, function(v) {
  d <- wide[!is.na(wide[[v]]), ]
  fixef_table(lm(reformulate("arm", v), data = d)) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    mutate(visit = v, n = nrow(d))
}))
per_visit |> mutate(across(c(estimate, se, lower, upper), \(x) round(x, 2)),
                    p = signif(p, 2))

#>     term estimate   se  lower upper       p   visit   n
#> 1  armSP     1.03 1.72  -2.34  4.39 0.55000  sbp_m0 360
#> 2  armEP     1.35 1.72  -2.01  4.71 0.43000  sbp_m0 360
#> 3  armSP     0.71 1.82  -2.85  4.27 0.70000  sbp_m1 324
#> 4  armEP    -0.89 1.80  -4.43  2.64 0.62000  sbp_m1 324
#> 5  armSP    -1.31 1.79  -4.81  2.19 0.46000  sbp_m3 319
#> 6  armEP    -3.72 1.82  -7.27 -0.16 0.04100  sbp_m3 319
#> 7  armSP    -2.97 1.85  -6.59  0.65 0.11000  sbp_m6 309
#> 8  armEP    -6.79 1.84 -10.39 -3.18 0.00027  sbp_m6 309
#> 9  armSP    -4.67 1.87  -8.33 -1.00 0.01300  sbp_m9 297
#> 10 armEP    -6.80 1.90 -10.52 -3.08 0.00039  sbp_m9 297
#> 11 armSP    -4.78 1.87  -8.44 -1.11 0.01100 sbp_m12 288
#> 12 armEP    -7.76 1.90 -11.49 -4.03 0.00006 sbp_m12 288


To quantify the multiplicity problem with realistic correlation, simulate trials with no treatment effect, using the observed covariance matrix of the six visits, and count how often at least one of the 12 tests is significant.

set.seed(3)
fwer <- mean(replicate(2000, {
  y <- MASS::mvrnorm(360, rep(145, 6), S_cc)
  arm <- factor(rep(c("UC", "SP", "EP"), each = 120), levels = c("UC", "SP", "EP"))
  p <- sapply(1:6, function(j) coef(summary(lm(y[, j] ~ arm)))[2:3, 4])
  any(p < 0.05)
}))
fwer

#> [1] 0.2475




Interpreting the output

per_visit |>
  mutate(month = as.numeric(sub("sbp_m", "", visit)),
         arm = ifelse(term == "armSP", "SP", "EP")) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, estimate, colour = arm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#888888") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Difference from usual care (mmHg)")







Figure 3.9: Difference in mean SBP from usual care (95% CI) at each scheduled visit, from separate regressions. The number of participants analysed falls from visit to visit.





The number of participants falls from 360 at baseline to 288 at month 12. In the simulated trials with no treatment effect at any visit, at least one of the 12 tests was significant in 25% of simulated trials, against the nominal 5% (and 46% if the tests were independent). At month 12 the per-visit estimate for EP (-7.76 mmHg, SE 1.90) is the follow-up-only analysis of Part 4, and its standard error is larger than that of ANCOVA (1.33). The pattern in Figure 3.9 looks informative, but the visit-to-visit changes partly reflect who remains in the study.


Checking the model
Each visit-specific regression can be checked with residual plots, but checking does not repair the design of the analysis. The useful check is to tabulate how many participants each test uses and whether those seen at later visits differed at baseline from those who dropped out.

seen12 <- wide |> mutate(seen_m12 = !is.na(sbp_m12)) |>
  group_by(seen_m12) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_sbp0 = mean(sbp_m0))
seen12

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   seen_m12     n mean_sbp0
#>   <lgl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 FALSE       72     150.4
#> 2 TRUE       288     146.1


Participants who were not seen at month 12 had higher baseline SBP on average (150.4 against 146.1 mmHg), so the month-12 comparisons are made in a selected group.


Reporting






TipReporting example



Visit-specific comparisons are best reported, if at all, as secondary descriptive results from a single longitudinal model: “Estimated differences from usual care at each scheduled visit were obtained as contrasts from the primary linear mixed model (Module 4) rather than from separate tests, which would each use a different subset of participants and inflate the number of comparisons.”




Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Declaring the time of “onset” of an effect from the first significant visit. Significance depends on sample size at that visit and on chance.
Ignoring multiplicity. Twelve tests at 5% give a much higher chance of at least one false positive.
Comparing estimates across visits as if they came from the same people. With dropout, they do not.
Correcting for multiplicity (for example Bonferroni) and believing the problem is solved. The inefficiency and the missing-data problem remain. Fit one model for all visits instead.

A linear mixed model (Module 4) answers the same question as ANCOVA, uses every observation of all 360 participants, uses actual visit times, models the correlation between repeated measurements, and is valid under MAR dropout when the model is correctly specified. title: 3  Statistical foundations and traditional approaches
text:
Summary
Traditional methods each take a narrow view of longitudinal data. Ordinary regression gives a useful mean structure but ignores the correlation between a participant’s measurements, so its standard errors cannot be trusted. A paired t-test describes change within one group and cannot, on its own, say whether an intervention worked. Repeated-measures ANOVA uses all the visits but only for participants who attended every one, assumes sphericity (which the WALK covariance matrix clearly violates, requiring the Greenhouse–Geisser or Huynh–Feldt correction), ignores actual visit times and time-varying covariates, and produces omnibus tests rather than estimates. For a single follow-up in a randomised trial, baseline-adjusted ANCOVA is the most precise of the simple analyses and is a sound primary analysis when data are complete; change scores are less efficient unless the baseline–follow-up correlation is high, and in non-randomised comparisons the two can disagree (Lord’s paradox). Separate tests at every visit multiply the chance of false positives and compare shifting subsets of participants. Module 4 shows how the linear mixed model keeps what is good in these methods and removes their main restrictions.

Further reading

Senn (2006) explains clearly why ANCOVA is preferred to change scores in randomised trials and discusses the role of baseline.
Vickers and Altman (2001) is a two-page summary of the same argument for clinical readers.
Twisk et al. (2018) compares the different ways of estimating treatment effects in trials with baseline and repeated follow-up measurements, including longitudinal mixed models.
Greenhouse and Geisser (1959) and Huynh and Feldt (1976) are the original sources for the sphericity corrections.
Fitzmaurice et al. (2011), chapters 1–3, places these methods in the wider history of longitudinal analysis.

title: 4  Linear mixed-effects models
text:
Learning outcomes
Module 3 ended with a list of things the traditional methods cannot do: use every participant whatever visits they missed, handle visits that happen at slightly different times for different people, describe how individuals differ in their rate of change, and give honest standard errors for the comparison of change between groups. The linear mixed-effects model does all of these with one coherent model. Its central idea is simple. Every participant has a trajectory of their own, the trajectories vary around an average trajectory in a way that can be described by a few variance parameters, and measurements scatter around each participant’s trajectory. The average trajectory carries the treatment comparison; the variation between and within participants determines how much the data tell us about it. This module builds the model in two steps (random intercepts, then random slopes), shows how the coding of time changes what each coefficient means, fits the course’s reference models to the WALK trial, and explains estimation by REML, predicted random effects and shrinkage. Linear mixed models are the core of most of the rest of the course, so the interpretation habits formed here matter.
By the end of this module participants will be able to:

title: 4  Linear mixed-effects models
text:
4.1 Part 1. Building the model

4.1.1 Fixed effects, random effects and residual variation
A linear mixed-effects model (LMM; also called a multilevel or hierarchical linear model) splits the variation in the outcome into three parts.
Fixed effects describe the average trajectory in the population and how it depends on covariates such as arm. They are the regression coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\) that you already know from Module 0, and they usually carry the research question. In WALK the fixed effects describe mean SBP over time in each arm.
Random effects describe how each participant’s own trajectory departs from the average one. A random intercept \(b_{0i}\) says that participant \(i\) sits \(b_{0i}\) mmHg above or below the average line throughout follow-up; a random slope \(b_{1i}\) says that participant \(i\) changes \(b_{1i}\) mmHg per month faster or slower than average. We do not estimate a separate fixed parameter for each participant. Instead we treat the participants as a sample from a population and estimate the variance of the random effects, for example \(\tau_0^2\), the variance of the intercepts. This is what makes the effects “random”: they are draws from a distribution whose spread is a parameter of the model.
Residual error \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) is what is left: the deviation of an individual measurement from the participant’s own line, caused by measurement error and by short-term fluctuation in blood pressure. Its variance is \(\sigma^2\).
The variances \(\tau_0^2\), \(\tau_1^2\) (and the covariance \(\tau_{01}\)) and \(\sigma^2\) are called variance components. They are the second set of parameters in the model, alongside the fixed effects.

m_demo <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk,
               control = lmer_ctrl)
set.seed(4)
nobs <- count(walk, id)
pick <- c(sample(nobs$id[nobs$n == 6], 2), sample(nobs$id[nobs$n %in% 4:5], 2),
          sample(nobs$id[nobs$n %in% 2:3], 2))
d6 <- walk |> filter(id %in% pick) |>
  mutate(panel = paste0(id, " (", arm, ", ", ave(sbp, id, FUN = length), " visits)"))
grid6 <- d6 |> distinct(id, arm, panel) |>
  tidyr::crossing(month = seq(0, 12, 0.5))
grid6$blup <- predict(m_demo, newdata = grid6)
grid6$mean <- predict(m_demo, newdata = grid6, re.form = NA)
ols6 <- d6 |> group_by(id) |>
  summarise(a = coef(lm(sbp ~ month))[1], b = coef(lm(sbp ~ month))[2])
grid6 <- grid6 |> left_join(ols6, by = "id") |> mutate(ols = a + b * month)
ggplot(d6, aes(month, sbp)) +
  geom_line(data = grid6, aes(y = mean), colour = "#AAAAAA", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = grid6, aes(y = ols), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = grid6, aes(y = blup), colour = course_colours["blue"],
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "SBP (mmHg)")







Figure 4.2: Six WALK participants (points), their own least-squares lines (dashed) and the lines predicted by the random-slope model fitted later in this module (solid). The grey line in each panel is the estimated mean trajectory for the participant’s arm. Participants with few observations are pulled more strongly toward their arm’s mean line.





Figure 4.2 illustrates the intuition. For each participant we could draw a least-squares line through their own points (dashed). With six visits that line is a reasonable summary; with two or three visits it is mostly noise, and with a single visit it cannot be drawn at all. The mixed model’s prediction for the participant (solid blue) is a compromise between the participant’s own line and the average line for their arm (grey). The compromise leans toward the participant’s own data when there are many precise observations and toward the average when there are few. This pulling toward the mean is called shrinkage, and Section 4.3.2 treats it formally. It is the reason mixed models handle unbalanced data so gracefully: every participant contributes what their data can support, and nobody is discarded.
The same model has two readings. Read subject-specific (conditional), it describes the trajectory of a participant with given random effects. Read population-average (marginal), it describes the mean trajectory averaged over participants. For a linear mixed model the two readings give the same fixed-effect coefficients, because averaging \(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + b_{0i} + b_{1i}t_{ij}\) over random effects with mean zero returns \(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta\). This is not true for the nonlinear links of Module 8, so it is worth remembering that the convenience is special to the linear case.






NoteWhy this matters



The random effects do two jobs. Scientifically, their variances describe how much participants differ in level and in rate of change. Statistically, they induce correlation between the repeated measurements of the same participant, which is what makes the standard errors of the fixed effects correct. Even when the individual differences are of no interest, the random effects are needed for valid inference about the mean.




4.1.2 The random-intercept model

The research question and estimand
We start with the simplest mixed model to see each part clearly. The question is the one from Module 3’s regression review: does mean SBP change at a different rate in each programme compared with usual care? If change is approximately linear over the year, the estimand is the difference in mean slope (mmHg per month) between SP and UC and between EP and UC.


Data structure and outcome types
The outcome is continuous (SBP in mmHg) and the data are in long format, one row per observation, with 1897 rows from 360 participants. Participants contribute between 1 and 6 observations. Time is the actual visit time month. Arm is a factor with UC as the reference. No participant needs to be complete, and the times need not be the same for everyone.


Intuition
Imagine shifting every participant’s data up or down so that all participants have the same average level. The remaining scatter around the arm’s mean line is the within-participant variation. The random-intercept model says exactly this: every participant has their own level, the levels are spread around the population mean with variance \(\tau_0^2\), and around their own level each participant’s measurements scatter with variance \(\sigma^2\). All participants in an arm share the same slope.


The model
For participant \(i\) at occasion \(j\),
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{SP}_i + \beta_3 \text{EP}_i + \beta_4 t_{ij}\text{SP}_i + \beta_5 t_{ij}\text{EP}_i + b_{0i} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
\[
b_{0i} \sim N(0, \tau_0^2), \qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
\]
with the \(b_{0i}\) independent across participants, the \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) independent across participants and occasions, and \(b_{0i}\) independent of \(\varepsilon_{ij}\).

\(y_{ij}\) is the SBP of participant \(i\) at occasion \(j\), and \(t_{ij}\) the actual time in months since randomisation.
\(\text{SP}_i\) and \(\text{EP}_i\) are indicators (1 or 0) for the participant’s arm. UC is the reference.
\(\beta_0\) is the mean SBP at \(t = 0\) in UC; \(\beta_1\) is the mean slope (mmHg/month) in UC.
\(\beta_2\), \(\beta_3\) are the differences in mean SBP at \(t = 0\) between SP or EP and UC. In a randomised trial these should be close to zero.
\(\beta_4\), \(\beta_5\) are the differences in mean slope between SP or EP and UC: the estimands.
\(b_{0i}\) is participant \(i\)’s random intercept: how far their whole trajectory sits above or below the mean trajectory of their arm.
\(\tau_0^2\) is the between-participant variance of the intercepts, and \(\sigma^2\) the within-participant (residual) variance.

The model implies a particular marginal covariance for the measurements of one participant. Two measurements of the same participant share \(b_{0i}\), so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(y_{ij}) = \tau_0^2 + \sigma^2, \qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(y_{ij}, y_{ik}) = \tau_0^2 \quad (j \ne k), \qquad
\operatorname{Corr}(y_{ij}, y_{ik}) = \frac{\tau_0^2}{\tau_0^2 + \sigma^2} = \rho_I .
\]
The correlation \(\rho_I\) is the intraclass correlation (ICC): the share of the total variance that lies between participants. It is the same for every pair of occasions, however far apart. This pattern of equal variances and equal correlations is compound symmetry, the same structure that repeated-measures ANOVA assumes (Module 3).


Assumptions and limitations
The mean is assumed linear in time within each arm. The random intercepts and residuals are assumed normal, independent of each other and of the covariates, with constant variances. The implied compound-symmetry correlation means that measurements one month apart are assumed to be no more correlated than measurements twelve months apart, and that the variance of SBP is the same at every time. Both are testable, and the second limitation is the main reason to move on to random slopes. Under these assumptions, and provided the model is correct, likelihood-based estimates are valid when data are missing at random (MAR), which is the reason the model can use all 360 participants without imputation (Module 10 discusses this in detail).


Fitting the model in R
The lme4 formula adds random-effects terms in brackets: (1 | id) means “a random intercept (1) for each level of id”. Loading lmerTest (done by setup.R) adds Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and p-values to the summary.

m_ri <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 | id), data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)

Interpreting the output
The fixed effects read exactly as in ordinary regression. Mean SBP in UC at randomisation is estimated at 145.0 mmHg, and the mean slope in UC is -0.024 mmHg/month, essentially flat. The interaction terms are the estimands: compared with UC, mean SBP falls faster by 0.49 mmHg/month in SP (95% CI 0.32 to 0.66) and by 0.72 mmHg/month in EP (0.55 to 0.89). Over 12 months these slopes imply differences in mean change of about -5.9 and -8.6 mmHg.
The random-effects block is new. The standard deviation of the random intercepts is \(\hat\tau_0 =\) 12.1 mmHg: participants’ typical levels vary around their arm’s mean with a standard deviation of about 12 mmHg, so roughly 95% of participants have a level within \(\pm\) 24 mmHg of the mean. The residual standard deviation is \(\hat\sigma =\) 6.4 mmHg: a single measurement typically differs from the participant’s own line by about this much. The ICC is
\[
\hat\rho_I = \frac{146.0}{146.0 + 40.6} = 0.78,
\]
so 78% of the variation in SBP around the arm-specific mean lines is between participants. Note that lme4 reports variances and standard deviations side by side; the standard deviations are on the scale of the outcome and are usually easier to interpret.
Compared with the ordinary regression of Module 3, the slope differences are similar but their meaning for inference is not. The random intercept accounts for the strong correlation within participants, so the standard errors are now model-based standard errors that respect the design. Within-participant comparisons, such as slopes, gain precision because each participant serves as their own control.

Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Calling the ICC “the correlation of the data” without saying that it is the correlation implied by the model. In a random-intercept model it is the same for every pair of visits, which the WALK data contradict.
Interpreting \(\tau_0\) as a standard error. It describes how much participants differ, not how uncertain an estimate is.
Fitting a fixed effect for every participant (sbp ~ month * arm + id). The arm effect is then not estimable, because arm is constant within participant, and the model describes only these participants rather than the population.
Forgetting that the random intercept assumes parallel lines within arm. If participants change at different rates, the model is misspecified and the standard errors of the slope differences are too small (see the next section).






4.1.3 The random-slope model: the linear-time reference model

The research question and estimand
The question and estimand are unchanged: the difference in mean slope between each programme and UC, and the implied difference in mean change over 12 months. The random-slope model adds a second question that it can also answer: how much do participants differ in their rate of change?


Data structure and outcome types
As before: continuous SBP in long format, actual times, unbalanced follow-up. To estimate between-participant variation in slopes, a reasonable number of participants need at least three observations, and the observation times need to be spread over follow-up. In WALK, 332 of the 360 participants have three or more observations.


Intuition
Now each participant has their own line with their own intercept and their own slope. The lines fan out or fan in over time, depending on whether participants who start high tend to change faster or slower. Because the spread of the lines changes with time, the variance of SBP and the correlation between visits now also depend on time. This is what allows the model to match the decaying correlations seen above.


The model
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{SP}_i + \beta_3 \text{EP}_i + \beta_4 t_{ij}\text{SP}_i + \beta_5 t_{ij}\text{EP}_i + b_{0i} + b_{1i} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
\[
\mathbf{b}_i = \begin{pmatrix} b_{0i} \\ b_{1i} \end{pmatrix} \sim N\!\left(\mathbf{0},\; G\right), \qquad
G = \begin{pmatrix} \tau_0^2 & \tau_{01} \\ \tau_{01} & \tau_1^2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2).
\]
The fixed effects \(\beta_0, \dots, \beta_5\) mean the same as before. The new terms are:

\(b_{1i}\), participant \(i\)’s random slope: the difference between their rate of change and the mean rate of change in their arm (mmHg/month);
\(\tau_1^2\), the variance of the random slopes;
\(\tau_{01}\), the covariance between random intercepts and slopes. Its correlation version \(\tau_{01}/(\tau_0\tau_1)\) says whether participants who start high tend to change faster (negative correlation, if SBP falls) or slower;
\(G\), the covariance matrix of the random effects.

In matrix form for participant \(i\), with \(X_i\) the fixed-effects design matrix and \(Z_i\) the random-effects design matrix (a column of ones and a column of times),
\[
\mathbf{y}_i = X_i\boldsymbol\beta + Z_i\mathbf{b}_i + \boldsymbol\varepsilon_i, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{y}_i) = V_i = Z_i G Z_i^\top + \sigma^2 I_{n_i}.
\]
Writing out the elements of \(V_i\) shows how the variance and covariance depend on time:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(y_{ij}) = \tau_0^2 + 2\tau_{01}t_{ij} + \tau_1^2 t_{ij}^2 + \sigma^2, \qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(y_{ij}, y_{ik}) = \tau_0^2 + \tau_{01}(t_{ij} + t_{ik}) + \tau_1^2 t_{ij}t_{ik}.
\]
The variance is a quadratic function of time. When \(\tau_{01} < 0\) it first falls and then rises, with its minimum at \(t = -\tau_{01}/\tau_1^2\). There is therefore no single ICC in a random-slope model: the correlation between two visits depends on when they are.


Assumptions and limitations
The assumptions of the random-intercept model carry over, with \(\mathbf{b}_i\) now bivariate normal. The mean trajectory in each arm is still assumed linear; departures from linearity in the mean are a separate issue from the random slopes, and we return to them in the section on coding time. The residuals are still assumed independent given the random effects, so short-term correlation between visits close in time is not modelled (Module 5 adds residual correlation structures). The variance pattern is constrained to be quadratic in time. Random slopes need enough observations per participant spread over time; with very few, the slope variance may be estimated at zero (a singular fit, see Module 11).


Fitting the model in R
(1 + month | id) requests a correlated random intercept and random slope on month for each participant. This is the course’s linear-time reference model.

The fixed effects tell the familiar story. The baseline differences are small and their confidence intervals include zero, as randomisation leads us to expect. Mean SBP is roughly flat in UC and falls by an extra 0.49 mmHg/month in SP (95% CI 0.28 to 0.70) and 0.72 mmHg/month in EP (0.51 to 0.93). Is the random slope needed? The random-intercept model is the random-slope model with \(\tau_1^2 = 0\) and \(\tau_{01} = 0\), so the two can be compared with a likelihood-ratio test. Both models have the same fixed effects, so the REML likelihoods can be compared (see Section 4.3.1):

anova(m_ri, m_lin, refit = FALSE)

#> Data: walk
#> Models:
#> m_ri: sbp ~ month * arm + (1 | id)
#> m_lin: sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id)
#>       npar   AIC   BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
#> m_ri     8 13482 13527  -6733     13466                        
#> m_lin   10 13439 13494  -6709     13419  47.3  2    5.3e-11 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The statistic is 47.3 on 2 degrees of freedom. Because a variance cannot be negative, the null value \(\tau_1^2 = 0\) lies on the boundary of the parameter space and the usual \(\chi^2_2\) reference distribution is conservative. The correct reference is a 50:50 mixture of \(\chi^2_1\) and \(\chi^2_2\) (Self and Liang 1987; Stram and Lee 1994), which gives p < 0.001 (p_boundary_mixture(chisq, df_mix = c(1, 2))). Either way the evidence for differences in slopes is overwhelming, and AIC agrees (13482 versus 13439). In a randomised trial there is a further argument for keeping random slopes whatever the test says: if participants vary in their rate of change and the model ignores it, the standard errors of the slope differences are too small (Barr et al. 2013). Basic residual checks are shown for the primary model below.

We fitted a linear mixed model with fixed effects for time (actual months since randomisation), arm and their interaction, and a correlated random intercept and random slope on time for each participant (REML; lme4, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom). Compared with usual care, mean SBP declined faster by 0.49 mmHg/month (95% CI 0.28 to 0.70) with the standard programme and by 0.72 mmHg/month (0.51 to 0.93) with the enhanced programme.
