Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Quoting a single ICC for a random-slope model. The correlation depends on the times involved; report \(G\) and \(\sigma^2\), or the implied correlations at chosen times.
Forgetting that the intercept variance refers to time zero. \(\tau_0^2\) and \(\tau_{01}\) change if time is shifted (see the next section). Only the implied \(V_i\) is invariant.
Testing the random slope with the naive \(\chi^2_2\) p-value and deciding that a borderline result means “no slope variation”. Use the mixture reference distribution, and keep random slopes when the design and question make them plausible.
Adding a random slope without the matching fixed slope. The random slope describes variation around a mean slope; the fixed slope should almost always be in the model.
Comparing models with different fixed effects using REML likelihoods. REML likelihoods are only comparable when the fixed effects are identical.






4.1.4 Coding time
The same data can be described with time coded in several ways. The choice changes what the intercept and the arm coefficients mean, and sometimes changes the fit. This section works through four codings. The first two give the same model in different clothes; the last two change the model.
Continuous time from randomisation (month), as above: the intercept is the mean at month 0 and the arm coefficients are differences at month 0. In a trial these are the least interesting quantities in the model, because randomisation makes them zero in expectation.
Centred time. Subtracting a constant from time moves the origin. With month12 = month - 12, the “zero” of time is month 12:

walk <- walk |> mutate(month12 = month - 12)
m_c12 <- lmer(sbp ~ month12 * arm + (1 + month12 | id), data = walk,
              control = lmer_ctrl)
cbind(origin_month0 = fixef(m_lin), origin_month12 = fixef(m_c12))

#>             origin_month0 origin_month12
#> (Intercept)     145.00959      144.60561
#> month            -0.03366       -0.03366
#> armSP             0.30530       -5.57438
#> armEP            -0.76422       -9.44648
#> month:armSP      -0.48997       -0.48997
#> month:armEP      -0.72352       -0.72352


The slopes and slope differences are unchanged (-0.490 and -0.724), and so are the log-likelihood and fitted values: this is the same model. But the arm “main effects” now mean something different. armSP = -5.57 and armEP = -9.45 are the differences in mean SBP at month 12, which equal \(\beta_2 + 12\beta_4\) from the uncentred model. Centring did not create an effect; it changed which question the coefficient answers. The random-effects parameters change too: \(\hat\tau_0\) is now the SD of participants’ levels at month 12 (12.52 mmHg) and the intercept-slope correlation becomes 0.26. Centring at the mean follow-up time is also common because it reduces the correlation between the intercept and slope estimates.
Categorical time (visit_f, the scheduled visit as a factor) estimates a separate mean for each arm at each scheduled visit, with no assumption about the shape of the trajectory. The interaction coefficients then compare the change from baseline to each visit between arms. This is the primary model of the course and has its own section below. Note that the random slope still uses actual time month, so the covariance part of the model respects the actual timing of visits.
Nonlinear time. If the mean trajectory curves, a straight line misrepresents it. A quadratic term is the simplest extension:

m_quad <- lmer(sbp ~ (month + I(month^2)) * arm + (1 + month | id),
               data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
anova(m_lin, m_quad)

#> refitting model(s) with ML (instead of REML)


#> Data: walk
#> Models:
#> m_lin: sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id)
#> m_quad: sbp ~ (month + I(month^2)) * arm + (1 + month | id)
#>        npar   AIC   BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
#> m_lin    10 13435 13491  -6708     13415                        
#> m_quad   13 13326 13399  -6650     13300   115  3     <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The quadratic model fits much better. Because the two models have different fixed effects, anova() refits both by ML before comparing them (refitting model(s) with ML). Figure 4.4 shows why: in the programme arms SBP falls quickly over the first six months and then levels off, which a straight line cannot follow. The linear-time model understates the decline over the first months and keeps falling after the estimated means have levelled off, so it overstates the decline at month 12 in SP. The quadratic follows the means more closely but bends upward at the end, which is a property of the quadratic form rather than of the data. Module 9 develops polynomial, piecewise and spline models for curved trajectories.

m_cat <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk,
              control = lmer_ctrl)
nd <- expand.grid(month = seq(0, 12, 0.25), arm = levels(walk$arm))
nd$lin  <- predict(m_lin,  newdata = nd, re.form = NA)
nd$quad <- predict(m_quad, newdata = nd, re.form = NA)
cat_means <- as.data.frame(emmeans(m_cat, ~ visit_f | arm)) |>
  mutate(month = as.numeric(as.character(visit_f)))
ggplot(nd, aes(month, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lin, linetype = "Linear")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = quad, linetype = "Quadratic")) +
  geom_point(data = cat_means, aes(month, emmean, shape = "Categorical"), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_arm(labels = walk_arm_labels, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Months since randomisation", y = "Estimated mean SBP (mmHg)",
       linetype = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme(legend.box = "vertical")







Figure 4.4: Estimated mean SBP by arm under three codings of time: a straight line (solid), a quadratic (dashed) and categorical time (points, one mean per arm and scheduled visit). Categorical time makes no assumption about shape.





Which coding to use depends on the question and the design. With a few fixed visits and a pre-specified estimand at one visit, categorical time is the safe default for the mean: it cannot be wrong about the shape. With many or irregular measurement times, or when the rate of change is itself the question, continuous time (possibly with curvature) is more natural and more efficient. Whatever the choice, centre time where the coefficients answer the question you care about, or, more simply, compute the quantity of interest with emmeans so that the coding does not matter.

title: 4  Linear mixed-effects models
section: 4.2 Part 2. The primary analysis of WALK
text:
4.2 Part 2. The primary analysis of WALK

4.2.1 The primary model: categorical time by arm

The research question and estimand
Does each walking programme lower SBP over 12 months compared with usual care? The estimand is the difference in mean change from baseline to month 12 between each programme and UC, in the population of randomised participants, with the missing data assumed to be MAR given the observed SBP history and arm. It is measured in mmHg; negative values favour the programme.


Data structure and outcome types
Continuous SBP in long format; the mean is indexed by scheduled visit (visit_f, six levels) and arm, while the random slope uses actual time month. All 360 participants contribute, including the 72 who have no month-12 measurement.


Intuition
The model estimates a mean for each arm at each scheduled visit, without forcing the means onto a line or curve. Participants with missing visits still inform the means at the visits they missed, through their correlation with the visits they attended. A participant last seen at month 6 with a high SBP tells the model something about where that participant was likely to be at month 12, and the model uses that information in proportion to the estimated correlation. This is how a likelihood analysis under MAR uses incomplete cases, and it is why the estimate can differ from a completers-only analysis.


The model
Let \(V_{kij}\) be 1 if occasion \(j\) of participant \(i\) is scheduled visit \(k\) (\(k = 2, \dots, 6\) for months 1, 3, 6, 9, 12) and 0 otherwise. Then
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=2}^{6}\gamma_k V_{kij} + \beta_{\text{SP}}\text{SP}_i + \beta_{\text{EP}}\text{EP}_i
+ \sum_{k=2}^{6}\left(\delta^{\text{SP}}_k V_{kij}\text{SP}_i + \delta^{\text{EP}}_k V_{kij}\text{EP}_i\right)
+ b_{0i} + b_{1i}t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
with \(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, G)\) and \(\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) as before.

\(\beta_0\) is mean SBP at baseline in UC, and \(\gamma_k\) the mean change from baseline to visit \(k\) in UC.
\(\beta_{\text{SP}}\), \(\beta_{\text{EP}}\) are the baseline differences between arms.
\(\delta^{\text{SP}}_k\) is the difference between SP and UC in mean change from baseline to visit \(k\). The primary estimands are \(\delta^{\text{SP}}_6\) and \(\delta^{\text{EP}}_6\) (month 12).
\(b_{0i}\), \(b_{1i}\), \(G\), \(\sigma^2\) and \(t_{ij}\) (actual time) are as in the random-slope model.

The mean model has 18 parameters, one per arm and visit, so it is saturated in arm and visit: it reproduces any pattern of means.


Assumptions and limitations
The mean model makes no shape assumption. The assumptions are in the covariance part (random intercept and slope with independent residuals, normality) and the missing-data mechanism (MAR). A misspecified covariance does not bias the mean estimates when data are complete, but with dropout under MAR the covariance model matters because it determines how incomplete participants are used; Module 5 compares covariance structures and Module 10 studies sensitivity to MAR. Using the scheduled visit for the mean ignores the small differences between scheduled and actual times; with visits a few weeks off schedule, this is a minor approximation.


Fitting the model in R
The model was fitted above as m_cat. Here is its summary.

summary(m_cat)

#> Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
#> lmerModLmerTest]
#> Formula: sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id)
#>    Data: walk
#> Control: lmer_ctrl
#> 
#> REML criterion at convergence: 13248
#> 
#> Scaled residuals: 
#>     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#> -3.0687 -0.5489 -0.0019  0.5535  2.6790 
#> 
#> Random effects:
#>  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr  
#>  id       (Intercept) 153.089  12.373         
#>           month         0.294   0.542   -0.23 
#>  Residual              31.580   5.620         
#> Number of obs: 1897, groups:  id, 360
#> 
#> Fixed effects:
#>                 Estimate Std. Error       df t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)      146.190      1.240  429.861  117.85  < 2e-16 ***
#> visit_f1          -1.626      0.761 1246.439   -2.14  0.03284 *  
#> visit_f3          -2.602      0.776 1396.965   -3.35  0.00082 ***
#> visit_f6          -1.608      0.833 1486.703   -1.93  0.05363 .  
#> visit_f9          -1.281      0.908  913.762   -1.41  0.15863    
#> visit_f12         -1.326      1.013  489.731   -1.31  0.19122    
#> armSP              1.042      1.754  429.849    0.59  0.55301    
#> armEP              1.347      1.754  429.832    0.77  0.44315    
#> visit_f1:armSP    -0.852      1.075 1246.773   -0.79  0.42824    
#> visit_f3:armSP    -2.603      1.090 1396.070   -2.39  0.01708 *  
#> visit_f6:armSP    -4.868      1.172 1482.821   -4.15  3.5e-05 ***
#> visit_f9:armSP    -5.933      1.276  913.380   -4.65  3.8e-06 ***
#> visit_f12:armSP   -5.377      1.422  483.194   -3.78  0.00017 ***
#> visit_f1:armEP    -3.363      1.070 1244.285   -3.14  0.00171 ** 
#> visit_f3:armEP    -5.225      1.102 1391.779   -4.74  2.3e-06 ***
#> visit_f6:armEP    -9.007      1.170 1481.381   -7.70  2.6e-14 ***
#> visit_f9:armEP    -8.859      1.291  908.650   -6.86  1.2e-11 ***
#> visit_f12:armEP   -8.969      1.437  490.778   -6.24  9.3e-10 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


#> 
#> Correlation matrix not shown by default, as p = 18 > 12.
#> Use print(x, correlation=TRUE)  or
#>     vcov(x)        if you need it


The coefficient table is long and most of it is not the answer. The cleanest way to get the estimand is with estimated marginal means (EMMs) from emmeans (Lenth and Piaskowski 2026): first the model-based mean at each visit in each arm, then the change from baseline to month 12 within each arm, then the contrast of each programme’s change with UC’s.

emm   <- emmeans(m_cat, ~ visit_f | arm)
chg12 <- contrast(emm, list(chg12 = c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)))   # month 12 minus month 0
dmc12 <- contrast(chg12, "trt.vs.ctrl", by = NULL, adjust = "none")
summary(chg12, infer = TRUE)

#> arm = UC:
#>  contrast estimate    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  chg12       -1.33 1.010 490    -3.32    0.665  -1.309  0.1912
#> 
#> arm = SP:
#>  contrast estimate    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  chg12       -6.70 0.997 476    -8.66   -4.744  -6.724 <0.0001
#> 
#> arm = EP:
#>  contrast estimate    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  chg12      -10.29 1.020 492   -12.30   -8.294 -10.109 <0.0001
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95

summary(dmc12, infer = TRUE)

#>  contrast            estimate   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  chg12 SP - chg12 UC    -5.38 1.42 483    -8.17    -2.58  -3.782  0.0002
#>  chg12 EP - chg12 UC    -8.97 1.44 491   -11.79    -6.15  -6.243 <0.0001
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95


The vector c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1) weights the six visit means: minus baseline plus month 12. trt.vs.ctrl subtracts the first arm (UC) from each of the others. We set adjust = "none" explicitly because emmeans applies a Dunnett-type adjustment to trt.vs.ctrl by default; whether to adjust for the two comparisons is a design decision discussed in Module 6.


Interpreting the output
Mean SBP changed from baseline to month 12 by -1.3 mmHg in UC (95% CI -3.3 to 0.7), -6.7 mmHg in SP and -10.3 mmHg in EP. The differences in mean change compared with UC are

SP: -5.38 (-8.17 to -2.58) mmHg, p < 0.001;
EP: -8.97 (-11.79 to -6.15) mmHg, p < 0.001.

Both programmes lowered SBP more than usual care, and the enhanced programme’s effect is roughly 1.7 times the standard programme’s. The confidence intervals are wide (each about 6 mmHg), but both exclude zero.
The estimates of the primary estimand are identical to the interaction coefficients visit_f12:armSP (-5.377) and visit_f12:armEP (-8.969). With UC and baseline as reference levels, \(\delta_6\) is the difference in mean change. emmeans is still the safer route: it does not depend on the reference levels, and it extends directly to adjusted models and other contrasts.
Comparison with the truth (possible only because the data are simulated). The data were generated with true differences in mean change at month 12 of -4.6 mmHg (SP) and -8.1 mmHg (EP). The estimates (-5.38 and -8.97) are within about one standard error of the true values, and both 95% confidence intervals contain them. The estimated change in UC (-1.3, true -2.1) is a little smaller than the truth, which is why both differences are slightly larger in magnitude than the true values. This is ordinary sampling error in one trial; one dataset can never show bias. In a real study none of this can be checked: the truth is unknown, and the confidence interval is all we have.



Quantity (mmHg, month 12)
Estimate (95% CI)
True value




Change, UC
-1.3 (-3.3 to 0.7)
-2.1


Change, SP
-6.7 (-8.7 to -4.7)
-6.7


Change, EP
-10.3 (-12.3 to -8.3)
-10.2


SP minus UC
-5.4 (-8.2 to -2.6)
-4.6


EP minus UC
-9.0 (-11.8 to -6.1)
-8.1



The linear-time model, which forces straight lines, gives -5.88 (SP) and -8.68 (EP) for the same estimand. These are not far off here, because the curvature is similar in all arms, but they rest on an assumption that Figure 4.4 shows is false. The primary analysis should not depend on a shape assumption that is not needed.
The variance components are close to those of the linear-time model (\(\hat\tau_0 =\) 12.37 mmHg, \(\hat\tau_1 =\) 0.542 mmHg/month, correlation -0.23, \(\hat\sigma =\) 5.62 mmHg). The residual SD is smaller because the flexible mean absorbs the curvature that the linear model left in the residuals.






NoteWhy the variance components do not match the generating values



The WALK data were generated with an intercept SD of 11 mmHg, a slope SD of 0.35 mmHg/month, a clinic SD of 3 mmHg, serially correlated deviations (SD 5 mmHg) and measurement error (SD 4 mmHg). The fitted model has no clinic effect and no serial correlation, so these sources are absorbed into the components it does have: the clinic variance into \(\tau_0^2\), part of the serial correlation into the random slopes and the rest into \(\sigma^2\). Variance components describe the model you fitted, not “the” variation in nature. Modules 5 and 13 add the missing structures.




Checking the model
Full diagnostics are the topic of Module 11. Three basic plots should accompany every LMM: conditional residuals (\(y_{ij}\) minus the participant-specific fitted value) against fitted values, a normal Q-Q plot of the residuals, and normal Q-Q plots of the predicted random effects.

diag_df <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_cat), resid = resid(m_cat))
re_df <- ranef(m_cat)$id
p1 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#888888") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = course_colours["orange"]) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (mmHg)", y = "Conditional residual (mmHg)")
p2 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(sample = resid)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#888888") + labs(x = "Normal quantile", y = "Residual (mmHg)")
p3 <- ggplot(re_df, aes(sample = `(Intercept)`)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#888888") + labs(x = "Normal quantile", y = "Predicted b0i (mmHg)")
p4 <- ggplot(re_df, aes(sample = month)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#888888") + labs(x = "Normal quantile", y = "Predicted b1i (mmHg/month)")
(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4)







Figure 4.5: Basic checks of the primary model. Top: conditional residuals against fitted values (with a smoother) and their normal Q-Q plot. Bottom: normal Q-Q plots of the predicted random intercepts and slopes.





The residuals show no fanning, so a constant residual variance looks reasonable. The smoother tilts upward: residuals tend to be negative at low fitted values and positive at high ones. This is an expected artefact of shrinkage, not a sign of a wrong mean model. Participants with extreme levels have their random intercepts pulled toward the mean, so their fitted values are less extreme than their data and their residuals point away from the centre. Module 11 shows residuals that avoid this artefact. The Q-Q plots are close to straight lines; SBP values are recorded as whole numbers, which gives the residuals a slightly granular look but does not matter. The predicted random effects are roughly normal, with some departure in the tails (the lowest predicted intercepts are less extreme than a normal distribution would give, and the predicted slopes have slightly heavy tails); nothing here suggests a serious problem. Remember that predicted random effects are shrunken (Section 4.3.2), so their Q-Q plots are only a rough guide; fixed-effect estimates are in any case fairly insensitive to non-normal random effects. The conditional residuals cannot detect serial correlation; Module 5 shows how to look for it.


Reporting






TipReporting example



SBP was analysed with a linear mixed model including scheduled visit (as a factor), arm and their interaction as fixed effects, and a correlated random intercept and random slope on actual time since randomisation for each participant, fitted by REML in lme4 (Bates et al. 2015). All 360 randomised participants and 1897 measurements contributed; the analysis is valid if missing data are missing at random given the observed SBP history and arm. The difference in mean change from baseline to month 12 was estimated with emmeans (Lenth and Piaskowski 2026) with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (Kuznetsova et al. 2017). Compared with usual care, SBP fell by an additional 5.4 mmHg with the standard programme (95% CI 2.6 to 8.2; p < 0.001) and by an additional 9.0 mmHg with the enhanced programme (95% CI 6.1 to 11.8; p < 0.001). Mean change in the usual-care arm was -1.3 mmHg (-3.3 to 0.7).


A complete report would also give the number of participants with month-12 data in each arm, state whether the two comparisons were adjusted for multiplicity, and report a sensitivity analysis for the MAR assumption (Modules 10 and 12).


Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Reading armSP as “the treatment effect”. In this model it is the difference at baseline. The treatment effect at month 12 is visit_f12:armSP, or better, the emmeans contrast.
Using the scheduled visit in the random slope ((1 + month_sched | id)) when actual times are available. Actual times describe the covariance better; scheduled visits are used for the mean only.
Leaving the emmeans default adjustment in place without saying so. trt.vs.ctrl is Dunnett-adjusted by default; state what you report.
Reporting the p-value of the global arm or visit_f:arm test instead of the pre-specified estimand with its confidence interval.
Fitting the model to completers only. This throws away the main advantage of the mixed model and gives biased estimates when dropout depends on observed outcomes.






4.2.2 The same model in nlme
nlme (Pinheiro and Bates 2000) is the older of the two main R packages for mixed models. It is still essential because it supports residual correlation structures and heterogeneous variances (Module 5), which lme4 does not. Its syntax separates the fixed and random parts: random = ~ 1 + month | id.

m_cat_lme <- lme(sbp ~ visit_f * arm, random = ~ 1 + month | id,
                 data = walk, method = "REML")
VarCorr(m_cat_lme)

#> id = pdLogChol(1 + month) 
#>             Variance StdDev  Corr  
#> (Intercept) 153.0838 12.3727 (Intr)
#> month         0.2938  0.5421 -0.235
#> Residual     31.5800  5.6196



agree <- data.frame(
  lmer = fixef(m_cat), lme = nlme::fixef(m_cat_lme),
  se_lmer = sqrt(diag(as.matrix(vcov(m_cat)))), se_lme = sqrt(diag(vcov(m_cat_lme))))
round(agree[c("(Intercept)", "visit_f12", "visit_f12:armSP", "visit_f12:armEP"), ], 4)

#>                    lmer     lme se_lmer se_lme
#> (Intercept)     146.190 146.190   1.240  1.240
#> visit_f12        -1.326  -1.326   1.013  1.013
#> visit_f12:armSP  -5.377  -5.377   1.421  1.421
#> visit_f12:armEP  -8.969  -8.969   1.437  1.437

c(max_abs_diff_estimates = max(abs(agree$lmer - agree$lme)),
  max_abs_diff_se = max(abs(agree$se_lmer - agree$se_lme)))

#> max_abs_diff_estimates        max_abs_diff_se 
#>              8.481e-06              2.472e-05



ds_lme <- summary(contrast(contrast(emmeans(m_cat_lme, ~ visit_f | arm),
                                    list(chg12 = c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))),
                           "trt.vs.ctrl", by = NULL, adjust = "none"), infer = TRUE)
ds_lme

#>  contrast            estimate   SE   df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  chg12 SP - chg12 UC    -5.38 1.42 1522    -8.16    -2.59  -3.782  0.0002
#>  chg12 EP - chg12 UC    -8.97 1.44 1522   -11.79    -6.15  -6.243 <0.0001
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: containment 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95


The two packages maximise the same REML criterion and agree on every fixed effect and standard error to within numerical tolerance (largest absolute difference 8.5e-06 mmHg for the estimates), and on the variance components (\(\hat\tau_0 =\) 12.37 in both). The one visible difference is the degrees of freedom. lme uses a simple “containment” rule that gives 1522 degrees of freedom for the month-12 contrast, whereas lmerTest uses the Satterthwaite approximation (483). With 360 participants both are large and the confidence intervals agree to the first decimal place: SP -5.38 (-8.17 to -2.59) with lme against -5.38 (-8.17 to -2.58) with lmer. In small samples the choice of degrees of freedom matters more, and Satterthwaite or Kenward-Roger approximations are preferred. Note also that setup.R makes fixef(), ranef() and VarCorr() the lme4 versions; for lme objects, VarCorr() still works through method dispatch, but use nlme::fixef() explicitly.

title: 4  Linear mixed-effects models
text:
4.3 Part 3. Estimation and prediction

4.3.1 Estimation by ML and REML

The research question and estimand
Every mixed model has two sets of parameters: the fixed effects \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and the variance components \(\boldsymbol\theta\) (here \(\tau_0^2\), \(\tau_1^2\), \(\tau_{01}\), \(\sigma^2\)). Estimation answers a technical question: which values of these parameters best explain the data? The choice between maximum likelihood (ML) and restricted maximum likelihood (REML) affects mainly the variance components and, through them, the standard errors, and it decides which models can be compared by likelihood-ratio tests.


Data structure and outcome types
Both methods apply to any linear mixed model for a continuous outcome with normally distributed random effects and residuals, balanced or unbalanced.


Intuition
You already know the simplest case. The ML estimate of a variance from a sample of size \(n\) divides the sum of squares by \(n\); the usual unbiased estimate divides by \(n - 1\). The ML version is too small because it measures spread around the estimated mean \(\bar y\), which is closer to the data than the true mean is. One degree of freedom has been “used up” estimating the mean. ML for a mixed model makes the same mistake on a larger scale: it estimates variance components as if \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) were the true \(\boldsymbol\beta\), ignoring the \(p\) degrees of freedom used by the fixed effects. REML corrects this by basing the estimation of \(\boldsymbol\theta\) only on the part of the data that carries no information about \(\boldsymbol\beta\) (the residual contrasts), which is the multivariate generalisation of dividing by \(n - 1\).


The model
Under the model \(\mathbf{y}_i \sim N(X_i\boldsymbol\beta, V_i(\boldsymbol\theta))\), independent across participants, the ML log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta, \boldsymbol\theta) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[ \log|V_i| + (\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\boldsymbol\beta)^\top V_i^{-1}(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\boldsymbol\beta) \right] + \text{constant}.
\]
For given \(\boldsymbol\theta\), the \(\boldsymbol\beta\) that maximises it is the generalized least squares estimate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}(\boldsymbol\theta) = \left(\sum X_i^\top V_i^{-1}X_i\right)^{-1}\sum X_i^\top V_i^{-1}\mathbf{y}_i\). The REML log-likelihood for the variance components is
\[
\ell_R(\boldsymbol\theta) = \ell\big(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}(\boldsymbol\theta), \boldsymbol\theta\big) - \frac{1}{2}\log\left|\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^\top V_i^{-1}X_i\right| + \text{constant}.
\]
The extra term penalises the uncertainty in \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). REML estimates \(\boldsymbol\theta\) by maximising \(\ell_R\), then estimates \(\boldsymbol\beta\) by generalized least squares at that \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\) (Laird and Ware 1982; Verbeke and Molenberghs 2000). Here \(\boldsymbol\theta\) is the vector of variance components and \(|\cdot|\) a determinant; the other symbols are as before.


Assumptions and limitations
Both rely on the normality of random effects and residuals for the likelihood, though the estimates remain consistent under moderate non-normality. The REML likelihood depends on the fixed-effects design \(X_i\). That is the price of the bias correction: REML likelihoods of models with different fixed effects are not comparable, so likelihood-ratio tests and AIC/BIC comparisons of fixed effects need ML fits.


Fitting the model in R
lmer() uses REML by default (REML = TRUE); lme() uses method = "REML" by default. Set REML = FALSE or method = "ML" for ML. anova() on two lmer fits refits them by ML automatically, unless refit = FALSE is given.

m_cat_ml <- update(m_cat, REML = FALSE)
cbind(REML = varcomp_table(m_cat)$value, ML = varcomp_table(m_cat_ml)$value)

#>         REML      ML
#> [1,] 12.3729 12.3216
#> [2,]  0.5421  0.5394
#> [3,] -0.2347 -0.2350
#> [4,]  5.6196  5.5922

cbind(REML = fixef(m_cat)[c("visit_f12:armSP", "visit_f12:armEP")],
      ML   = fixef(m_cat_ml)[c("visit_f12:armSP", "visit_f12:armEP")])

#>                   REML     ML
#> visit_f12:armSP -5.377 -5.377
#> visit_f12:armEP -8.969 -8.969


The rows of the first table are \(\tau_0\), \(\tau_1\), their correlation and \(\sigma\).


Interpreting the output
With 360 participants and 18 fixed effects, ML and REML hardly differ: \(\hat\tau_0\) is 12.37 (REML) versus 12.32 (ML), and \(\hat\sigma\) is 5.620 versus 5.592. As expected, the ML estimates are slightly smaller. The fixed effects are the same to three decimals, and the ML standard error of the EP contrast is a little smaller (1.430 versus 1.437) because it is computed from the smaller variance estimates. The difference matters when the number of participants is small relative to the number of fixed effects. A small simulation shows this. We generate 500 small trials of 16 participants (8 per arm) with five visits, a true intercept variance \(\tau_0^2 = 121\) and residual variance \(\sigma^2 = 36\), and fit a random-intercept model by both methods.

set.seed(404)
sim_reml <- t(replicate(500, {
  d <- sim_two_arm(n_per_arm = 8, times = c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12),
                   sd_int = 11, sd_slope = 0, sd_resid = 6)
  f_reml <- suppressMessages(lmer(y ~ time * trt + (1 | id), data = d))
  f_ml   <- suppressMessages(lmer(y ~ time * trt + (1 | id), data = d, REML = FALSE))
  c(tau2_reml = as.numeric(VarCorr(f_reml)$id), tau2_ml = as.numeric(VarCorr(f_ml)$id),
    s2_reml = sigma(f_reml)^2, s2_ml = sigma(f_ml)^2)
}))

#> Warning in checkConv(attr(opt, "derivs"), opt$par, ctrl = control$checkConv, : Model failed to converge with max|grad| = 0.00241426 (tol = 0.002, component 1)
#>   See ?lme4::convergence and ?lme4::troubleshooting.


#> Warning in checkConv(attr(opt, "derivs"), opt$par, ctrl = control$checkConv, : Model failed to converge with max|grad| = 0.00418164 (tol = 0.002, component 1)
#>   See ?lme4::convergence and ?lme4::troubleshooting.

sim_summary <- data.frame(parameter = c("tau0^2", "tau0^2", "sigma^2", "sigma^2"),
                          method = c("REML", "ML", "REML", "ML"),
                          truth = c(121, 121, 36, 36),
                          mean_estimate = colMeans(sim_reml),
                          mcse = apply(sim_reml, 2, sd) / sqrt(nrow(sim_reml)))
sim_summary

#>           parameter method truth mean_estimate   mcse
#> tau2_reml    tau0^2   REML   121        121.67 2.0680
#> tau2_ml      tau0^2     ML   121        105.79 1.8100
#> s2_reml     sigma^2   REML    36         35.83 0.2809
#> s2_ml       sigma^2     ML    36         34.71 0.2722


Averaged over the 500 trials, REML estimates the intercept variance at 121.7 (Monte Carlo SE 2.1), close to the true 121, while ML gives 105.8, about 13% too small. The residual variance is estimated well by both (35.8 and 34.7 against 36), because there are many more within-participant degrees of freedom than fixed effects. The bias of ML falls on the between-participant variance, which is estimated from only 16 participants, two of whose degrees of freedom are used by the between-participant fixed effects (intercept and arm). Underestimated variance components lead to standard errors that are too small, so with few participants REML is the safer default. (The convergence warnings printed above come from a few of the 1,000 small-sample fits, whose gradient is only just above the lme4 tolerance. Borderline warnings like these are expected occasionally in simulations with very small datasets and do not change the averages; Module 11 explains how to investigate them in a real analysis.)
The practical rules are short:

Use REML for the final model, to report variance components and standard errors, and to compare models that differ only in their random effects or covariance structure (same fixed effects).
Use ML to compare models that differ in their fixed effects (likelihood-ratio tests, AIC, BIC). Then refit the chosen model with REML for reporting.



Checking the model
There is little to check about the estimation method itself. Check convergence messages, and if the ML and REML variance estimates differ markedly, take that as a sign that the number of participants is small relative to the fixed-effects model, so that small-sample degrees of freedom (Satterthwaite or Kenward-Roger) matter too.


Reporting






TipReporting example



Models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Nested models differing in their fixed effects were compared by likelihood-ratio tests on maximum-likelihood fits; the final model was refitted by REML. Degrees of freedom for tests and confidence intervals were approximated by the Satterthwaite method.




Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Comparing REML fits with different fixed effects (for example linear versus quadratic time) with anova(..., refit = FALSE) or with AIC. The comparison is meaningless.
Reporting the ML fit used for a model comparison as the final result. Refit with REML.
Believing REML changes the fixed effects substantially. It changes them only through the variance estimates; the main effect is on variance components and standard errors.






4.3.2 Predicted random effects (BLUPs) and shrinkage

The research question and estimand
Sometimes the individual trajectories are of interest in themselves: which participants respond most to the programme, what is a given participant’s likely SBP at month 12, or how much do individual slopes vary? The target is the participant-specific trajectory \(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + b_{0i} + b_{1i}t_{ij}\), and in particular the participant’s own slope.


Data structure and outcome types
The same long data. The precision of each participant’s prediction depends on how many observations they have and how spread out in time those observations are.


Intuition
Random effects are not parameters, so they are not “estimated”; they are predicted from the data given the fitted model. The best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of \(\mathbf{b}_i\) combines two sources of information: the participant’s own data, which say where their line is, and the population distribution \(N(\mathbf{0}, G)\), which says that extreme lines are rare. A participant with many observations and little residual noise is predicted close to their own least-squares line. A participant with one or two observations is predicted close to the mean line of their arm. This is shrinkage (also called partial pooling): the estimates of all participants borrow strength from each other (Gelman and Hill 2007).


The model
Given the fitted model, the BLUP of participant \(i\)’s random effects is
\[
\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i = \hat G Z_i^\top \hat V_i^{-1}\left(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\right).
\]
It is the participant’s vector of residuals from the mean trajectory, \(\mathbf{y}_i - X_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\), transformed and scaled down. The random-intercept model makes the shrinkage explicit. There,
\[
\hat b_{0i} = \frac{n_i\tau_0^2}{n_i\tau_0^2 + \sigma^2}\left(\bar y_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\right),
\]
where \(n_i\) is the participant’s number of observations and \(\bar y_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) the participant’s mean residual from the population line. The factor in front lies between 0 and 1. It approaches 1 (little shrinkage) when \(n_i\) is large or \(\sigma^2\) small relative to \(\tau_0^2\), and approaches 0 (strong shrinkage) when the participant has few, noisy observations.


Assumptions and limitations
BLUPs depend on the model being correct, including the normality of the random effects, which pulls unusual participants toward the centre. Because of shrinkage, the spread of the BLUPs is smaller than \(\hat\tau\), so the BLUPs should not be used as if they were data in a second-stage analysis (for example by correlating predicted slopes with another variable). Each BLUP has a prediction error that should be considered before ranking or classifying individuals.


Fitting the model in R
ranef() returns the predicted random effects \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i\); coef() returns the participant-specific coefficients, which add the fixed effects. Separate least-squares lines for each participant (“no pooling”) come from lme4::lmList().

ols <- coef(lme4::lmList(sbp ~ month | id, data = walk)) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("id") |>
  rename(ols_slope = month)
blup <- coef(m_lin)$id |> tibble::rownames_to_column("id")
shrink <- count(walk, id, arm, name = "n_obs") |>
  left_join(ols |> select(id, ols_slope), by = "id") |>
  left_join(blup, by = "id") |>
  mutate(blup_slope = month + (arm == "SP") * `month:armSP` + (arm == "EP") * `month:armEP`,
         n_group = cut(n_obs, c(0, 3, 5, 6), labels = c("2-3 visits", "4-5 visits", "6 visits")))
head(ranef(m_lin)$id, 3)

#>      (Intercept)   month
#> W001      0.4578 -0.3084
#> W002     22.9738 -0.2382
#> W003    -25.6002 -0.5240

shrink |> group_by(n_group) |>
  summarise(n = n(), sd_ols = sd(ols_slope, na.rm = TRUE), sd_blup = sd(blup_slope))

#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   n_group        n sd_ols sd_blup
#>   <fct>      <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 2-3 visits    42 6.209   0.3260
#> 2 4-5 visits    80 0.9690  0.4664
#> 3 6 visits     238 0.8021  0.4479



shrink |> filter(!is.na(ols_slope)) |>
  ggplot(aes(ols_slope, blup_slope, colour = n_group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#AAAAAA") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(course_colours[c("orange", "blue", "grey")]), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "Separate OLS slope (mmHg/month)", y = "Model-based slope, BLUP (mmHg/month)")







Figure 4.6: Participant-specific slopes from separate least-squares fits (x-axis) against the model’s predicted slopes (BLUPs, y-axis), by number of observations. Points on the grey line would show no shrinkage. The x-axis is truncated at ±6 mmHg/month; a few least-squares slopes from two or three visits lie further out.







Interpreting the output
The least-squares slopes are extremely variable: their SD is 0.80 mmHg/month among participants with all six visits and 6.21 among those with two or three. The BLUP slopes are much more tightly concentrated (SD 0.45 and 0.33). Figure 4.6 shows the pattern: every point lies on a line much flatter than the identity line, and the line is flattest for participants with few visits. A participant with two visits whose two measurements happen to differ by 20 mmHg has an OLS slope of several mmHg per month, but the model recognises that most of that difference is probably measurement noise and short-term fluctuation and predicts a slope near the arm mean. The 15 participants with a single visit have no OLS slope at all; their BLUP slope is the arm mean plus a small adjustment driven by the intercept-slope correlation.
Why do the slopes shrink so much more than the intercepts? In the random-intercept model the shrinkage factor for a participant with six visits is 0.96 and with one visit 0.78, because the intercept variance (146 mmHg²) is large compared with the residual variance divided by the number of visits. For the slopes the opposite holds: the slope variance (0.265 (mmHg/month)²) is small compared with the sampling variance of an individual’s least-squares slope over a year of noisy measurements. Individual rates of change are much harder to pin down than individual levels, and the BLUPs reflect that honestly.
Also note the small but systematic difference between the spread of the BLUP slopes for complete participants (0.45) and the model’s \(\hat\tau_1 =\) 0.51: shrunken predictions always vary less than the random effects themselves.


Checking the model
Plot the BLUPs (normal Q-Q plots as in Figure 4.5) to look for outlying participants or clear departures from normality, and plot each participant’s data with their predicted line, as in Figure 4.2, for a sample of participants and for any participant flagged as unusual. Module 11 adds influence diagnostics.


Reporting






TipReporting example



Participant-specific trajectories were predicted from the random-slope model as best linear unbiased predictors. Predicted slopes were strongly shrunk toward the arm means, particularly for participants with few visits (SD of predicted slopes 0.33 mmHg/month for participants with two or three visits against 6.21 for separate least-squares slopes), reflecting the limited information about individual rates of change. The model-estimated SD of true individual slopes was 0.51 mmHg/month.




Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Calling BLUPs “estimated random effects” and treating them as data, for example correlating BLUP slopes with an outcome in a second step. Shrinkage biases such analyses; include the variable in the model instead.
Ranking individuals (“responders”) by BLUPs without their prediction uncertainty. Most participants’ slopes are not distinguishable from each other.
Using ranef() when you need the participant’s full coefficient. ranef() gives the deviation \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i\); coef() adds the fixed effects, but for a model with arm-by-time interactions you still need to add the arm-specific terms, as in the code above.
Expecting the SD of the BLUPs to equal \(\hat\tau\). It is always smaller.






4.3.3 Choosing the random-effects structure: a short guide
In a randomised trial with a continuous outcome measured repeatedly over time, a random intercept and a random slope on time is a sensible starting point, because participants almost always differ in both level and rate of change. Omitting a random slope that exists makes the standard errors of time-related fixed effects (including the arm-by-time interaction) too small (Barr et al. 2013). Adding random effects that the data cannot support leads to singular fits and convergence problems; Matuschek et al. (2017) discuss the balance between these risks. The covariance of the random effects (\(\tau_{01}\)) should normally be estimated rather than set to zero, because setting it to zero makes the model depend on where time zero is. Decide the structure in advance where possible, from the design and the question, rather than by repeated testing. Module 5 compares random-effects and residual correlation structures more systematically, and Module 11 shows what to do when the fit is singular.


4.3.4 Adjusting for baseline covariates
The covariate-adjusted version of the primary model adds age, sex and BMI, centred so that the intercept refers to a 60-year-old man with a BMI of 29 kg/m².

walk <- walk |> mutate(age10 = (age - 60) / 10, bmi_c = bmi - 29)
m_adj <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + age10 + sex + bmi_c + (1 + month | id),
              data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
ds_adj <- summary(contrast(contrast(emmeans(m_adj, ~ visit_f | arm),
                                    list(chg12 = c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))),
                           "trt.vs.ctrl", by = NULL, adjust = "none"), infer = TRUE)
ds_adj

#>  contrast            estimate   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  chg12 SP - chg12 UC    -5.37 1.42 485    -8.16    -2.58  -3.780  0.0002
#>  chg12 EP - chg12 UC    -9.02 1.44 492   -11.84    -6.20  -6.285 <0.0001
#> 
#> Results are averaged over the levels of: sex 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95

round(as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_adj))$sdcor, 3)

#> [1] 11.896  0.541 -0.235  5.620


The estimated differences in mean change hardly move (-5.37 and -9.02 mmHg against -5.38 and -8.97 unadjusted), as expected in a randomised trial. The covariates explain between-participant differences in level, so the random-intercept SD falls from 12.37 to 11.90 mmHg. Unlike in ANCOVA for a single follow-up (Module 3), the precision of the change contrast barely improves (standard errors 1.436 against 1.437 for EP), because a within-participant change is already free of the stable between-participant differences that the covariates explain. Module 6 discusses the interpretation of adjusted estimates.

title: 4  Linear mixed-effects models
text:
Summary
A linear mixed-effects model describes longitudinal data with a mean trajectory (the fixed effects), participant-specific departures from it (the random effects) and measurement-level noise (the residual error). A random intercept alone implies compound symmetry, one ICC for every pair of visits; adding a random slope lets the variance and correlation change with time, through \(V_i = Z_iGZ_i^\top + \sigma^2 I\). The coding of time decides what the intercept and arm coefficients mean: centring at month 12 turns the arm main effects into month-12 differences, categorical time removes all shape assumptions from the mean, and curvature can be added when a line is too simple. For WALK, the primary model with categorical time and a random slope on actual time uses all 360 participants and estimates a difference in mean change at month 12 of -5.4 mmHg for the standard programme and -9.0 mmHg for the enhanced programme compared with usual care, obtained with emmeans and reproduced exactly by nlme::lme. REML is the default estimation method because it corrects the downward bias of ML variance estimates; ML is needed for comparing fixed effects. Predicted random effects are shrunk toward the mean, much more for slopes than for intercepts, and that shrinkage is a feature, not a flaw.

title: 4  Linear mixed-effects models
text:
Further reading

Laird and Ware (1982) introduced the random-effects model for longitudinal data in the form used here.
Fitzmaurice et al. (2011), chapters on linear mixed effects models, give an applied account with many examples.
Verbeke and Molenberghs (2000) is the standard reference on linear mixed models for longitudinal data, including REML and BLUPs.
Pinheiro and Bates (2000) explains nlme and the theory of linear mixed models; Bates et al. (2015) describes lme4.
Barr et al. (2013) and Matuschek et al. (2017) discuss how to choose the random-effects structure.

title: 4  Linear mixed-effects models
text:
Exercises
Work through the Module 4 workbook (workbook/wb04-linear-mixed-models.qmd). The guided exercises fit the random-intercept and random-slope models, compute the ICC and implied correlations, centre time, obtain the primary estimand with emmeans and draw a shrinkage plot. The independent exercises look at the month-6 estimand, model comparison by ML, a smaller subset of the trial and the covariate-adjusted model. The practical assessment (assessments/pa04-linear-mixed-models.qmd) asks you to plan, fit and report a complete mixed-model analysis.

title: 5  Modelling covariance and choosing a model
text:
Learning outcomes
Repeated measurements on the same participant are correlated, and every longitudinal model makes an assumption about that correlation, whether or not the analyst states it. Module 4 introduced one way to describe it: random intercepts and slopes. This module looks at the covariance of the repeated measurements directly. You will meet the standard residual correlation structures (compound symmetry, autoregressive, continuous-time exponential and unstructured), see how random effects and residual correlation combine into a single marginal covariance matrix, and learn to compare candidate models with likelihood-ratio tests and information criteria. The covariance model is rarely the scientific target, but it decides how efficiently the data are used, whether the standard errors can be trusted, and whether an analysis that ignores dropout is valid under missing at random. The module ends with an argument that matters in practice: the most complicated covariance model is not automatically the most useful one.
By the end of this module participants will be able to:

text:
5.1 Describe compound symmetry, AR(1), continuous-time exponential correlation and unstructured covariance, and fit each with nlme::gls() or nlme::lme().
5.2 Model heterogeneous residual variances over time.
5.3 Derive and compute the marginal covariance implied by a combination of random effects and residual correlation, and compare it with the observed covariance.
5.4 Compare models with likelihood-ratio tests and information criteria, using REML only for models with the same fixed effects and ML for comparing fixed effects.
5.5 Recognise boundary problems, convergence failures and singular fits, and respond to them sensibly.
5.6 Justify a final covariance model using both statistical evidence and substantive judgement, not complexity for its own sake.

title: 5  Modelling covariance and choosing a model
text:
Prerequisites
Modules 1 and 3 (within-subject correlation, the limits of repeated-measures ANOVA and sphericity) and Module 4 (linear mixed-effects models, REML and ML). Matrix notation is used throughout, but every matrix is also written out for the WALK visit schedule.






WarningSimulated data



All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
crumbs: 5  Modelling covariance and choosing a model

title: 5  Modelling covariance and choosing a model
text:
5.1 Why the covariance model matters
The WALK trial randomised 360 participants to usual care (UC), a standard programme (SP) or an enhanced programme (EP) and measured systolic blood pressure (SBP) at months 0, 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12. The primary estimand, used in every module of this course, is the difference in mean change in SBP from baseline to month 12 between each programme and usual care. That is a statement about the mean. Why, then, spend a whole module on the covariance?
The quickest answer is a demonstration. Below, the same mean model (a separate mean for each arm at each scheduled visit, written visit_f * arm) is fitted twice with generalized least squares (nlme::gls()): once assuming that the six measurements on a participant are independent, and once allowing them to be correlated in the simplest possible way.

f_mean <- sbp ~ visit_f * arm
m_ind <- gls(f_mean, data = walk)
m_cs  <- gls(f_mean, data = walk, correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))

# difference in mean change baseline -> month 12, programme minus usual care
cells  <- expand.grid(visit_f = levels(walk$visit_f), arm = levels(walk$arm))
cell_w <- function(a, v) as.numeric(cells$arm == a & cells$visit_f == v)
chg12  <- function(a) cell_w(a, "12") - cell_w(a, "0")
L_dic  <- list("SP - UC" = chg12("SP") - chg12("UC"),
               "EP - UC" = chg12("EP") - chg12("UC"))

dic <- function(m) {
  e <- if (inherits(m, "gls")) emmeans(m, ~ visit_f * arm, mode = "df.error") else
    emmeans(m, ~ visit_f * arm)
  summary(contrast(e, L_dic), infer = TRUE)
}
dic(m_ind)

#>  contrast estimate   SE   df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  SP - UC     -5.80 2.55 1879    -10.8   -0.808  -2.279  0.0228
#>  EP - UC     -9.11 2.57 1879    -14.2   -4.062  -3.541  0.0004
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: df.error 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95

dic(m_cs)

#>  contrast estimate   SE   df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  SP - UC     -5.41 1.21 1878    -7.78    -3.04  -4.474 <0.0001
#>  EP - UC     -8.99 1.22 1878   -11.39    -6.59  -7.343 <0.0001
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: df.error 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95


The point estimates are close (-9.11 and -8.99 mmHg for EP versus UC), but the standard errors are not: 2.57 under independence and 1.22 with correlation. The independence model treats the month-12 and baseline measurements of one participant as if they came from different people, so it cannot see that much of the person-to-person variation in SBP cancels when we take a within-person change. Module 1 showed the same effect by simulation: ignoring positive correlation inflates standard errors for within-subject comparisons. The covariance model therefore matters for the estimand directly, because the estimand is a within-subject change.
There are three further reasons. First, when visits are missing the estimates of the means themselves depend on the covariance model, because the model uses each participant’s observed measurements to inform the missing ones. A likelihood-based analysis is valid under missing at random (MAR) only if the covariance model is approximately right (Module 10). Second, a covariance model that is too simple can give standard errors that are too small, and that is worse than standard errors that are too large. Third, the covariance often answers questions of its own: how stable is a participant’s blood pressure over a year, and how much of the variation is measurement error?

title: 5  Modelling covariance and choosing a model
section: 5.2 Looking at the observed covariance first
text:
5.2 Looking at the observed covariance first
Before fitting covariance models, look at the data. With a common visit schedule we can estimate the covariance between visits directly. One detail matters: SBP falls faster in the programme arms, so if we compute covariances of raw SBP across all participants, differences between the arm means inflate them. We therefore first remove the arm-by-visit means (the residuals from an ordinary least squares fit of visit_f * arm) and then compute the covariance of these residuals between visits, using all pairs of visits that a participant attended.

sched <- c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)
walk$res_ols <- residuals(lm(sbp ~ visit_f * arm, data = walk))
res_wide <- walk |>
  select(id, visit_f, res_ols) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit_f, values_from = res_ols) |>
  select(-id)
obs_cov <- cov(res_wide, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
obs_cor <- cov2cor(obs_cov)
round(obs_cov, 1)

#>        0     1     3     6     9    12
#> 0  175.8 149.9 132.5 120.0 126.3 118.1
#> 1  149.9 175.3 144.1 133.1 130.8 125.4
#> 3  132.5 144.1 171.1 130.3 128.3 125.1
#> 6  120.0 133.1 130.3 173.0 133.3 127.8
#> 9  126.3 130.8 128.3 133.3 174.3 145.0
#> 12 118.1 125.4 125.1 127.8 145.0 169.0

round(obs_cor, 2)

#>       0    1    3    6    9   12
#> 0  1.00 0.85 0.76 0.69 0.72 0.69
#> 1  0.85 1.00 0.83 0.76 0.75 0.73
#> 3  0.76 0.83 1.00 0.76 0.74 0.74
#> 6  0.69 0.76 0.76 1.00 0.77 0.75
#> 9  0.72 0.75 0.74 0.77 1.00 0.84
#> 12 0.69 0.73 0.74 0.75 0.84 1.00


Three features stand out, and each points to a component of a covariance model:

The variances are roughly constant, between 169 and 176 mmHg², so the standard deviation of SBP around the arm mean is about 13.2 mmHg at every visit. There is little sign of heterogeneous variances.
Every correlation is high, at least 0.69. Some participants have high blood pressure throughout the year and others low: a stable person-level component, which a random intercept describes.
Correlations decline with the time between visits, from 0.85 between months 0 and 1 to 0.69 between months 0 and 12, but they do not decline towards zero. They level off. Correlation that decays with time separation is called serial correlation. Correlation that levels off at a high value suggests serial correlation sitting on top of a stable person-level component.


mat_long <- function(M, label) {
  data.frame(row = factor(rep(rownames(M), ncol(M)), levels = rownames(M)),
             col = factor(rep(colnames(M), each = nrow(M)), levels = colnames(M)),
             value = as.vector(M), model = label)
}
ggplot(mat_long(obs_cor, "Observed"), aes(col, row, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", value)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F7FBFF", high = "#2171B5", limits = c(0.3, 1),
                      breaks = c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1), name = "Correlation") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Scheduled month") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm"))







Figure 5.1: Observed correlation between scheduled visits of SBP residuals (after removing arm-by-visit means). Correlations are high everywhere and fall slowly with the gap between visits.





This empirical summary is possible here because WALK has a fixed visit schedule and 360 participants. The pairwise-complete covariances use different subsets of participants for different cells, and under MAR dropout they are not unbiased estimates of the population covariances, so treat them as a guide rather than a gold standard. With irregular visit times and no schedule, the semivariogram introduced later plays the same role.
Because the data are simulated we know the truth, which is not possible with real data. WALK was generated with a random intercept (SD 11 mmHg), a random slope (SD 0.35 mmHg/month, correlation −0.25 with the intercept), a clinic effect (SD 3 mmHg), a serially correlated residual process (SD 5 mmHg, correlation \(\exp(-|\Delta t|/3)\) with \(\Delta t\) in months) and independent measurement error (SD 4 mmHg). The observed pattern matches that recipe: a large stable component plus serial correlation that fades over a few months, plus noise.

title: 5  Modelling covariance and choosing a model
text:
5.3 Residual correlation structures
The first family of covariance models describes the correlation of the residuals directly, without random effects. These are sometimes called marginal or covariance-pattern models. They are fitted with nlme::gls().

5.3.1 The research question and estimand
The scientific question does not change: what is the difference in mean change in SBP from baseline to month 12 between each programme and usual care? The covariance structure is a means to that end. It also answers secondary descriptive questions, such as how quickly the correlation between two measurements of the same person fades as the time between them grows.


5.3.2 Data structure and outcome types
These models are for a continuous outcome measured repeatedly, assumed approximately normal given the covariates. Data are in long format, one row per observation, with a participant identifier and a time variable. Compound symmetry and unstructured models need no particular timing. AR(1) as used here needs a visit index (integer order of the measurements). The exponential structure uses actual measurement times and is the natural choice when visits are irregular, as they are in WALK (month differs from month_sched).


5.3.3 Intuition
Think of the \(n_i \times n_i\) covariance matrix of one participant’s measurements. A covariance structure is a rule that fills in that matrix with a few parameters.

Compound symmetry (CS): every pair of measurements has the same correlation \(\rho\), whatever the time between them. This is the pattern produced by a random intercept and nothing else, and it is the sphericity-type assumption behind repeated-measures ANOVA (Module 3).
First-order autoregressive, AR(1): correlation falls by a constant factor \(\rho\) with each step between visits, so visits \(k\) steps apart have correlation \(\rho^k\). Neighbours are strongly correlated; distant visits are almost uncorrelated.
Continuous-time exponential: correlation depends on the actual time gap \(|t_{ij} - t_{ik}|\) and decays as \(\exp(-|t_{ij}-t_{ik}|/\phi)\), where the range \(\phi\) is measured in months. A nugget adds independent measurement error, so that even two measurements taken on the same day are not perfectly correlated.
Unstructured (UN): every variance and every correlation is a separate parameter. Nothing is assumed except that the covariance matrix is the same for all participants with the same visits.



5.3.4 The model
All four models share the same form. For participant \(i\) with \(n_i\) observations,
\[
\mathbf{y}_i = X_i \boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon_i, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, R_i),
\]
where \(\mathbf{y}_i\) is the vector of SBP measurements, \(X_i\) is the fixed-effects design matrix (here indicators for each visit, arm and visit-by-arm combination), \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is the vector of fixed effects and \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i\) the vector of residual errors. There are no random effects, so the marginal covariance \(V_i\) equals the residual covariance \(R_i\). Write \(R_i = \sigma^2 C_i\), with \(\sigma^2\) the residual variance and \(C_i\) a correlation matrix. The structures differ only in \(C_i\). For measurements \(j\) and \(k\) of participant \(i\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{CS:}\quad & [C_i]_{jk} = \rho \quad (j \neq k) \\
\text{AR(1):}\quad & [C_i]_{jk} = \rho^{|j-k|} \\
\text{Exponential with nugget } c:\quad & [C_i]_{jk} = (1-c)\exp\!\left(-|t_{ij}-t_{ik}|/\phi\right) \quad (j \neq k) \\
\text{UN:}\quad & [R_i]_{jk} = \sigma_{jk}, \text{ a separate parameter for each pair, with } \sigma_{jj} = \sigma_j^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\rho\) is a correlation parameter, \(|j-k|\) is the number of visits between two measurements, \(t_{ij}\) is the actual time of occasion \(j\), \(\phi > 0\) is the range (larger means slower decay) and \(0 \le c < 1\) is the nugget, the proportion of the residual variance that is uncorrelated measurement error. With six scheduled visits CS and AR(1) have one correlation parameter, the exponential has two, and UN has \(6 + 15 = 21\) variance and covariance parameters.
To see what the structures say for WALK, take a participant measured exactly on schedule (months 0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12). AR(1) by visit index gives months 0 and 1 the same correlation \(\rho\) as months 9 and 12, even though the second gap is three times longer. The exponential structure uses the actual gaps, so \(C_{12} = (1-c)e^{-1/\phi}\) for months 0 and 1 but \(C_{56} = (1-c)e^{-3/\phi}\) for months 9 and 12.


5.3.5 Assumptions and limitations
All four assume that the mean model is correct, that the residuals are normally distributed (estimates of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) are fairly insensitive to this, but prediction intervals are not), and that the same covariance applies to every participant (or every participant in a group, if you let it vary by arm). CS assumes correlation does not depend on the time gap, which is rarely true for long follow-up. AR(1) by visit index ignores unequal spacing; AR(1) correlations also fall towards zero, which contradicts the stable person-level component seen in most human data. The exponential structure without a random intercept has the same problem, which it can only escape by estimating a very long range. UN is the most flexible but needs a common set of scheduled visits, uses many parameters (it grows as \(n(n+1)/2\)), can fail to converge with few participants per visit, and says nothing about times between the scheduled visits.


5.3.6 Fitting the model in R
gls() takes the mean model as a formula, a correlation argument for \(C_i\) and a weights argument for heterogeneous variances (next section). Inside the correlation constructors, the formula ~ time | group names the time (or order) variable and the grouping variable.

m_ar1 <- gls(f_mean, data = walk,
             correlation = corAR1(form = ~ visit | id))          # visit index 1-6
m_exp <- gls(f_mean, data = walk,
             correlation = corExp(form = ~ month | id, nugget = TRUE))
m_un  <- gls(f_mean, data = walk,
             correlation = corSymm(form = ~ visit | id),         # free correlations
             weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit_f))           # free variances

Three details are easy to get wrong. corAR1() needs an integer position variable, so we use visit (1 to 6), not month. If a participant misses visit 3, visit still tells nlme that visits 2 and 4 are two steps apart. corSymm() needs the same integer index so that it knows which correlation belongs to which pair of visits. corExp() takes the actual times (month), so unequal and irregular spacing is used exactly. All models are fitted by REML, the default in gls(), which is appropriate because they share the same fixed effects.


5.3.7 Interpreting the output
The summary of a gls fit has three parts: the information criteria, the estimated correlation parameters, and the fixed effects. Here is the exponential model, with the long correlation matrix of the estimates suppressed.

s_exp <- summary(m_exp)
s_exp$modelStruct

#> corStruct  parameters:
#>  range nugget 
#>  4.102 -1.857

c(sigma = m_exp$sigma, logLik = logLik(m_exp), AIC = AIC(m_exp), BIC = BIC(m_exp))

#>    sigma   logLik      AIC      BIC 
#>    13.48 -6612.56 13267.12 13383.43










Output line
What it means
Value here




range
\(\hat\phi\): months over which the correlated part decays by a factor \(e\)
60.4 months


nugget
\(\hat c\): share of residual variance that is uncorrelated noise
0.135


sigma
\(\hat\sigma\): residual SD (here the total SD, as there are no random effects)
13.48 mmHg


implied correlation, 1 month apart
\((1-\hat c)e^{-1/\hat\phi}\)
0.85


implied correlation, 12 months apart
\((1-\hat c)e^{-12/\hat\phi}\)
0.71



The estimated range of about 60 months may look strange when the true serial process decays over 3 months. It is not an error. Without a random intercept, the exponential structure has to produce correlations that stay around 0.7 over a year, and the only way it can do so is with a very slow decay. The single exponential is absorbing both the stable person-level component and the short-term serial component. We return to this when random effects and serial correlation are combined.
For the other structures the key numbers are the CS correlation \(\hat\rho = 0.79\) and the AR(1) correlation between adjacent visits \(\hat\rho = 0.83\). The AR(1) model therefore implies a correlation of \(0.83^5 = 0.39\) between baseline and month 12, far below the observed 0.69. The unstructured model returns 15 correlations and 6 variances, too many to read one by one, so we compare its implied matrix with the observed one graphically below.
The fixed effects are the arm-by-visit means; the estimand is a combination of them, computed with emmeans as in the first section. All structures give a similar difference in mean change, with different standard errors:

bind_rows(lapply(list(Independence = m_ind, CS = m_cs, `AR(1)` = m_ar1,
                      Exponential = m_exp, Unstructured = m_un),
                 function(m) as.data.frame(dic(m))[, c("contrast", "estimate", "SE")]),
          .id = "structure")

#>       structure contrast estimate    SE
#> 1  Independence  SP - UC   -5.802 2.546
#> 2  Independence  EP - UC   -9.106 2.572
#> 3            CS  SP - UC   -5.409 1.209
#> 4            CS  EP - UC   -8.990 1.224
#> 5         AR(1)  SP - UC   -5.386 2.001
#> 6         AR(1)  EP - UC   -9.087 2.017
#> 7   Exponential  SP - UC   -5.426 1.422
#> 8   Exponential  EP - UC   -8.985 1.438
#> 9  Unstructured  SP - UC   -5.453 1.343
#> 10 Unstructured  EP - UC   -9.044 1.358




5.3.8 Checking the model
The most direct check for a scheduled design is to compare the correlation matrix implied by each model with the observed one. The function below computes the implied marginal covariance at the scheduled months for any gls or lme fit. It is written out by hand so that the formula \(V = ZGZ^\top + \sigma^2 S C S\) is visible (\(S\) is a diagonal matrix of standard-deviation ratios, introduced in the next section). Note that nlme stores corAR1() objects with class corARMA.

implied_cov <- function(model, times = sched) {
  k <- length(times); C <- diag(k)
  cs <- model$modelStruct$corStruct
  if (!is.null(cs)) {
    if (inherits(cs, "corCompSymm")) {
      C <- matrix(coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE), k, k); diag(C) <- 1
    } else if (inherits(cs, c("corAR1", "corARMA"))) {
      C <- coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE)^abs(outer(1:k, 1:k, "-"))
    } else if (inherits(cs, "corExp")) {
      p <- coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE)
      nug <- if ("nugget" %in% names(p)) p[["nugget"]] else 0
      C <- (1 - nug) * exp(-abs(outer(times, times, "-")) / p[["range"]])
      diag(C) <- 1
    } else if (inherits(cs, "corSymm")) {
      C[lower.tri(C)] <- coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE)
      C <- C + t(C) - diag(k)
    }
  }
  vs <- model$modelStruct$varStruct
  s <- if (is.null(vs)) rep(1, k) else
    coef(vs, unconstrained = FALSE, allCoef = TRUE)[as.character(times)]
  V <- model$sigma^2 * diag(s) %*% C %*% diag(s)          # R_i
  if (inherits(model, "lme")) {                              # + Z G Z'
    G <- as.matrix(getVarCov(model))
    Z <- cbind(1, times)[, seq_len(ncol(G)), drop = FALSE]
    V <- Z %*% G %*% t(Z) + V
  }
  dimnames(V) <- list(times, times)
  V
}
round(cov2cor(implied_cov(m_ar1)), 2)

#>       0    1    3    6    9   12
#> 0  1.00 0.83 0.69 0.57 0.47 0.39
#> 1  0.83 1.00 0.83 0.69 0.57 0.47
#> 3  0.69 0.83 1.00 0.83 0.69 0.57
#> 6  0.57 0.69 0.83 1.00 0.83 0.69
#> 9  0.47 0.57 0.69 0.83 1.00 0.83
#> 12 0.39 0.47 0.57 0.69 0.83 1.00


Figure 5.2 places the observed correlation matrix next to the matrices implied by the four structures. CS gets the overall level right but misses the decline with lag. AR(1) by visit index decays far too fast. The exponential model with a nugget follows the decline well, and the unstructured model reproduces the observed matrix closely (it should: it has a parameter for every cell), although even UN is not identical to the pairwise-complete matrix, because the likelihood uses the information from incomplete participants differently.

heat_gls <- bind_rows(
  mat_long(obs_cor, "Observed"),
  mat_long(cov2cor(implied_cov(m_cs)),  "Compound symmetry"),
  mat_long(cov2cor(implied_cov(m_ar1)), "AR(1) by visit"),
  mat_long(cov2cor(implied_cov(m_exp)), "Exponential + nugget"),
  mat_long(cov2cor(implied_cov(m_un)),  "Unstructured")) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = unique(model)))
plot_heat <- function(d, ncol = 5) {
  ggplot(d, aes(col, row, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", value)), size = 2.2) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F7FBFF", high = "#2171B5", limits = c(0.3, 1),
                        breaks = c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1), name = "Correlation") +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
    facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = ncol) +
    labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Scheduled month") +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm"),
          axis.text = element_text(size = 7))
}
plot_heat(heat_gls)







Figure 5.2: Observed correlation of SBP residuals between scheduled visits and the correlation implied by four residual correlation structures fitted with gls (REML).





Two further checks are useful. Normalized residuals (residuals(m, type = "normalized")) should look like uncorrelated noise with constant variance if the covariance model is right; plot them against time and fitted values. And the semivariogram, shown later, checks serial correlation when the times are irregular.


5.3.9 Reporting
State the structure, why it was chosen, and its estimated parameters. A methods paragraph might read:






TipReporting example



SBP was analysed with a generalized least squares model with a separate mean for each arm at each scheduled visit. The within-participant correlation was modelled with a continuous-time exponential structure in actual months since randomisation, with a nugget for measurement error, fitted by REML. The estimated range was 60.4 months and the nugget 0.14, implying correlations of 0.85 between measurements one month apart and 0.71 between measurements twelve months apart. The difference in mean change from baseline to month 12 was -9.0 (-11.8 to -6.2) mmHg for the enhanced programme versus usual care.




5.3.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Using corAR1(form = ~ month | id) with non-integer times. AR(1) needs an integer order; with irregular times use corExp() (or corCAR1()) on actual time.
Using corSymm() without an index. corSymm(form = ~ 1 | id) assumes each participant’s rows are in visit order with no gaps. With missed visits the correlations are then attached to the wrong pairs. Always give ~ visit | id.
Computing the observed covariance on raw outcomes. Differences between group means inflate covariances; remove the mean model first.
Reading AR(1) by visit as a continuous-time model. With unequal spacing (1, 2, 3, 3, 3 months in WALK) the same parameter is applied to gaps of different lengths.
Treating the unstructured model as automatically correct. It is flexible but costly in parameters, fragile with small samples, and cannot interpolate between scheduled times.

title: 5  Modelling covariance and choosing a model
text:
5.4 Heterogeneous residual variances

5.4.1 The research question and estimand
The estimand is unchanged. The question here is narrower: does the variability of SBP around the arm mean change over follow-up? In many studies it does. Variance can grow as participants diverge in their response to treatment, or shrink after a run-in period removes the most variable participants. Getting the variances wrong mainly affects the standard errors of visit-specific contrasts and the weight each visit gets.


5.4.2 Data structure and outcome types
As before: a continuous outcome in long format. Heterogeneous variances by visit need a variable that defines the variance strata, here the scheduled visit visit_f. Variances can also differ by arm or depend on a continuous covariate.


5.4.3 Intuition
Instead of one residual variance \(\sigma^2\), allow a different variance at each scheduled visit. The correlations stay as before; only the diagonal of the covariance matrix changes. It is a stretching of each row and column of the matrix.


5.4.4 The model
\[
R_i = \sigma^2\, S_i C_i S_i, \qquad S_i = \operatorname{diag}(\delta_{v(i1)}, \dots, \delta_{v(in_i)}),
\]
where \(\sigma^2\) is the residual variance at the reference visit (baseline), \(\delta_v\) is the ratio of the residual standard deviation at visit \(v\) to that at baseline (\(\delta_{0} = 1\)), \(v(ij)\) is the scheduled visit of observation \(j\), and \(C_i\) is any correlation structure from the previous section. The variance at visit \(v\) is \(\sigma^2\delta_v^2\). With six visits this adds five parameters. Combined with corSymm() it gives the fully unstructured covariance.


5.4.5 Assumptions and limitations
The variance ratios are assumed common to all participants. The ratios are estimated from the participants seen at each visit, so with MAR dropout they rely on the model being right in the same way as the means. Each extra parameter costs information; with six visits and 360 participants that is cheap, but with many visits it may not be.


5.4.6 Fitting the model in R

m_cs_het <- gls(f_mean, data = walk,
                correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id),
                weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit_f))

varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit_f) estimates one SD ratio per level of visit_f. Other variance functions exist (varPower(), varExp(), varIdent(form = ~ 1 | arm)), and they combine with varComb(); Pinheiro and Bates (2000) describe them.


5.4.7 Interpreting the output

coef(m_cs_het$modelStruct$varStruct, unconstrained = FALSE, allCoef = TRUE)

#>      0      1      3      6      9     12 
#> 1.0000 0.9992 1.0090 1.0432 1.0317 1.0294

m_cs_het$sigma

#> [1] 13.29

het_lrt <- anova(m_cs, m_cs_het)
het_lrt

#>          Model df   AIC   BIC logLik   Test L.Ratio p-value
#> m_cs         1 20 13353 13464  -6656                       
#> m_cs_het     2 25 13360 13499  -6655 1 vs 2   2.639  0.7555


The ratios are all close to 1, between 0.999 and 1.043. The estimated residual SD at baseline is 13.29 mmHg, so the SD at month 12 is 13.29 × 1.029 = 13.69 mmHg. The likelihood-ratio test of the two REML fits (same mean model, so REML is legitimate) gives \(\chi^2 = 2.64\) on 5 degrees of freedom, p = 0.755, and AIC rises from 13352.8 to 13360.1. There is no evidence that the variance changes over follow-up, which agrees with the observed variances and with the simulation, where every visit has the same variance apart from the small contribution of the random slope.


5.4.8 Checking the model
Plot the standard deviation of residuals by visit (or the square root of the diagonal of obs_cov). If you have fitted varIdent, the normalized residuals should have similar spread at every visit. A boxplot of residuals(m_cs_het, type = "normalized") by visit_f does this.


5.4.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Allowing a separate residual variance at each scheduled visit did not improve the fit (likelihood-ratio test on REML fits, \(\chi^2_{5} = 2.64\), p = 0.755; estimated SD ratios relative to baseline 1.00 to 1.04), so a common residual variance was retained.




5.4.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Comparing the sigma of a varIdent model with that of a homogeneous model. With varIdent, sigma is the SD at the reference level only.
Using weights = ~ visit_f. In gls() a one-sided formula in weights means varFixed() (variance proportional to the covariate). Use varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit_f).
Adding heterogeneity without looking. Check whether residual SDs actually differ before spending parameters.
