1.76



For a given participant on placebo, the odds of moderate or severe itch are multiplied by 0.909 each week. On active treatment they are multiplied by a further 0.878 per week (95% CI 0.804 to 0.960). Over 12 weeks, a participant on active treatment has odds of itch 0.21 times those of a participant on placebo with the same random intercept and the same baseline odds (95% CI 0.07 to 0.61).
The random-intercept SD of 1.76 is large on the logit scale. Two participants one SD apart in their random intercepts differ in their odds of itch by a factor \(e^{1.76} \approx 5.8\) at every visit. Another way to express this is the latent-scale ICC, \(\tau_0^2 / (\tau_0^2 + \pi^2/3)\), which treats the binary outcome as a dichotomised continuous latent variable with logistic residuals of variance \(\pi^2/3\): here 0.49. About 49% of the latent variation in itch propensity is between participants.
Comparison with the truth. Because the data are simulated, we can compare with the generating values. The unadjusted model above omits age and sex, which the generating model includes, so its intercept refers to an average mix of ages and sexes and its random-intercept variance absorbs some of their effect. A model with the same covariates as the truth (age centred at 45 and in units of 10 years) gives directly comparable estimates.

glmm_adj <- glmer(itch ~ week * arm + age45 + sex + (1 | id), data = clear,
                  family = binomial, nAGQ = 25)
truth_tab <- data.frame(
  truth = c(-truth_clear$cuts[2], truth_clear$beta_week, truth_clear$beta_trtweek,
            truth_clear$beta_age, truth_clear$beta_female, truth_clear$sd_b),
  estimate = c(fixef(glmm_adj)[c("(Intercept)", "week", "week:armActive",
                                 "age45", "sexFemale")],
               attr(VarCorr(glmm_adj)$id, "stddev")),
  se = c(sqrt(diag(as.matrix(vcov(glmm_adj))))[c("(Intercept)", "week",
                                                  "week:armActive", "age45",
                                                  "sexFemale")], NA),
  row.names = c("(Intercept)", "week", "week:armActive", "age45", "sexFemale",
                "SD random intercept"))
round(truth_tab, 3)

#>                     truth estimate    se
#> (Intercept)          0.00    0.200 0.306
#> week                -0.06   -0.096 0.029
#> week:armActive      -0.16   -0.131 0.045
#> age45                0.20    0.207 0.119
#> sexFemale            0.30   -0.134 0.312
#> SD random intercept  2.00    1.744    NA


Every fixed effect is within 1.5 standard errors of its true value (the largest discrepancy is for female sex, 1.4 standard errors). The estimated weekly slope on placebo (-0.096) is somewhat steeper than the truth (−0.06), the interaction (-0.131) somewhat smaller in magnitude than −0.16, and the random-intercept SD (1.74) a little below 2.0. These are the kinds of differences that sampling variation produces in a trial of 200 participants; they are not biases of the method.


8.2.8 Checking the model
Residuals of binary data are hard to read directly, because each observation is 0 or 1. The DHARMa package simulates many new datasets from the fitted model, and for each observation computes where the observed value falls within its simulated distribution (Hartig 2026). If the model is right, these scaled residuals are uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, whatever the outcome type, and they can be plotted and tested like ordinary residuals. Since version 0.5.0, DHARMa simulates by default conditionally on the fitted random effects, so the residuals check the observation-level part of the model given each participant’s estimated random effect; that suits the observation-level checks below. For checks aggregated by participant (for example recalculateResiduals(res, group = clear$id) followed by a dispersion test), simulate unconditionally with simulateResiduals(fit, simulateREs = "unconditional"), so that new random effects are drawn in each simulation. With conditional simulation such grouped tests reject correctly specified GLMMs far too often; Module 11 investigates this.

res_clear <- simulateResiduals(glmm_clear, n = 1000, seed = 8)
plot(res_clear, quantreg = FALSE)







Figure 8.1: DHARMa simulation-based residuals for the CLEAR logistic GLMM. Left: QQ plot of the scaled residuals against the uniform distribution, with tests of uniformity, dispersion and outliers. Right: scaled residuals against the rank-transformed model predictions.





The QQ plot follows the diagonal. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of uniformity gives p = 0.178, and the dispersion test (ratio 1.01, p = 0.456) shows no sign of over- or underdispersion. (For binary data, overdispersion at the observation level cannot exist; DHARMa’s dispersion test is still useful because it detects misspecification of the random-effects part.) It is also worth plotting the residuals against week and arm to look for curvature in time:

data.frame(week = factor(clear$week), arm = clear$arm,
           r = residuals(res_clear)) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, r, colour = arm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Scaled (DHARMa) residual")







Figure 8.2: DHARMa scaled residuals of the CLEAR GLMM by scheduled week. Under a correct model each box should be centred on 0.5 with quartiles near 0.25 and 0.75.





The boxes are centred near 0.5 at all weeks in both arms, so the linear-in-week logit is adequate. A further check specific to GLMMs is the one already done: the stability of the estimates across quadrature settings.


8.2.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Moderate or severe itch (yes/no) was analysed with a logistic mixed model including week, arm and their interaction as fixed effects and a random intercept for each participant, fitted by maximum likelihood with adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (25 points; lme4::glmer). Results were stable across 5 to 25 quadrature points; the Laplace approximation gave a smaller random-intercept SD (1.67 against 1.76). For a given participant, the odds of itch decreased by a factor of 0.909 per week on placebo and by an additional factor of 0.878 per week on active treatment (95% CI 0.804 to 0.960). The between-participant SD of the log-odds was 1.76 (latent-scale ICC 0.49). Simulation-based residuals (DHARMa) showed no evidence of misfit.




8.2.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Interpreting GLMM odds ratios as population-average effects. They compare situations for the same participant. For the population, use marginal predictions or GEE.
Relying on the Laplace approximation for binary data with few observations per participant and a large random-effect variance without checking AGQ. Compare nAGQ = 1 with a larger value.
Comparing log-likelihoods across different nAGQ settings as if they were different models.
Reporting the intercept as “the baseline probability”. \(\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0)\) is the probability for a participant with \(b_{0i} = 0\), which is not the average probability in the population.
Ignoring the random-effect SD. It is a key result: it tells readers how heterogeneous participants are, and it drives the gap between conditional and marginal effects.

title: 8  Generalized linear mixed models
section: 8.3 Why logistic GLMM and GEE coefficients differ
text:
8.3 Why logistic GLMM and GEE coefficients differ

8.3.1 The research question and estimand
The GEE analysis of CLEAR in Module 7 gave a weekly log-odds slope on placebo of about −0.06 and an interaction of about −0.08; the GLMM gives about −0.10 and −0.13. Neither analysis is wrong. They estimate different quantities: the GEE coefficients describe the population-average (marginal) curve, the GLMM coefficients the subject-specific (conditional) curves. This section shows numerically how the two are related and when each is the right target (Zeger et al. 1988; Neuhaus et al. 1991).


8.3.2 Data structure and outcome types
The relationship below applies to binary outcomes with a logit link and a normally distributed random intercept. For a probit link there is an exact version; for a log link with a random intercept the slopes are identical and only the intercept differs; for an identity link the two coincide.


8.3.3 Intuition
Averaging changes the shape of curves on the logit scale. Imagine participants whose individual probability curves all have the same steep slope on the logit scale but are shifted left or right by their random intercepts. At any week, the population proportion is the average of their probabilities. Participants far from the middle have probabilities near 0 or 1 that barely change over time, so they dilute the average change. The averaged curve is therefore flatter than any individual curve, and the larger the spread of the random intercepts, the flatter it is.


8.3.4 The model
For a logistic random-intercept model with conditional coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta_C\) and random-intercept variance \(\tau_0^2\), the implied marginal probability is
\[
P(Y_{ij} = 1) = \int \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_C + b)\, \varphi(b; 0, \tau_0^2)\, db .
\]
This is not exactly a logistic function of \(\mathbf{x}_{ij}\), but it is very close to one with attenuated coefficients (Zeger et al. 1988):
\[
\boldsymbol\beta_M \approx \frac{\boldsymbol\beta_C}{\sqrt{1 + c^2 \tau_0^2}}, \qquad c^2 = \left(\frac{16\sqrt{3}}{15\pi}\right)^2 \approx 0.346 .
\]
The constant comes from approximating the logistic function by a normal distribution function. The attenuation factor depends only on the random-intercept variance: with \(\tau_0 = 1\) it is 0.86, with \(\tau_0 = 2\) it is 0.65. When \(\tau_0 = 0\) (no between-participant variation) marginal and conditional coefficients coincide.


8.3.5 Assumptions and limitations
The approximation assumes a normal random intercept and a logit link, and is accurate for moderate variances; for large variances or extreme probabilities, the exact integral should be used. With random slopes the attenuation depends on time, so a single factor no longer applies. The relationship holds for the true parameters; for estimates it holds approximately, because GEE and GLMM estimates are also subject to different sampling errors and, under MAR dropout, to different biases.


8.3.6 Fitting the model in R
We compute the approximate marginal coefficients from the GLMM, the exact marginal coefficients implied by the GLMM (by integrating numerically over the random intercept at the observed weeks and fitting the marginal logistic model to the resulting probabilities), the GEE estimates, and the corresponding true values. Numerical integration uses Gauss–Hermite quadrature, which approximates \(\int f(b)\varphi(b; 0, \tau_0^2)\,db\) by a weighted sum \(\sum_k (w_k/\sqrt{\pi}) f(\sqrt{2}\tau_0 x_k)\) over fixed nodes \(x_k\) and weights \(w_k\):

gauss_hermite <- function(n) {               # Golub-Welsch algorithm
  i <- seq_len(n - 1)
  J <- matrix(0, n, n); J[cbind(i, i + 1)] <- J[cbind(i + 1, i)] <- sqrt(i / 2)
  e <- eigen(J, symmetric = TRUE)
  list(x = e$values, w = sqrt(pi) * e$vectors[1, ]^2)
}
gh <- gauss_hermite(30)
marginal_p <- function(eta, sigma) {         # average of plogis(eta + b)
  sapply(eta, function(e) sum(gh$w / sqrt(pi) * plogis(e + sqrt(2) * sigma * gh$x)))
}
# check against simulation: P(Y = 1) when eta = 0.5 and SD = 2
set.seed(1)
c(quadrature = marginal_p(0.5, 2),
  simulation = mean(plogis(0.5 + rnorm(1e6, 0, 2))))

#> quadrature simulation 
#>     0.5752     0.5753



gee_clear <- geeglm(itch ~ week * arm, id = factor(id), waves = visit,
                    data = clear, family = binomial, corstr = "exchangeable")
atten <- 1 / sqrt(1 + 0.346 * sig^2)
grid <- expand.grid(week = truth_clear$weeks,
                    arm = factor(c("Placebo", "Active"), levels = c("Placebo", "Active")))
X <- model.matrix(~ week * arm, grid)
grid$p_marg <- marginal_p(X %*% fc, sig)
implied <- coef(suppressWarnings(glm(p_marg ~ week * arm, family = binomial, data = grid)))
true_c <- c(0, truth_clear$beta_week, 0, truth_clear$beta_trtweek)
atten_tab <- data.frame(
  glmm_conditional = fc,
  approx_marginal = fc * atten,
  exact_marginal = implied,
  gee = coef(gee_clear),
  truth_conditional = true_c,
  truth_approx_marginal = true_c / sqrt(1 + 0.346 * truth_clear$sd_b^2))
round(atten_tab, 4)

#>                glmm_conditional approx_marginal exact_marginal     gee
#> (Intercept)              0.1331          0.0924         0.0875  0.0849
#> week                    -0.0959         -0.0666        -0.0628 -0.0634
#> armActive               -0.1128         -0.0784        -0.0637 -0.0634
#> week:armActive          -0.1299         -0.0902        -0.0895 -0.0844
#>                truth_conditional truth_approx_marginal
#> (Intercept)                 0.00                0.0000
#> week                       -0.06               -0.0389
#> armActive                   0.00                0.0000
#> week:armActive             -0.16               -0.1036


geeglm is fitted exactly as in Module 7 (sorted data, id = factor(id), exchangeable working correlation).


8.3.7 Interpreting the output
With \(\hat\tau_0\) = 1.76, the attenuation factor is \(1/\sqrt{1 + 0.346 \times 3.10}\) = 0.695. Multiplying the GLMM’s placebo slope (-0.0959) by this factor gives -0.0666, the exact integration gives -0.0628, and GEE estimates -0.0634. For the interaction the three numbers are -0.0902, -0.0895 and -0.0844, against the conditional -0.1299. The approximation is close to the exact integral, and both are close to GEE. The two methods agree once we recognise that they estimate different things.
For the truth, the attenuation factor with \(\tau_0 = 2\) is 0.648, so the true conditional slopes of −0.06 and −0.16 correspond to marginal slopes of about -0.039 and -0.104. Module 7 computed the true marginal coefficients exactly (integrating also over age and sex) as about −0.036 and −0.100. The GEE estimates (-0.063 and -0.084) are compared with these marginal values, and the GLMM estimates (-0.096 and -0.130) with −0.06 and −0.16. Comparing a GEE estimate with a conditional true value, or a GLMM estimate with a marginal one, would wrongly suggest bias.

wk <- seq(0, 12, by = 0.25)
arms <- factor(c("Placebo", "Active"), levels = c("Placebo", "Active"))
curves <- expand.grid(week = wk, b = qnorm(c(0.05, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 0.95)) * sig,
                      arm = arms)
curves$p <- plogis(model.matrix(~ week * arm, curves) %*% fc + curves$b)
avg <- expand.grid(week = wk, arm = arms)
Xa <- model.matrix(~ week * arm, avg)
avg$`Participant with b = 0` <- plogis(Xa %*% fc)
avg$`Population average` <- marginal_p(Xa %*% fc, sig)
avg_long <- pivot_longer(avg, -c(week, arm), names_to = "curve", values_to = "p")
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(week, p, group = b), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = avg_long, aes(week, p, linetype = curve), colour = "#222222",
            linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Probability of moderate or severe itch", linetype = NULL)







Figure 8.3: Conditional and marginal probability curves from the CLEAR logistic GLMM. Grey lines are individual curves for participants at the 5th, 15th, 30th, 50th, 70th, 85th and 95th percentiles of the random-intercept distribution. The solid line is the curve of a participant with random intercept 0; the dashed line is the population average, obtained by integrating over the random intercepts. The population-average curve is flatter than the individual curves.





The figure makes the mechanism visible. On active treatment, the curve for a participant with \(b_{0i} = 0\) falls from about 0.51 to 0.06 over 12 weeks; the population-average curve falls from 0.50 to 0.14. Participants at the extremes contribute probabilities near 0 or 1 that barely change.


8.3.8 Checking the model
The comparison is itself a check: if a GLMM’s implied marginal coefficients were far from the GEE estimates, that would suggest that one of the models is misspecified (for example, a non-normal random-effects distribution, a missing random slope, or MAR dropout biasing GEE). Here the agreement is good.


8.3.9 Reporting
When reporting a binary longitudinal analysis, say which kind of effect is reported, and do not compare effect sizes across studies that used different kinds. A sentence such as the following helps readers:






TipReporting example



Odds ratios from the mixed model are subject-specific: they compare the odds of itch for the same participant under different conditions. Population-average odds ratios, which compare proportions in the treated and untreated populations, are smaller in magnitude; the population-average odds ratio for the additional weekly change on active treatment implied by the mixed model was 0.914 (GEE estimate 0.919), compared with the subject-specific 0.878.


Which is the right target? Use the population-average effect when the question concerns populations: public-health impact, the proportion of patients who will respond, regulatory endpoints defined as proportions. Use the subject-specific effect when the question concerns change within individuals, when individual predictions are needed, or when the model is a step towards understanding mechanisms. In a randomised trial both are valid summaries of the treatment effect, but they are different numbers, and the estimand should be stated in the protocol. A practical advantage of the GLMM is that it gives both: conditional coefficients directly and marginal summaries by integration (next section), and it is valid under MAR dropout.


8.3.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Calling the difference between GLMM and GEE odds ratios “bias”. They estimate different parameters.
Comparing a GLMM estimate with a published population-average effect (or the reverse) without converting.
Using the attenuation formula with random slopes, where the attenuation varies over time.
Forgetting that the attenuation depends on \(\tau_0^2\): adding covariates that explain between-participant variation changes the conditional coefficients of other variables in a logistic GLMM, even in a randomised trial.

title: 8  Generalized linear mixed models
section: 8.4 Predicted probabilities and interpretable effect summaries
text:
8.4 Predicted probabilities and interpretable effect summaries

8.4.1 The research question and estimand
Odds ratios are hard to communicate. Readers want to know: what proportion of patients will have moderate or severe itch at week 12 on each treatment, and how many fewer per 100 on active treatment? Two kinds of prediction answer different versions of this question. The conditional prediction at \(b_{0i} = 0\) is the probability for a “typical” participant (one with a random intercept of zero, the median participant). The marginal (population-averaged) prediction is the proportion in the population, the average of the individual probabilities. Effect summaries such as risk differences and risk ratios are usually wanted on the marginal scale.


8.4.2 Data structure and outcome types
The same CLEAR data and the fitted GLMM glmm_clear. The approach extends to any GLMM: for a log link the marginal mean has a closed form (below); for a logit link it requires numerical integration.


8.4.3 Intuition
The conditional prediction plugs \(b_{0i} = 0\) into the inverse link. The marginal prediction averages the inverse link over all values of \(b_{0i}\), weighted by their normal density. Because the inverse logit is S-shaped, the average is pulled towards 0.5 compared with the value at \(b_{0i} = 0\). Uncertainty comes from two sources: the fixed effects and the random-effect SD, both estimated.


8.4.4 The model
\[
p^{C}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta),
\qquad
p^{M}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + b)\,\varphi(b; 0, \tau_0^2)\,db ,
\]
and the marginal risk difference at week 12 is \(p^M(\mathbf{x}_{\text{Active},12}) - p^M(\mathbf{x}_{\text{Placebo},12})\). For uncertainty we draw \((\tau_0, \boldsymbol\beta)\) many times from their approximate joint sampling distribution (a multivariate normal centred at the estimates with the inverse-Hessian covariance), compute the marginal quantities for each draw, and take percentiles. This is a simulation version of the delta method. A parametric bootstrap (simulate new datasets from the fitted model, refit, recompute) is the more thorough alternative and accounts for non-normality of the estimates; it is shown at the end of this section but not run, because 1,000 refits with 25 quadrature points take several minutes.


8.4.5 Assumptions and limitations
The simulation approach relies on approximate normality of \((\hat\tau_0, \hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\), which is reasonable here (200 participants, \(\hat\tau_0\) far from zero) but can fail when the random-effect variance is near zero. Predictions refer to the covariate values chosen; for an unadjusted model in a randomised trial these are just arm and week.


8.4.6 Fitting the model in R
Conditional predictions with delta-method intervals come directly from emmeans:

emm_cond <- emmeans(glmm_clear, ~ arm | week, at = list(week = c(0, 12)),
                    type = "response")
emm_cond

#> week =  0:
#>  arm       prob     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo 0.5332 0.0631 Inf    0.4101     0.652
#>  Active  0.5051 0.0650 Inf    0.3801     0.629
#> 
#> week = 12:
#>  arm       prob     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo 0.2655 0.0596 Inf    0.1657     0.397
#>  Active  0.0636 0.0215 Inf    0.0324     0.121
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95 
#> Intervals are back-transformed from the logit scale


For the marginal predictions we need the joint covariance of \(\hat\tau_0\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). When glmer uses quadrature, its final optimisation is over \((\theta, \boldsymbol\beta)\) together, where \(\theta\) is the random-intercept SD (for a single random intercept, \(\theta = \tau_0\)), and it stores the Hessian of the deviance (\(-2\log L\)). Twice its inverse is the covariance matrix; its \(\boldsymbol\beta\) block reproduces vcov():

H <- glmm_clear@optinfo$derivs$Hessian
V_joint <- 2 * solve(H)
max(abs(V_joint[-1, -1] - as.matrix(vcov(glmm_clear))))   # beta block matches

#> [1] 1.735e-18

sqrt(V_joint[1, 1])                                         # SE of tau_0

#> [1] 0.1772



set.seed(808)
draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(4000, mu = c(getME(glmm_clear, "theta"), fc), Sigma = V_joint)
pg <- expand.grid(arm = factor(c("Placebo", "Active"), levels = c("Placebo", "Active")),
                  week = c(0, 12))
Xp <- model.matrix(~ week * arm, pg)
marg_draws <- apply(draws, 1, function(d) marginal_p(Xp %*% d[-1], abs(d[1])))
cond_draws <- apply(draws, 1, function(d) plogis(Xp %*% d[-1]))
pg$conditional <- plogis(Xp %*% fc)
pg$marginal <- marginal_p(Xp %*% fc, sig)
pg$marg_lower <- apply(marg_draws, 1, quantile, 0.025)
pg$marg_upper <- apply(marg_draws, 1, quantile, 0.975)
pg |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !week, \(x) round(x, 3)))

#>       arm week conditional marginal marg_lower marg_upper
#> 1 Placebo    0       0.533    0.522      0.438      0.600
#> 2  Active    0       0.505    0.503      0.422      0.585
#> 3 Placebo   12       0.265    0.339      0.255      0.431
#> 4  Active   12       0.064    0.139      0.087      0.210

# week-12 effect summaries on the marginal scale (rows 3 = Placebo, 4 = Active)
summ <- function(x) c(estimate = x[1], quantile(x[-1], c(0.025, 0.975)))
eff <- rbind(
  risk_difference = summ(c(pg$marginal[4] - pg$marginal[3],
                           marg_draws[4, ] - marg_draws[3, ])),
  risk_ratio = summ(c(pg$marginal[4] / pg$marginal[3],
                      marg_draws[4, ] / marg_draws[3, ])),
  odds_ratio_marginal = summ(c(exp(qlogis(pg$marginal[4]) - qlogis(pg$marginal[3])),
                               exp(qlogis(marg_draws[4, ]) - qlogis(marg_draws[3, ])))),
  risk_difference_b0 = summ(c(pg$conditional[4] - pg$conditional[3],
                              cond_draws[4, ] - cond_draws[3, ])))
round(eff, 3)

#>                     estimate   2.5%  97.5%
#> risk_difference       -0.200 -0.303 -0.091
#> risk_ratio             0.409  0.244  0.673
#> odds_ratio_marginal    0.314  0.165  0.592
#> risk_difference_b0    -0.202 -0.333 -0.086


emmeans also offers an approximate marginal prediction through its bias adjustment, which uses a second-order Taylor expansion:

summary(regrid(emmeans(glmm_clear, ~ arm | week, at = list(week = c(0, 12))),
               bias.adjust = TRUE, sigma = sig))

#> week =  0:
#>  arm      prob     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo 0.508 0.0148 Inf     0.478     0.537
#>  Active  0.501 0.0146 Inf     0.472     0.530
#> 
#> week = 12:
#>  arm      prob     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo 0.407 0.0439 Inf     0.321     0.493
#>  Active  0.144 0.0430 Inf     0.060     0.228
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95




8.4.7 Interpreting the output
At week 12, a participant with a random intercept of zero has a probability of itch of 0.27 on placebo (95% CI 0.17 to 0.40) and 0.06 on active treatment (0.03 to 0.12). The population proportions are quite different: 0.34 (0.25 to 0.43) on placebo and 0.14 (0.09 to 0.21) on active treatment. The marginal proportions are pulled towards 0.5 because they average over participants with very high and very low propensities. They are close to the GEE estimates of Module 7 (about 0.34 and 0.15), as they should be.
The marginal risk difference at week 12 is -0.200 (95% interval -0.303 to -0.091): about 20 fewer people per 100 with moderate or severe itch if everyone were treated. The marginal risk ratio is 0.41 (0.24 to 0.67), and the marginal odds ratio 0.31 (0.17 to 0.59), against a conditional odds ratio at week 12 of 0.19. The risk difference for a participant with \(b_{0i} = 0\) is -0.202, which describes a median participant, not the population.
The emmeans bias adjustment gives 0.407 and 0.144 at week 12, against 0.339 and 0.139 by numerical integration. The second-order approximation works for active treatment, where the probability is low, but overstates the placebo proportion by 0.07. With a random-intercept SD as large as 1.76, a Taylor expansion around \(b_{0i} = 0\) is not accurate enough; numerical integration is exact up to the quadrature error and is just as easy once the function is written.


8.4.8 Checking the model
Check that predictions are consistent with the data: the marginal predicted proportions should be close to the observed proportions at visits where few participants are missing (week 0: observed 0.57 placebo, 0.52 active; predicted 0.52 and 0.50). At later visits, observed proportions are affected by dropout and the model-based marginal predictions are preferable. Check also that the simulation draws are numerous enough (re-running with another seed should change the intervals only in the third decimal place).
For a parametric bootstrap, lme4::bootMer() simulates new outcomes from the fitted model, refits, and applies a function to each refit. The code below is not run in these notes because of its run time:

marg_rd <- function(m) {
  b <- fixef(m); s <- getME(m, "theta")
  p <- marginal_p(Xp %*% b, s)
  p[4] - p[3]                                # marginal risk difference, week 12
}
boot_rd <- bootMer(glmm_clear, marg_rd, nsim = 1000, seed = 1)
quantile(boot_rd$t, c(0.025, 0.975))



8.4.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Population-averaged probabilities were obtained from the mixed model by integrating over the random-intercept distribution (Gauss–Hermite quadrature), with 95% intervals from 4,000 draws from the approximate joint sampling distribution of the fixed effects and random-intercept SD. At week 12 the estimated proportion of participants with moderate or severe itch was 0.34 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.43) on placebo and 0.14 (0.09 to 0.21) on active treatment: a risk difference of -0.20 (-0.30 to -0.09) and a risk ratio of 0.41 (0.24 to 0.67).




8.4.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Presenting emmeans(..., type = "response") from a GLMM as population proportions. They are probabilities at \(b_{0i} = 0\).
Computing a marginal prediction by plugging the average random effect into the inverse link. The average of the inverse link is not the inverse link of the average.
Ignoring the uncertainty in the random-effect variance when computing marginal quantities; it contributes to their uncertainty.
Reporting only relative measures. Give absolute risks and risk differences as well.

title: 8  Generalized linear mixed models
section: 8.5 Count outcomes: Poisson and negative binomial GLMMs for DIARY
text:
8.5 Count outcomes: Poisson and negative binomial GLMMs for DIARY

8.5.1 The research question and estimand
Does the preventive treatment reduce the rate of migraine days, and by how much? The estimand is the ratio of the post-baseline to baseline migraine rate on active treatment divided by the same ratio on placebo (a ratio of rate ratios), and, for reporting, the expected number of migraine days per 28-day period in each arm.


8.5.2 Data structure and outcome types
DIARY has 1026 diary periods from 160 participants: a baseline period (0) and up to six 28-day treatment periods. The outcome migraine_days is a count; the exposure days (14 to 28) is the number of days with a completed diary. Counts are non-negative integers whose variance usually grows with the mean. 11% of periods have no migraine days.


8.5.3 Intuition
A Poisson GLMM says that, given a participant’s random intercept, their migraine days in a period follow a Poisson distribution with mean equal to (diary days) × (their personal rate). The random intercept allows some participants to have more migraines than others. The Poisson distribution forces the variance to equal the mean given the random intercept. Migraines cluster in time, so counts within a participant often vary more than that, which is overdispersion. The negative binomial (NB) distribution adds a parameter that lets the variance exceed the mean: in the nbinom2 parameterisation, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid b) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the size (dispersion) parameter.


8.5.4 The model
\[
\log E(Y_{ij} \mid b_{0i}) = \log(\text{days}_{ij}) + \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{post}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Active}_i + \beta_3 \text{post}_{ij}\text{Active}_i + b_{0i},
\qquad b_{0i} \sim N(0, \tau_0^2),
\]
with \(Y_{ij} \mid b_{0i}\) Poisson or negative binomial. \(\log(\text{days}_{ij})\) is the offset (a term with coefficient fixed at 1), so that \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the baseline migraine rate per diary day on placebo for a participant with \(b_{0i} = 0\), \(\exp(\beta_1)\) the placebo rate ratio after versus before baseline, \(\exp(\beta_2)\) the baseline rate ratio between arms (near 1 after randomisation), and \(\exp(\beta_3)\) the treatment effect (ratio of rate ratios), all within participant. For a log link with a random intercept, the conditional and marginal rate ratios are identical: \(E(Y_{ij}) = \exp(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta)\,E\{\exp(b_{0i})\} = \exp(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \tau_0^2/2)\), so only the intercept differs, by \(\tau_0^2/2\).
The DIARY data were generated from a negative binomial model of this form with \(\theta = 5\), \(\tau_0 = 0.55\), a baseline rate of 0.18 per diary day, \(\beta_1 = -0.10\) and \(\beta_3 = -0.40\), and no excess zeros (see the data dictionary).


8.5.5 Assumptions and limitations
The model assumes a constant rate within each phase (baseline, treatment) for each participant, independence of counts within participant given the random intercept, normally distributed random intercepts, and for the NB model a common dispersion parameter. Counts in DIARY cannot exceed the number of diary days, which neither distribution respects exactly, but rates are low enough for this to matter little. Dropout in DIARY is MCAR; under MAR, the likelihood-based GLMM remains valid.


8.5.6 Fitting the model in R

pois_glmm <- glmmTMB(migraine_days ~ post * arm + offset(log(days)) + (1 | id),
                     data = diary, family = poisson)
nb_glmm <- glmmTMB(migraine_days ~ post * arm + offset(log(days)) + (1 | id),
                   data = diary, family = nbinom2)
summary(nb_glmm)

#>  Family: nbinom2  ( log )
#> Formula:          migraine_days ~ post * arm + offset(log(days)) + (1 | id)
#> Data: diary
#> 
#>       AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
#>      4827      4857     -2408      4815      1020 
#> 
#> Random effects:
#> 
#> Conditional model:
#>  Groups Name        Variance Std.Dev.
#>  id     (Intercept) 0.27     0.519   
#> Number of obs: 1026, groups:  id, 160
#> 
#> Dispersion parameter for nbinom2 family (): 4.46 
#> 
#> Conditional model:
#>                Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)     -1.7126     0.0956  -17.92   <2e-16 ***
#> post            -0.1811     0.0832   -2.18     0.03 *  
#> armActive       -0.1141     0.1362   -0.84     0.40    
#> post:armActive  -0.1966     0.1196   -1.64     0.10    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Overdispersion. Two checks are common. The Pearson statistic divided by its residual degrees of freedom should be near 1 for a well-fitting Poisson model. DHARMa’s dispersion test compares the spread of the observed residuals with that of simulated ones.

pearson_ratio <- function(m) sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m)
res_pois <- simulateResiduals(pois_glmm, n = 1000, seed = 8)
res_nb <- simulateResiduals(nb_glmm, n = 1000, seed = 8)
disp <- data.frame(
  model = c("Poisson GLMM", "NB GLMM"),
  pearson_ratio = c(pearson_ratio(pois_glmm), pearson_ratio(nb_glmm)),
  dharma_dispersion = c(testDispersion(res_pois, plot = FALSE)$statistic,
                        testDispersion(res_nb, plot = FALSE)$statistic),
  p_dispersion = c(testDispersion(res_pois, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
                   testDispersion(res_nb, plot = FALSE)$p.value))
disp

#>          model pearson_ratio dharma_dispersion p_dispersion
#> 1 Poisson GLMM        1.5787             1.511        0.000
#> 2      NB GLMM        0.8489             1.145        0.112


Zero inflation. Zero-inflated models add a separate process that produces “structural” zeros (for example, people who cannot have the event). They should be considered only when there is a substantive reason for such a process, and tested against a model that already handles overdispersion. A Poisson model that cannot accommodate overdispersion will also under-predict zeros, so a zero-inflation test on a Poisson model mostly detects overdispersion.

zi <- data.frame(
  model = c("Poisson GLMM", "NB GLMM"),
  obs_to_sim_zeros = c(testZeroInflation(res_pois, plot = FALSE)$statistic,
                       testZeroInflation(res_nb, plot = FALSE)$statistic),
  p_value = c(testZeroInflation(res_pois, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
              testZeroInflation(res_nb, plot = FALSE)$p.value))
zi

#>          model obs_to_sim_zeros p_value
#> 1 Poisson GLMM            1.575   0.000
#> 2      NB GLMM            1.057   0.568

zinb_glmm <- glmmTMB(migraine_days ~ post * arm + offset(log(days)) + (1 | id),
                     ziformula = ~ 1, data = diary, family = nbinom2)
summary(zinb_glmm)$coefficients$zi

#>             Estimate Std. Error  z value Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)   -18.57       2036 -0.00912   0.9927
#> attr(,"ddf")
#> [1] "asymptotic"

data.frame(model = c("Poisson", "NB", "ZINB"),
           df = sapply(list(pois_glmm, nb_glmm, zinb_glmm), \(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
           logLik = sapply(list(pois_glmm, nb_glmm, zinb_glmm), \(m) as.numeric(logLik(m))),
           AIC = sapply(list(pois_glmm, nb_glmm, zinb_glmm), AIC))

#>     model df logLik  AIC
#> 1 Poisson  5  -2528 5065
#> 2      NB  6  -2408 4827
#> 3    ZINB  7  -2408 4829


Rate ratios and expected counts. emmeans with offset = log(28) gives expected counts in a full 28-day period. With type = "response" alone these are for a participant with \(b_{0i} = 0\); adding bias.adjust = TRUE with the random-intercept SD gives the population mean count, which for a log link is exactly \(\exp(\tau_0^2/2)\) times larger.

sig_nb <- attr(VarCorr(nb_glmm)$cond$id, "stddev")
fixef_table(nb_glmm, exponentiate = TRUE)

#>             term estimate      se  lower  upper         p
#> 1    (Intercept)   0.1804 0.09559 0.1496 0.2176 8.859e-72
#> 2           post   0.8344 0.08321 0.7088 0.9822 2.954e-02
#> 3      armActive   0.8922 0.13615 0.6832 1.1650 4.020e-01
#> 4 post:armActive   0.8215 0.11958 0.6499 1.0385 1.001e-01

emm_c <- emmeans(nb_glmm, ~ arm | post, offset = log(28), type = "response")
emm_m <- emmeans(nb_glmm, ~ arm | post, offset = log(28), type = "response",
                 bias.adjust = TRUE, sigma = sig_nb)
emm_c

#> post = 0:
#>  arm     response    SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo     5.05 0.483 Inf      4.19      6.09
#>  Active      4.51 0.438 Inf      3.73      5.45
#> 
#> post = 1:
#>  arm     response    SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo     4.21 0.288 Inf      3.69      4.82
#>  Active      3.09 0.216 Inf      2.69      3.54
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95 
#> Intervals are back-transformed from the log scale

emm_m

#> post = 0:
#>  arm     response    SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo     5.73 0.548 Inf      4.75      6.91
#>  Active      5.11 0.497 Inf      4.23      6.19
#> 
#> post = 1:
#>  arm     response    SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  Placebo     4.78 0.327 Inf      4.18      5.47
#>  Active      3.50 0.245 Inf      3.06      4.02
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95 
#> Intervals are back-transformed from the log scale 
#> Bias adjustment applied based on sigma = 0.51924

rr_int <- confint(contrast(emmeans(nb_glmm, ~ post * arm),
                           interaction = c("revpairwise", "revpairwise")),
                  type = "response")
rr_int

#>  post_revpairwise arm_revpairwise  ratio     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
#>  1 / 0            Active / Placebo 0.822 0.0982 Inf      0.65      1.04
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95 
#> Intervals are back-transformed from the log scale


The interaction contrast reproduces \(\exp(\hat\beta_3)\) and confirms which coefficient is the treatment effect.


8.5.7 Interpreting the output
Overdispersion. For the Poisson GLMM the Pearson ratio is 1.58 and the DHARMa dispersion ratio 1.51 (p < 0.001): even after allowing for differences between participants, the counts vary more than a Poisson model allows. For the NB GLMM the DHARMa ratio is 1.15 (p = 0.112), with no evidence of remaining overdispersion. (The NB Pearson ratio, 0.85, is less useful because the Pearson residuals already use the estimated NB variance.) The estimated NB size parameter is \(\hat\theta\) = 4.46 (truth 5). The NB model also fits much better: AIC 4827 against 5065.
Overdispersion matters for inference. The Poisson GLMM estimates the treatment effect as -0.227 with SE 0.080; the NB GLMM gives -0.197 with SE 0.120. The Poisson SE is too small because the model believes the counts are less variable than they are. The Poisson model would declare a “significant” effect (p = 0.005) that the NB model does not (p = 0.100).
Zero inflation. The DHARMa zero-inflation test on the Poisson model reports 1.57 times as many zeros as expected (p < 0.001), which looks like zero inflation. On the NB model the ratio is 1.06 (p = 0.568): once overdispersion is modelled, the zeros are as frequent as the model predicts. Fitting a zero-inflated NB model confirms this: the estimated zero-inflation log-odds is -18.6 (a probability of structural zeros indistinguishable from zero, with an enormous SE that signals the parameter is on the boundary), the log-likelihood is unchanged and the AIC is higher (4829). The truth has no excess zeros, so this is the right conclusion. Zero inflation should be tested against the NB model, and only when the subject matter suggests a structural-zero process.
Rate ratios. For a given participant, the migraine rate after baseline on placebo is 0.83 times the baseline rate (95% CI 0.71 to 0.98). On active treatment, the post-baseline rate relative to baseline is multiplied by a further 0.82 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.04): the reduction in rate attributable to treatment is about 18%, but the interval is wide and includes no effect. The true value, exp(−0.40) = 0.67, lies within the interval; the estimate is closer to 1 than the truth, which is within the range of sampling variation (the difference is about 1.7 standard errors). Because the link is log, the same rate ratio applies to the population mean: there is no attenuation for counts with a random intercept.
Expected counts. For a participant with \(b_{0i} = 0\), the expected migraine days per 28 days during treatment are 4.2 (placebo) and 3.1 (active). Averaged over participants they are 4.8 and 3.5, larger by the factor \(\exp(\hat\tau_0^2/2)\) = 1.144. The population means are the quantities to compare with GEE: the Module 7 GEE gave about 4.7 and 3.5. Note that the arm comparison of expected counts during treatment, 0.73, also includes the small baseline difference between arms; the treatment effect proper is the ratio of rate ratios.
Comparison with GEE. The Module 7 GEE treatment effect was -0.239 on the log scale (rate ratio 0.79), the NB GLMM gives -0.197 (0.82). For a log link both estimate the same parameter, and the difference reflects different weighting of the data. The intercepts differ as expected: GLMM -1.713, plus \(\hat\tau_0^2/2\) = 0.135 gives -1.578, close to GEE’s -1.620.


8.5.8 Checking the model

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plotQQunif(res_pois, testDispersion = TRUE, testOutliers = FALSE)
plotResiduals(res_pois, quantreg = FALSE)

#> DHARMa:testOutliers with type = binomial may have inflated Type I error rates for integer-valued distributions. To get a more exact result, it is recommended to re-run testOutliers with type = 'bootstrap'. See ?testOutliers for details

plotQQunif(res_nb, testDispersion = TRUE, testOutliers = FALSE)
plotResiduals(res_nb, quantreg = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))







Figure 8.4: DHARMa residuals for the DIARY Poisson GLMM (top) and negative binomial GLMM (bottom). The Poisson model shows a QQ plot bent away from the diagonal and significant dispersion; the negative binomial model does not.





The Poisson model’s QQ plot departs clearly from the diagonal, and its residuals pile up at 0 and 1, the signature of overdispersion. The NB model’s residuals are close to uniform (KS test p = 0.169). Further checks: plot residuals by period and arm to assess the constant-rate assumption, and compare observed and predicted counts of zeros, ones, twos and so on.


8.5.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Migraine days per diary period were analysed with a negative binomial mixed model (glmmTMB, nbinom2) with log link, an offset for the log number of diary days, fixed effects for treatment phase (baseline vs treatment), arm and their interaction, and a random intercept for each participant. A Poisson mixed model showed overdispersion (DHARMa dispersion ratio 1.51); the negative binomial model fitted better (AIC 4827 vs 5065) and showed no residual overdispersion or excess zeros, and a zero-inflated model did not improve the fit. Relative to baseline, the migraine rate during treatment was 0.82 times as large on active treatment as on placebo (95% CI 0.65 to 1.04). The estimated mean number of migraine days per 28 days during treatment was 4.8 (95% CI 4.2 to 5.5) on placebo and 3.5 (3.1 to 4.0) on active treatment.




8.5.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Leaving out the offset, or including log(days) as a covariate with an estimated coefficient without a reason.
Fitting a Poisson GLMM without checking overdispersion. The random intercept does not remove within-participant overdispersion; standard errors can be badly underestimated.
Adding zero inflation because a Poisson model has “too many zeros”. Test against the negative binomial, and only with a substantive reason.
Reporting emmeans counts at \(b_{0i} = 0\) as population means. Use bias.adjust = TRUE (exact for the log link) for population means.
Reading armActive as the treatment effect when a baseline period is in the model.









NoteAdvanced extension



Zero-inflated and hurdle models (ziformula in glmmTMB, or family = truncated_nbinom2 for the non-zero part of a hurdle model) are needed when a subgroup cannot experience the event during a period, for example participants whose migraines have stopped entirely. Their parameters answer two questions (whether any events occur, and how many when they do), and the overall treatment effect on the mean count must be computed from both parts.

title: 8  Generalized linear mixed models
text:
Summary
Generalized linear mixed models combine a generalized linear model for each observation with random effects for each participant. Their coefficients are conditional: they describe change within a participant. For binary outcomes with a logit link, conditional odds ratios are further from 1 than population-average odds ratios, by a factor close to \(\sqrt{1 + 0.346\,\tau_0^2}\); in CLEAR the GLMM’s implied marginal effects match the GEE estimates of Module 7 closely. Fitting binary GLMMs with few observations per participant needs accurate integration, and adaptive quadrature changed the random-effect SD noticeably compared with the Laplace approximation. Predicted probabilities can be reported for a typical participant (\(b_{0i} = 0\)) or for the population (by integrating over the random effects), and the two answer different questions. For counts, the log link makes conditional and marginal rate ratios equal; the main practical issues are the exposure offset and overdispersion, which in DIARY called for a negative binomial model, while the apparent excess of zeros in the Poisson model disappeared once overdispersion was modelled. DHARMa’s simulation-based residuals provide one framework for checking all these models.

title: 8  Generalized linear mixed models
text:
Further reading

Molenberghs and Verbeke give a comprehensive treatment of models for discrete longitudinal data, including GLMMs, marginal models and their relationship (Molenberghs and Verbeke 2005).
Zeger, Liang and Albert, and Neuhaus, Kalbfleisch and Hauck, explain the difference between subject-specific and population-averaged effects (Zeger et al. 1988; Neuhaus et al. 1991).
Fitzmaurice, Laird and Ware cover GLMMs and their interpretation for applied researchers (Fitzmaurice et al. 2011).
Bates and colleagues describe lme4 (Bates et al. 2015), Brooks and colleagues glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017), and Hartig the DHARMa residuals (Hartig 2026).

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
text:
Learning outcomes
So far the course has used covariates that are fixed at baseline (arm, age, sex, body mass index) and has described time either as a set of scheduled visits or as a straight line. Real longitudinal studies are richer than that. Some predictors change from visit to visit: the number of steps a participant walks, the dose of a drug, a symptom score. Their association with the outcome has two parts, one that compares people with each other and one that compares occasions within the same person, and the two parts usually answer different scientific questions. Change itself is rarely linear either. In the WALK trial, blood pressure falls quickly in the first few months of the walking programme and then levels off; in the KIDNEY cohort, kidney function declines at an accelerating rate. This module shows how to separate within-person from between-person associations, how to use actual measurement times when visits are irregular, how to describe curved trajectories with polynomials, piecewise lines, splines and generalized additive mixed models, and why associations with time-varying covariates should be interpreted causally only with great care.
By the end of this module participants will be able to:

9.1 Distinguish time-invariant from time-varying covariates.
9.2 Separate within-person and between-person associations with person-mean centring, and interpret the contextual effect.
9.3 Analyse data with unequal measurement intervals using actual measurement times.
9.4 Fit and compare polynomial, piecewise linear and spline trajectories.
9.5 Fit an introductory generalized additive mixed model with mgcv and interpret the smooth time effects.
9.6 Explain why associations with time-varying covariates may reflect confounding, reverse causation or mediation, and state the limits of causal interpretation.

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
text:
Prerequisites
Module 4 (linear mixed models with random intercepts and slopes), Module 5 (covariance structures and comparing models with AIC and BIC) and Module 6 (estimated marginal means, contrasts and the WALK primary estimand). Module 2 introduced the distinction between scheduled and actual time.






WarningSimulated data



All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
crumbs: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
text:
9.1 Time-invariant and time-varying covariates
A time-invariant covariate takes one value per participant for the whole study. In WALK these are arm, clinic, age at baseline, sex and baseline body mass index (BMI). In long format the value is simply repeated on every row of the participant. A time-varying covariate can take a different value at each measurement occasion. In WALK the average daily step count in the week before each visit (steps, in thousands per day) is time-varying; so are time itself and anything measured at every visit.

walk |>
  filter(id %in% c("W001", "W130")) |>
  select(id, arm, age, bmi, month, steps, sbp)

#> # A tibble: 12 × 7
#>    id    arm     age   bmi month steps   sbp
#>    <chr> <fct> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 W001  EP       69  32.8  0      4.5   150
#>  2 W001  EP       69  32.8  1.09   6.5   148
#>  3 W001  EP       69  32.8  2.95   7.7   133
#>  4 W001  EP       69  32.8  6.04   7.2   140
#>  5 W001  EP       69  32.8  9.68   7     132
#>  6 W001  EP       69  32.8 11.13   8.2   132
#>  7 W130  EP       69  27.5  0      4.3   140
#>  8 W130  EP       69  27.5  0.76   2.6   134
#>  9 W130  EP       69  27.5  3.05   4     130
#> 10 W130  EP       69  27.5  6.12   6.4   126
#> 11 W130  EP       69  27.5  9.17   5.9   135
#> 12 W130  EP       69  27.5 11.17   4.3   132


Participant W001 (enhanced programme) has the same arm, age and BMI on every row, but their steps rise from 4.5 to over 8 thousand a day while their SBP falls. The table already shows the two kinds of information that a time-varying covariate carries. W001’s average step count tells us where W001 sits relative to other people (a between-person comparison). The visit-to-visit fluctuations around that average tell us what happens to W001’s blood pressure in weeks when W001 walks more than usual (a within-person comparison).
The distinction matters for three reasons. First, time-invariant covariates can explain only differences between participants (they can shift the intercept, or the slope if interacted with time), whereas time-varying covariates can also explain changes within a participant. Second, a time-varying covariate measured after randomisation can itself be affected by the treatment, which changes what adjusting for it means (see the section on mediation below). Third, the within-person part of the association is automatically protected against confounding by any stable characteristic of the person, because each person serves as their own control; the between-person part has no such protection.

walk |>
  group_by(arm, month_sched) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(steps), se = sd(steps) / sqrt(n())) |>
  ggplot(aes(month_sched, mean, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
                width = 0.25) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Mean daily steps (thousands)")







Figure 9.1: Mean daily steps (thousands) by arm and scheduled visit in WALK, with 95% confidence intervals. Steps rise in both programme arms after randomisation, so steps is affected by the treatment.





Figure 9.1 shows that steps rise in the two programme arms after randomisation and barely change under usual care. Steps is therefore not just a characteristic of participants: it is partly an outcome of the intervention. Keep this in mind; it returns when we ask what happens to the treatment effect when steps is added to the model.
crumbs: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
text:
9.2 Within-person and between-person associations

9.2.1 The research question and estimand
Two different questions can be asked about steps and blood pressure.

Between-person: do people who habitually walk more have lower blood pressure than people who habitually walk less? The estimand is the difference in mean SBP between two participants whose usual step counts differ by 1,000 steps a day.
Within-person: when a given participant walks more than usual, is their blood pressure lower than usual? The estimand is the expected change in a participant’s SBP for an increase of 1,000 steps a day above their own average.

Because the WALK data are simulated, we know both answers: the between-person effect is -1.5 mmHg and the within-person effect is -0.6 mmHg per 1,000 steps a day. The two differ by a factor of more than two. In real data the two can even have opposite signs: people who exercise a lot have lower heart rates at rest, but any one person’s heart rate is higher while they exercise (Curran and Bauer 2011).


9.2.2 Data structure and outcome types
We need long-format data with a participant identifier, the time-varying covariate at each occasion, and a continuous outcome. Person-mean centring works for any outcome type (it is just a construction of two covariates), but this section uses the linear mixed model for SBP. Each participant must contribute at least one observation to estimate a person mean, and at least two for the within-person deviation to vary.


9.2.3 Intuition
A single coefficient for steps in a mixed model, the “naive” approach, mixes the two kinds of comparison. The model uses both the differences between participants and the fluctuations within participants, and returns a weighted blend whose weights depend on how much variation there is at each level and on the random-effects variance. The blend is neither the within-person nor the between-person effect; it answers no clearly stated question.
Person-mean centring splits the covariate into two new variables (Enders and Tofighi 2007; Curran and Bauer 2011):

the person mean \(\bar x_i\) (here centred at the grand mean of the person means), which varies only between participants;
the within-person deviation \(x_{ij} - \bar x_i\), which varies only within participants and has mean zero for every participant.

Entering both in the model gives each its own coefficient. The deviation variable is uncorrelated with anything that is constant within a person, including the random intercept, so its coefficient is a purely within-person estimate.


9.2.4 The model
For participant \(i\) at occasion \(j\),
\[
y_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \beta_W\,(s_{ij} - \bar s_i) + \beta_B\,(\bar s_i - \bar s) + b_{0i} + b_{1i} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
where \(y_{ij}\) is SBP, \(\mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta\) is the primary mean structure (a mean for each arm at each scheduled visit, plus age, sex and BMI in the adjusted model), \(s_{ij}\) is the step count (thousands per day) at the occasion, \(\bar s_i\) the participant’s mean over their observed occasions and \(\bar s\) the mean of the \(\bar s_i\). The coefficient \(\beta_W\) is the within-person effect and \(\beta_B\) the between-person effect. As in Module 4, \(b_{0i}\) and \(b_{1i}\) are the random intercept and random slope on actual time \(t_{ij}\), with covariance matrix \(G\), and \(\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) is the residual error.
An equivalent parameterisation enters the raw covariate and the person mean:
\[
y_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \beta_W\, s_{ij} + \beta_C\,(\bar s_i - \bar s) + b_{0i} + b_{1i} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \beta_C = \beta_B - \beta_W .
\]
Here \(\beta_C\) is the contextual effect: the difference in expected SBP between two participants with the same step count at this occasion but whose usual step counts differ by 1,000 a day. It tests directly whether the between-person and within-person effects differ. The two parameterisations fit the data identically; they only label the parameters differently.


9.2.5 Assumptions and limitations
The usual mixed-model assumptions apply (Module 4): a correctly specified mean, normally distributed random effects and residuals, and missingness that is at most missing at random (Module 10). In addition:

The within-person effect is assumed to be the same for everyone. A random slope on the deviation variable relaxes this.
The person mean is computed from the observed occasions only. Participants who drop out early have person means based on fewer visits, and in WALK these early visits are before the programme raised step counts. The observed person mean is also an imperfect measure of the habitual level, which slightly attenuates \(\beta_B\).
The between-person effect is open to confounding by any characteristic that differs between people and is related to both steps and SBP. In WALK, people with a higher BMI walk less, and BMI raises SBP.
The within-person effect is protected against stable confounders but not against time-varying confounders, reverse causation or mediation (see the final section and Module 13).



9.2.6 Fitting the model in R

walk <- walk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(steps_pm = mean(steps)) |>                 # person mean
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(steps_wc = steps - steps_pm,               # within-person deviation
         steps_gm = steps_pm - mean(steps_pm[!duplicated(id)]),  # centred person mean
         age10 = (age - 60) / 10,
         bmi_c = bmi - 29)


m_naive  <- lmer(sbp ~ steps + visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
m_wb     <- lmer(sbp ~ steps_wc + steps_gm + visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
m_wb_adj <- lmer(sbp ~ steps_wc + steps_gm + visit_f * arm +
                   age10 + sex + bmi_c + (1 + month | id),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
m_ctx    <- lmer(sbp ~ steps + steps_gm + visit_f * arm +
                   age10 + sex + bmi_c + (1 + month | id),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)

All four models keep the primary mean structure (visit_f * arm), so the steps coefficients are estimated net of the average trajectory of each arm.


9.2.7 Interpreting the output

coef(summary(m_wb_adj))[c("steps_wc", "steps_gm", "age10", "sexFemale", "bmi_c"), ]

#>           Estimate Std. Error     df t value  Pr(>|t|)
#> steps_wc   -0.6206     0.1284 1484.0  -4.833 1.484e-06
#> steps_gm   -1.6905     0.3117  356.4  -5.423 1.084e-07
#> age10       1.5632     0.6791  343.9   2.302 2.194e-02
#> sexFemale  -3.9577     1.2200  346.9  -3.244 1.293e-03
#> bmi_c       0.4319     0.1484  347.5   2.910 3.842e-03



tab <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Naive: one coefficient", "Person-mean centred",
            "Person-mean centred", "Person-mean centred + age, sex, BMI",
            "Person-mean centred + age, sex, BMI",
            "Contextual parameterisation + age, sex, BMI"),
  Term = c("steps", "within", "between", "within", "between", "contextual"),
  `Estimate (95% CI)` = c(ci(nv), ci(w1), ci(b1), ci(w2), ci(b2), ci(cx)),
  Truth = c("none", truth$beta_steps_within, truth$beta_steps_between,
            truth$beta_steps_within, truth$beta_steps_between,
            truth$beta_steps_between - truth$beta_steps_within),
  check.names = FALSE)

The naive coefficient, -0.80, lies between the within-person and between-person estimates, as expected of a blend. It is not wrong arithmetic; it is an answer to an ill-posed question. The within-person estimate is -0.62 mmHg per 1,000 steps a day, close to the true -0.6, and it hardly changes when age, sex and BMI are added (-0.62 without them). That stability is expected: stable characteristics cannot confound a comparison of a person with themselves.
The between-person estimate behaves differently. Without adjustment it is -1.91; adjusting for age, sex and BMI moves it to -1.69, nearer the true -1.5. The unadjusted estimate is confounded by BMI: participants with a higher BMI walk less and have higher SBP, so part of the apparent benefit of walking more is really the benefit of a lower BMI. This is the general lesson. Between-person associations in longitudinal data are observational comparisons of different people and need the same confounder adjustment as a cross-sectional study.
The contextual effect, -1.07 (-1.73 to -0.41) mmHg, says that, among participants walking the same number of steps this week, those who usually walk 1,000 more steps a day have SBP about 1.1 mmHg lower. Its confidence interval excludes zero, so the data indicate that the between-person and within-person effects differ. Note how the estimate of steps in the contextual model equals the within-person estimate exactly; only the label of the second coefficient changes.
The person means vary more than the within-person deviations (SD 2.06 versus 1.18 thousand steps a day), so the between-person coefficient is estimated from more spread in the covariate; it is nevertheless less precise (SE 0.31 versus 0.13) because there are only 360 participants to compare but about 1,900 occasions.


9.2.8 Checking the model
Three checks are specific to this model. First, plot SBP against the deviation variable within a sample of participants to see whether the within-person relation looks linear. Second, check whether the within-person effect varies between participants by adding a random slope for steps_wc and comparing the fits. Third, check how sensitive the between-person estimate is to adjustment for plausible confounders, as done above.

m_wb_rs <- lmer(sbp ~ steps_wc + steps_gm + visit_f * arm + age10 + sex +
                  bmi_c + (1 + month + steps_wc | id),
                data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)

#> boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')

anova(m_wb_adj, m_wb_rs, refit = FALSE)

#> Data: walk
#> Models:
#> m_wb_adj: sbp ~ steps_wc + steps_gm + visit_f * arm + age10 + sex + bmi_c + (1 + month | id)
#> m_wb_rs: sbp ~ steps_wc + steps_gm + visit_f * arm + age10 + sex + bmi_c + (1 + month + steps_wc | id)
#>          npar   AIC   BIC logLik -2*log(L) Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
#> m_wb_adj   27 13222 13372  -6584     13168                    
#> m_wb_rs    30 13225 13392  -6583     13165  2.49  3       0.48


lmer() reports a singular fit for this model: the estimated random-effects covariance matrix lies on the boundary of the parameter space, a sign that the data carry little information about the extra variance component. The random slope for steps has an estimated SD of 0.26 mmHg per 1,000 steps/day and the likelihood-ratio test gives p = 0.477 (the test is conservative because the variance is tested on its boundary; Module 4). In the simulation every participant has the same within-person effect, so the absence of strong evidence for a random slope is the correct conclusion. Residual and random-effects checks are as in Module 11.


9.2.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Daily step count was decomposed into each participant’s mean over their visits (between-person component, centred at the sample mean) and the deviation of each visit from that mean (within-person component), and both were added to the primary linear mixed model together with age, sex and BMI (Curran and Bauer 2011). Within participants, SBP was 0.62 mmHg lower (95% CI 0.37 to 0.87) in weeks when a participant walked 1,000 more steps a day than usual. Between participants, a 1,000 steps/day higher average step count was associated with 1.69 mmHg lower SBP (95% CI 1.08 to 2.30). The difference between the two (contextual effect) was -1.07 mmHg (-1.73 to -0.41). These associations are observational and may reflect confounding or reverse causation.




9.2.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Reporting a single coefficient for a time-varying covariate and interpreting it as “the effect of walking more”. It mixes two questions. Decompose it.
Centring at the grand mean instead of the person mean. Subtracting the overall mean from \(s_{ij}\) changes the intercept but leaves the within/between blend intact.
Forgetting the person mean. A model with only the within-person deviation estimates \(\beta_W\) correctly, but leaves between-person variation in steps in the random intercept; adding \(\bar s_i\) makes the model complete and shows the contextual effect.
Treating the between-person effect as causal without adjusting for between-person confounders such as BMI.
Computing person means from a different set of rows than the model uses (for example, before removing rows with missing SBP).

section: 9.3 Time-varying covariates, mediation and the treatment effect
text:
9.3 Time-varying covariates, mediation and the treatment effect
In a randomised trial it is tempting to “adjust for” a time-varying covariate that predicts the outcome, in the hope of a more precise treatment effect. When the covariate is affected by the treatment, this changes the estimand. In WALK the programmes increase walking (Figure 9.1), and walking more lowers blood pressure. Part of each programme’s effect therefore acts through steps: steps is a mediator. Adjusting for steps removes that part and leaves an estimate of the effect of the programme other than through walking more, which is a different question from the trial’s primary one.

m_primary <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id),
                  data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
m_steps   <- lmer(sbp ~ steps_wc + visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id),
                  data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)

diff_change <- function(m) {
  e  <- emmeans(m, ~ visit_f | arm, at = list(visit_f = c("0", "12")))
  ch <- contrast(e, list(change = c(-1, 1)), by = "arm")
  summary(contrast(ch, "trt.vs.ctrl", by = NULL), infer = TRUE,
          adjust = "none")
}
diff_change(m_primary)

#>  contrast              estimate   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  change SP - change UC    -5.38 1.42 483    -8.17    -2.58  -3.782  0.0002
#>  change EP - change UC    -8.97 1.44 491   -11.79    -6.15  -6.243 <0.0001
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95

diff_change(m_steps)

#>  contrast              estimate   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL t.ratio p.value
#>  change SP - change UC    -4.83 1.42 487    -7.62    -2.04  -3.405  0.0007
#>  change EP - change UC    -7.93 1.45 508   -10.78    -5.09  -5.483 <0.0001
#> 
#> Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95



knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Contrast = c("SP vs UC", "EP vs UC"),
  `Primary model` = fmt_ci(d0$estimate, d0$lower.CL, d0$upper.CL),
  `True total effect` = f1(true_total),
  `Adjusted for steps` = fmt_ci(d1$estimate, d1$lower.CL, d1$upper.CL),
  `True effect not through steps` = f1(true_direct),
  check.names = FALSE))



Table 9.2: Difference in mean change in SBP from baseline to month 12 versus usual care (mmHg), with and without the within-person steps deviation in the model. True values are known only because the data are simulated.

Adjusting for within-person steps moves the SP contrast from -5.38 to -4.83 mmHg and the EP contrast from -8.97 to -7.93 mmHg, shifts of 0.54 and 1.04. In the simulation the parts of the effects that act through extra walking are -0.60 (SP) and -1.08 mmHg (EP), and the estimated shifts are close to these. Neither model is wrong, but they estimate different things:

the primary model estimates the total effect of being randomised to a programme, which is what the trial was designed to answer;
the steps-adjusted model estimates something like a direct effect: the effect of the programme among participants whose walking (relative to their own average) is held fixed.

The second interpretation needs much stronger assumptions. Randomisation protects the comparison of arms, but it does not protect the comparison of people with different step counts within an arm. If anything other than the programme affects both steps and SBP (illness, a change of medication, a stressful month), the “direct effect” is confounded. Formal mediation analysis with time-varying mediators requires the methods of Module 13 and Hernán and Robins (2020). The practical rule for trials is simple: do not adjust the primary treatment comparison for post-randomisation variables. Use them in secondary, clearly labelled analyses.

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
section: 9.4 Unequal measurement intervals and actual time
text:
9.4 Unequal measurement intervals and actual time

9.4.1 The research question and estimand
Most longitudinal questions are about change per unit of time: how much does SBP fall per month, how many units of eGFR are lost per year? The estimand is defined on the time scale, so the analysis must place each measurement at the correct time.


9.4.2 Data structure and outcome types
WALK visits are scheduled at months 0, 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12, which are unequally spaced: 1 month between the first two visits, 3 months between later ones. In addition, actual visit times (month) scatter around the schedule (month_sched). The KIDNEY cohort has no schedule at all: eGFR is measured at clinic visits whose timing is irregular and differs between patients.

walk |>
  mutate(dev = month - month_sched) |>
  group_by(month_sched) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_dev = mean(dev), sd_dev = sd(dev),
            min = min(month), max = max(month))

#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   month_sched     n  mean_dev sd_dev   min   max
#>         <dbl> <int>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1           0   360  0        0       0     0   
#> 2           1   324 -0.001574 0.1201  0.7   1.39
#> 3           3   319 -0.01746  0.2519  2.23  3.69
#> 4           6   309 -0.01508  0.3355  5.16  6.86
#> 5           9   297 -0.02946  0.4077  7.8  10.01
#> 6          12   288  0.02208  0.4452 10.81 13.3

kidney |> count(id) |> summarise(min = min(n), median = median(n), max = max(n))

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>     min median   max
#>   <int>  <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     10    24




9.4.3 Intuition
Using visit number (1, 2, …, 6) as if it were time treats the gap from month 0 to month 1 as equal to the gap from month 9 to month 12. A straight line in visit number is then a curve in real time, and the slope “per visit” has no stable meaning. Using scheduled time fixes the spacing but ignores the actual deviations. Using actual time puts every observation where it belongs. A mixed model with time as a continuous covariate needs no balance or common schedule: each participant contributes whatever measurements they have, at whatever times.


9.4.4 The model
The linear-time WALK model with actual time is
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t_{ij} + \beta_2\text{SP}_i + \beta_3\text{EP}_i + \beta_4 t_{ij}\text{SP}_i + \beta_5 t_{ij}\text{EP}_i + b_{0i} + b_{1i} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
where \(t_{ij}\) is the actual month of the visit. Replacing \(t_{ij}\) by the scheduled month or by visit number gives the alternatives compared below. The random slope \(b_{1i}\) should also use actual time, because the variance of \(y_{ij}\) implied by a random slope, \(\tau_0^2 + 2\tau_{01}t_{ij} + \tau_1^2 t_{ij}^2 + \sigma^2\), depends on the real time elapsed. For the same reason the primary model uses scheduled visit for the mean but actual time in the random part. Continuous-time residual correlation structures, such as the exponential structure of Module 5, also need actual times.


9.4.5 Assumptions and limitations
Using actual time assumes that the timing of a visit does not carry information about the outcome beyond what the model includes. If participants with worse outcomes are seen earlier or more often, the visit process is informative; Module 10 shows how that biases simple summaries and when a mixed model is protected. Actual time also cannot be used for a categorical-time mean model, where the mean is estimated separately at each scheduled visit; that is why the WALK primary model combines visit_f for the mean with actual month in the random part.


9.4.6 Fitting the model in R

m_actual <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
m_sched  <- lmer(sbp ~ month_sched * arm + (1 + month_sched | id),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
m_visit  <- lmer(sbp ~ I(visit - 1) * arm + (1 + I(visit - 1) | id),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)



9.4.7 Interpreting the output

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Time scale` = c("Actual month", "Scheduled month", "Visit number"),
  Unit = c("per month", "per month", "per visit"),
  `SP vs UC` = c(ci(a_sp), ci(s_sp), ci(v_sp)),
  `EP vs UC` = c(ci(a_ep), ci(s_ep), ci(v_ep)), check.names = FALSE))

With actual time, the EP slope is -0.72 mmHg per month steeper than usual care; with scheduled time it is -0.73. In WALK the two agree closely because the deviations from the schedule are small (SD at most about half a month) and unrelated to blood pressure. That is the best case. The visit-number model gives -1.92 mmHg “per visit”, a number with no stable meaning because a visit is one month early in the study and three months later. It cannot be converted to a monthly rate and it implies the wrong shape of change.
KIDNEY shows the problem more starkly because visits are irregular and patients with low eGFR are seen more often.

kidney <- kidney |>
  group_by(id) |> arrange(years, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(visit_no = row_number() - 1) |> ungroup()
mk_years <- lmer(egfr ~ years + (1 + years | id), data = kidney,
                 control = lmer_ctrl)
mk_visit <- lmer(egfr ~ visit_no + (1 + visit_no | id), data = kidney,
                 control = lmer_ctrl)
rbind(years = fixef(mk_years), visit_no = fixef(mk_visit))

#>          (Intercept)  years
#> years          49.75 -2.586
#> visit_no       49.42 -1.063


The estimated decline is -2.59 mL/min/1.73m² per year on the actual time scale and -1.06 per visit. A “visit” in KIDNEY lasts anything from a few weeks to more than a year, and it is shorter for patients with poor kidney function, so the per-visit slope mixes the rate of decline with the clinic’s scheduling policy. Only the per-year slope answers a clinical question.


9.4.8 Checking the model
Plot the observed times (a histogram of month - month_sched, or a dot plot of each participant’s visit times) to see how irregular the timing is and whether it differs by arm or by outcome level. Plot residuals against actual time to check the shape of the time trend; the next section shows what to do when the shape is not linear.

set.seed(9)
ids <- sample(unique(kidney$id), 40)
kidney |>
  filter(id %in% ids) |>
  add_count(id) |>
  ggplot(aes(years, reorder(id, n))) +
  geom_point(size = 1, colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = "Years since entry", y = "Participant") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())







Figure 9.2: Visit times for 40 randomly chosen KIDNEY participants, ordered by their number of visits. Timing is irregular and differs between participants.







9.4.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Time was measured as actual months since randomisation, calculated from visit dates; scheduled visits were used only to define the categorical-time mean in the primary model. In the linear-time model, SBP declined 0.72 mmHg per month faster in the enhanced programme than in usual care (95% CI 0.51 to 0.93). Results were almost identical with scheduled time (-0.73 mmHg per month).




9.4.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Using visit number as time when visits are unequally spaced or irregular.
Binning irregular times into windows and then treating the windows as if all measurements were taken at the window midpoint, when the mixed model can use exact times.
Using scheduled time in the random part of the model when actual times vary a lot: the implied variance and correlation depend on real elapsed time.
Ignoring the reason for irregular timing. If visits happen because the patient is unwell, the timing is informative (Module 10).
