title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
section: 9.5 Nonlinear trajectories: polynomials, piecewise lines and splines
text:
9.5 Nonlinear trajectories: polynomials, piecewise lines and splines

9.5.1 The research question and estimand
The WALK primary estimand, the difference in mean change at month 12, can be estimated with categorical time, which makes no assumption about the shape of change between visits. Many questions are about the shape itself: how fast does the effect develop, does it plateau, what is the mean change at month 4 (an unscheduled time)? Those questions need a model for the mean trajectory as a smooth function of time. With irregular times, such as KIDNEY, there is no alternative: categorical time is impossible because there are no common visits.


9.5.2 Data structure and outcome types
The same long-format WALK data with actual time month. The methods apply to any outcome; with a non-Gaussian outcome they are used inside a GLMM or GEE (Modules 7 and 8).


9.5.3 Intuition
Because the data are simulated, we know that the true mean change in each arm follows an exponential approach to a plateau,
\[
\mu(t) - \mu(0) = -A\,\{1 - \exp(-t/2)\},
\]
plus a small extra fall that acts through increased walking. Change develops quickly in the first three months and is nearly complete by month 6. No straight line can follow this. The three standard ways of bending a line within a linear mixed model are:

a polynomial, adding \(t^2\) (and possibly \(t^3\)) terms. Simple, but a quadratic is symmetric about its turning point, so it must turn back up after reaching its minimum;
a piecewise linear (linear spline) model, with a separate slope before and after a knot. Easy to interpret when there is a natural break (here: the intensive phase of the programme in the first three months);
a natural cubic spline, joining cubic pieces smoothly at several knots and constrained to be linear beyond the outer knots. Flexible and well-behaved, but its coefficients are not interpretable one by one.

All three remain linear in the parameters, so they are fitted by lmer() like any other fixed effect. Models that are nonlinear in their parameters, such as the exponential curve above with \(A\) and the rate as parameters, are covered in Module 13.


9.5.4 The model
Write \(f(t_{ij})\) for the shape of the mean trajectory in usual care and \(g(t_{ij})\) for the difference in shape for a programme arm. For each approach,
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \alpha_1\text{SP}_i + \alpha_2\text{EP}_i + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left(\beta_k + \gamma_{k1}\text{SP}_i + \gamma_{k2}\text{EP}_i\right) h_k(t_{ij}) + b_{0i} + b_{1i}t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
where the \(h_k(t)\) are basis functions of time:

quadratic: \(h_1(t) = t\), \(h_2(t) = t^2\);
piecewise linear with a knot at 3 months: \(h_1(t) = t\), \(h_2(t) = (t - 3)_+\), where \((t - 3)_+ = \max(t - 3, 0)\). The slope is \(\beta_1\) before month 3 and \(\beta_1 + \beta_2\) after it;
natural cubic spline: \(h_1, h_2, h_3\) are the columns returned by splines::ns(month, df = 3), with interior knots at the 33rd and 67th percentiles of the observed times.

The coefficients \(\beta_k\) describe usual care; \(\gamma_{k1}\) and \(\gamma_{k2}\) are the differences for SP and EP; \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2\) are baseline differences (expected to be near zero in a randomised trial). The random part is the same random intercept and slope on actual time as in the reference models.


9.5.5 Assumptions and limitations
Each model assumes that its family of curves contains (or closely approximates) the true mean trajectory. A misspecified shape biases the estimated mean at particular times, including month 12. Polynomials behave badly at the ends of the time range and should not be extrapolated. Piecewise models depend on knot placement; a knot chosen after looking at the data makes the model look better than it is. Splines need enough data across the time range, and their knots are placed by the software unless specified. The random part here allows only linear individual deviations, which is a simplification.


9.5.6 Fitting the model in R
The models differ in their fixed effects, so they are fitted by maximum likelihood (REML = FALSE) for comparison with AIC and BIC (Module 5).

walk <- walk |> mutate(month_p3 = pmax(month - 3, 0))   # (t - 3)+
fit_ml <- function(f) lmer(f, data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl, REML = FALSE)
m_lin  <- fit_ml(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id))
m_quad <- fit_ml(sbp ~ (month + I(month^2)) * arm + (1 + month | id))
m_pw   <- fit_ml(sbp ~ (month + month_p3) * arm + (1 + month | id))
m_ns   <- fit_ml(sbp ~ splines::ns(month, df = 3) * arm + (1 + month | id))
m_cat  <- fit_ml(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id))



9.5.7 Interpreting the output
The piecewise model has the most interpretable coefficients:

pw <- fixef_table(m_pw)
pw

#>             term estimate     se     df     lower    upper          p
#> 1    (Intercept) 145.8390 1.2086  396.7 143.46294 148.2151 8.693e-315
#> 2          month  -0.7179 0.2394 1440.0  -1.18745  -0.2484  2.751e-03
#> 3       month_p3   0.8868 0.2947 1261.1   0.30861   1.4649  2.673e-03
#> 4          armSP   1.1697 1.7094  396.8  -2.19086   4.5302  4.942e-01
#> 5          armEP   0.9337 1.7088  396.3  -2.42580   4.2932  5.851e-01
#> 6    month:armSP  -1.1703 0.3368 1438.5  -1.83092  -0.5097  5.254e-04
#> 7    month:armEP  -2.1524 0.3409 1439.0  -2.82118  -1.4837  3.619e-10
#> 8 month_p3:armSP   0.8756 0.4138 1256.8   0.06375   1.6874  3.455e-02

In the enhanced programme SBP falls by about 2.87 mmHg per month during the first three months and then by only 0.13 mmHg per month; the standard programme shows the same pattern (-1.89 then -0.13). This is the “fast then slow” shape of the true curve described by two straight lines.

ggplot(curves, aes(month, change, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line(data = true_curve, aes(group = arm), linetype = "dashed",
            colour = "black") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12)) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Month since randomisation", y = "Mean change in SBP (mmHg)")







Figure 9.3: Estimated mean change in SBP from baseline under four trajectory models (solid) and the true mean change (dashed; known only because the data are simulated).






m12 <- function(m) {
  p <- predict(m, newdata = filter(nd, month %in% c(0, 12)), re.form = NA)
  ch <- p[c(2, 4, 6)] - p[c(1, 3, 5)]
  c(SP = unname(ch[2] - ch[1]), EP = unname(ch[3] - ch[1]))
}
cat_ct <- fixef(m_cat)[c("visit_f12:armSP", "visit_f12:armEP")]
ic <- data.frame(
  Model = c(names(mods), "Categorical time"),
  Parameters = sapply(c(mods, list(m_cat)), function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  AIC = round(sapply(c(mods, list(m_cat)), AIC), 1),
  BIC = round(sapply(c(mods, list(m_cat)), BIC), 1),

  `EP vs UC` = f2(c(sapply(mods, m12)["EP", ], cat_ct[2])),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(ic)
best_aic <- ic$Model[which.min(ic$AIC)]; best_bic <- ic$Model[which.min(ic$BIC)]

Figure 9.3 and Table 9.4 tell a consistent story. The linear model misses the shape completely: it describes a steady decline that is far too slow in the first months and almost no change in usual care, and its AIC is about 128 points worse than the best model. The quadratic follows the early fall but curves back up after month 8, an artefact of its symmetric shape, so its month-12 values reflect the upturn rather than the plateau. The piecewise model captures the fast-then-slow pattern with a visible corner at month 3. The natural spline follows the true curves most closely in the programme arms but adds a small wiggle in usual care, where there is little change to describe.
By AIC the best model is the natural spline, by BIC the piecewise; the categorical-time model, which uses 22 parameters, is penalised by BIC for its flexibility. The month-12 contrasts of the smooth models range from -9.16 to -8.03 for EP. All are within sampling error of the truth (−8.1), but the spread shows that the shape assumption matters for a single time point. This is why the WALK primary analysis uses categorical time for the month-12 estimand, and smooth models are used to describe the shape.


9.5.8 Checking the model
Compare the fitted mean curves with the observed means at each scheduled visit, plot residuals against time (any curvature left over shows a misspecified shape), and compare candidate models by AIC/BIC fitted with ML. Prefer knots set in advance on substantive grounds (here: the end of the intensive phase at month 3) to knots chosen by searching.

bind_rows(
  walk |> mutate(res = resid(m_lin), model = "Linear"),
  walk |> mutate(res = resid(m_ns), model = "Natural spline")) |>
  group_by(model, arm, month_sched) |>
  summarise(res = mean(res)) |>
  ggplot(aes(month_sched, res, colour = arm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Mean residual (mmHg)")







Figure 9.4: Mean conditional residuals by scheduled visit for the linear and natural spline models. A systematic pattern indicates that the time trend is misspecified.





The linear model leaves systematic residual patterns, while the spline residuals stay close to zero at every visit. Conditional residuals are partly absorbed by the random slopes, so the pattern understates the misfit of the mean; the comparison of fitted and true curves in Figure 9.3 shows it more fully.


9.5.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



The shape of the mean SBP trajectory was described with a piecewise linear model with a knot at month 3 (the end of the intensive phase of the programmes), with separate slopes for each arm and a random intercept and slope on actual time. In the enhanced programme SBP fell by 2.87 mmHg per month during months 0–3 and by 0.13 mmHg per month thereafter; in usual care the corresponding slopes were -0.72 and 0.17 mmHg per month. A natural cubic spline (3 degrees of freedom) gave similar fitted curves (AIC 13306.9 vs 13317.5).




9.5.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Interpreting individual spline coefficients. Interpret the fitted curve and contrasts computed from it, not the basis coefficients.
Extrapolating a polynomial beyond the observed time range, or reading its turning point as a real feature.
Choosing knots by trying many and keeping the best fit, then reporting the model as if pre-specified.
Comparing models with different fixed effects using REML likelihoods. Use ML (REML = FALSE) for AIC/BIC comparisons, then refit the chosen model with REML for reporting.
Forgetting the interaction with arm. A common shape for all arms with only shifted levels cannot estimate a difference in change.

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
text:
9.6 Generalized additive mixed models

9.6.1 The research question and estimand
Splines require the analyst to choose the number and position of knots. A generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) lets the data choose how wiggly the curve should be, through a penalty on roughness (Wood 2017). The estimand is the same smooth mean trajectory (and contrasts derived from it) as in the previous section.


9.6.2 Data structure and outcome types
Long-format data with actual time. mgcv handles Gaussian, binomial, Poisson and other outcomes. We use WALK (SBP by arm) and KIDNEY (eGFR, a nonlinear decline in an observational cohort with irregular visits).


9.6.3 Intuition
A GAMM represents each smooth function with a rich spline basis (here 5 basis functions per arm) and adds a penalty that grows with the curvature of the function. The amount of penalty is estimated from the data by REML, in the same way as a variance component. In fact a penalised smooth is a mixed model in disguise: the wiggly part of the curve is treated as a random effect whose variance controls the smoothness. The result is summarised by the effective degrees of freedom (edf): an edf of 1 means a straight line, larger values mean more curvature.


9.6.4 The model
For WALK,
\[
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \alpha_1\text{SP}_i + \alpha_2\text{EP}_i + f_{a(i)}(t_{ij}) + b_{0i} + b_{1i}t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
where \(a(i)\) is the arm of participant \(i\) and \(f_{\text{UC}}, f_{\text{SP}}, f_{\text{EP}}\) are three smooth functions of actual time \(t_{ij}\), each centred to average zero over the data (so \(\alpha_1\), \(\alpha_2\) are average differences between arms, not baseline differences). Each \(f_a(t) = \sum_{k} \theta_{ak} B_k(t)\) is a combination of spline basis functions \(B_k\), with a penalty \(\lambda_a \int f_a''(t)^2\,dt\) on its roughness. The smoothing parameters \(\lambda_a\) are estimated by REML. The random effects \(b_{0i}, b_{1i}\) and residual \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) are as before.


9.6.5 Assumptions and limitations
The GAMM assumes that the true curves are smooth, that the basis dimension k is large enough to represent them, and the usual mixed-model assumptions. Confidence intervals for smooths are Bayesian credible intervals with good average coverage across the curve, not exact pointwise intervals. Smoothness is estimated: with sparse data near the ends, the curve may be over- or under-smoothed. GAMMs describe shapes well but are harder to report than parametric models, because there is no single coefficient for “the rate of change”.


9.6.6 Fitting the model in R
mgcv offers two routes. gamm() passes the random effects to nlme::lme(). gam() and bam() instead write the random effects as penalised smooths with bs = "re":

g_walk <- gamm(sbp ~ arm + s(month, by = arm, k = 5),
               random = list(id = ~ 1 + month),
               data = walk, method = "REML")


walk$idf <- factor(walk$id)        # bs = "re" needs a factor
g_bam <- bam(sbp ~ arm + s(month, by = arm, k = 5) +
               s(idf, bs = "re") + s(idf, month, bs = "re"),
             data = walk, method = "fREML")

The formula gam(sbp ~ arm + s(month, by = arm, k = 5) + s(id, bs = "re") + s(id, month, bs = "re"), method = "REML") is valid and gives the same model as bam() above (with id a factor). We do not run it here: with 360 participants it took about nine minutes on the authors’ computer, because gam() treats each of the 720 random coefficients as part of a dense penalised model. bam() is designed for large models and fits the same formula in well under a minute. Note one difference: s(idf) + s(idf, month) gives independent random intercepts and slopes (no correlation \(\tau_{01}\)), whereas gamm() with ~ 1 + month | id estimates the correlation.


9.6.7 Interpreting the output

summary(g_walk$gam)

#> 
#> Family: gaussian 
#> Link function: identity 
#> 
#> Formula:
#> sbp ~ arm + s(month, by = arm, k = 5)
#> 
#> Parametric coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)   144.83       1.13  128.27   <2e-16 ***
#> armSP          -2.09       1.60   -1.31   0.1910    
#> armEP          -4.36       1.60   -2.73   0.0064 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Approximate significance of smooth terms:
#>                 edf Ref.df     F p-value    
#> s(month):armUC 2.82   2.82  2.93    0.11    
#> s(month):armSP 3.23   3.23 26.52  <2e-16 ***
#> s(month):armEP 3.55   3.55 52.41  <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> R-sq.(adj) =  0.0568   
#>   Scale est. = 31.695    n = 1897










Output line
Meaning
Value here




armSP, armEP
Average SBP difference from UC over the follow-up (smooths are centred)
-2.09, -4.36 mmHg


s(month):armUC edf
Curvature of the usual-care trajectory
2.82


s(month):armSP edf

3.23


s(month):armEP edf

3.55


p-values for smooths
Test that the smooth is flat (zero everywhere)
p = 0.108 (UC), p < 0.001 (EP)



All three smooths have edf well above 1, so the data support curved trajectories, and the curvature is greatest in the enhanced programme. The UC smooth is only weakly distinguishable from a flat line (p = 0.108): usual care changes little. The parametric arm coefficients are averages over the whole follow-up, not baseline differences; this is a frequent source of misinterpretation.
To obtain the trial estimand from a GAMM, compute it from predictions. The linear predictor matrix (type = "lpmatrix") gives the design rows for months 0 and 12 in each arm; a contrast vector then gives the estimate and its standard error:

Xp <- predict(g_walk$gam, newdata = ndg, type = "lpmatrix")
L  <- (Xp[6, ] - Xp[5, ]) - (Xp[2, ] - Xp[1, ])     # EP change minus UC change
est <- sum(L * coef(g_walk$gam)); se <- sqrt(drop(t(L) %*% vcov(g_walk$gam) %*% L))

The GAMM estimates the difference in mean change at month 12 as -5.54 mmHg (SE 1.34) for SP and -8.66 mmHg (SE 1.36) for EP, close to the spline and categorical-time estimates. The bam() fit gives nearly identical smooths (edf 2.83, 3.23, 3.55).

ndp <- expand.grid(month = seq(0, 12, by = 0.1),
                   arm = factor(c("UC", "SP", "EP"), levels = c("UC", "SP", "EP")))
pp <- predict(g_walk$gam, newdata = ndp, se.fit = TRUE)
ndp <- ndp |> mutate(fit = pp$fit, lo = fit - 1.96 * pp$se.fit,
                     hi = fit + 1.96 * pp$se.fit)
obs_means <- walk |> group_by(arm, month_sched) |> summarise(sbp = mean(sbp))
ggplot(ndp, aes(month, fit, colour = arm, fill = arm)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = obs_means, aes(month_sched, sbp)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12)) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  scale_fill_arm(name = NULL, labels = walk_arm_labels) +
  labs(x = "Month since randomisation", y = "Mean SBP (mmHg)")







Figure 9.5: Population-average SBP trajectories from the WALK GAMM with 95% intervals (bands), and observed means at each scheduled visit (points).






KIDNEY: a nonlinear decline with irregular visits
The KIDNEY eGFR data have no schedule, so a GAMM on actual time is natural. We allow a different smooth decline for participants with and without diabetes and adjust for age.

kidney <- kidney |>
  mutate(age10 = (age - 60) / 10,
         dm = factor(diabetes, levels = 0:1, labels = c("No", "Yes")))
g_kid <- gamm(egfr ~ dm + age10 + s(years, by = dm, k = 6),
              random = list(id = ~ 1 + years), data = kidney, method = "REML")
summary(g_kid$gam)$s.table

#>                  edf Ref.df      F p-value
#> s(years):dmNo  2.547  2.547  77.82       0
#> s(years):dmYes 2.313  2.313 174.15       0



ktr <- readRDS(here("data", "kidney_truth.rds"))
ndk <- expand.grid(years = seq(0, 5, by = 0.05), dm = c("No", "Yes"), age10 = 0)
pk  <- predict(g_kid$gam, newdata = ndk, se.fit = TRUE)
ndk <- ndk |> mutate(fit = pk$fit, lo = fit - 1.96 * pk$se.fit, hi = fit + 1.96 * pk$se.fit,
                     true = ktr$b0 + (ktr$b1 + ktr$b1_dm * (dm == "Yes")) * years +
                       ktr$b2 * years^2)
ggplot(ndk, aes(years, fit, colour = dm, fill = dm)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = true), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(No = "#0072B2", Yes = "#D55E00"), name = "Diabetes") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(No = "#0072B2", Yes = "#D55E00"), name = "Diabetes") +
  labs(x = "Years since entry", y = "Mean eGFR (mL/min/1.73m²)")







Figure 9.6: Mean eGFR trajectories (age 60) from the KIDNEY GAMM by diabetes status, with 95% intervals. Dashed lines: the true quadratic mean trajectories (known only because the data are simulated).





Both smooths are clearly curved (edf 2.55 without diabetes, 2.31 with), and the decline accelerates over time. Over five years the estimated mean loss at age 60 is 9.9 units without diabetes and 18.4 with diabetes. The fitted curves track the true quadratic trajectories well, although they are less certain after year 4, where fewer patients remain under observation. KIDNEY measurements stop at kidney failure and visits are more frequent when eGFR is low; Module 10 examines what these features do to the analysis, and Module 13 fits a joint model for eGFR and kidney failure.



9.6.8 Checking the model
gam.check() reports, for each smooth, whether the basis dimension k may be too small (a low k-index with a small p-value suggests increasing k). Refit with a larger k and check that the curve changes little. Residual checks are as for any mixed model; for gamm() fits use g$lme for the mixed-model residuals.

k_check <- gam.check(g_walk$gam)

#> 
#> 'gamm' based fit - care required with interpretation.
#> Checks based on working residuals may be misleading.
#> Basis dimension (k) checking results. Low p-value (k-index<1) may
#> indicate that k is too low, especially if edf is close to k'.
#> 
#>                  k'  edf k-index p-value
#> s(month):armUC 4.00 2.82    1.08       1
#> s(month):armSP 4.00 3.23    1.08       1
#> s(month):armEP 4.00 3.55    1.08       1


The k-index is above 1 for all three smooths with large p-values, so there is no sign that k = 5 is too small. The EP smooth uses 3.55 of its 4 available degrees of freedom; with visits clustered around six scheduled times there is little information for a more flexible curve, so increasing k would change little.


9.6.9 Reporting






TipReporting example



Mean SBP trajectories were described with a generalized additive mixed model with a separate penalised regression spline of actual time for each arm (basis dimension 5, smoothness estimated by REML) and a correlated random intercept and slope for each participant, fitted with mgcv::gamm() (Wood 2017). The trajectories were curved in the programme arms (effective degrees of freedom 3.23 for SP and 3.55 for EP), with most of the reduction occurring in the first three months. The difference in mean change from baseline to month 12, derived from the fitted curves, was -8.66 mmHg (95% CI -11.34 to -5.99) for EP versus usual care.




9.6.10 Common mistakes






ImportantCommon mistakes




Reading the parametric arm coefficients as baseline differences. Smooths are centred, so arm coefficients are averages over follow-up.
Using s(id, bs = "re") with a character id. It must be a factor; otherwise mgcv treats it as a numeric covariate or stops.
Running gam() with hundreds of random-effect levels and waiting a long time. Use gamm() or bam().
Choosing k larger than the number of distinct time points (scheduled designs have few).
Reporting only p-values for smooths. Show the fitted curves with intervals and derive the estimands of interest from predictions.

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
section: 9.7 Confounding, reverse causation and the limits of causal interpretation
text:
9.7 Confounding, reverse causation and the limits of causal interpretation
Within-person associations are often described as “each person is their own control”, which is true but only for characteristics that do not change. Three problems remain, and the WALK example illustrates each.
Time-varying confounding. Anything that changes over time and affects both steps and SBP confounds the within-person association. A bout of illness reduces walking and may also raise blood pressure (through pain, stress, or a change in medication). Comparing a participant’s ill weeks with their well weeks then attributes the effect of illness to walking. Person-mean centring does nothing about this, because the confounder varies within the person. Measuring and adjusting for such variables helps only if they are not themselves affected by earlier steps or SBP; when they are, ordinary adjustment fails (Module 13).
Reverse causation. The direction of influence may run from the outcome to the covariate. Suppose a participant’s SBP is high at one visit and the nurse responds by advising them to walk more. Their steps at the next visit then increase because SBP was high. If SBP then remains somewhat high (because of the serial correlation of SBP), weeks with more steps coincide with weeks of higher SBP, which pulls the within-person association towards zero or even reverses it. Lagging the covariate (using steps before the previous visit to predict SBP at this one) reduces but does not remove the problem, because the lagged covariate may itself have been influenced by earlier SBP.
Mediation. As shown above, steps lie on the causal pathway from the programme to SBP. Adjusting for a mediator changes the estimand from a total to a (controlled) direct effect and can introduce bias if mediator and outcome share causes.
What can be said with confidence? In WALK the arm comparison is protected by randomisation, so the primary estimand (difference in mean change at month 12) has a causal interpretation under the usual trial assumptions. The within-person and between-person associations of steps with SBP are observational associations. They are useful for description and for generating hypotheses, and the within-person version is protected against stable confounders, but neither is an estimate of “the effect of walking 1,000 more steps” without assumptions that the data cannot verify. We know the true effects here only because we simulated the data. Methods for causal effects of time-varying exposures, including marginal structural models with inverse probability weighting and g-methods, are introduced in Module 13 (Hernán and Robins 2020; Robins et al. 1995).






NoteWhy this matters



A report that says “each 1,000 additional steps per day lowered SBP by 0.6 mmHg” makes a causal claim. A report that says “SBP was on average 0.6 mmHg lower at visits when participants walked 1,000 more steps a day than their own average” describes an association. Use the second kind of sentence unless the design or a causal method justifies the first.

title: 9  Time-varying predictors and nonlinear change
text:
9.8 Summary
Time-varying covariates carry two kinds of information, and person-mean centring separates them: in WALK, walking more than one’s own average was associated with a smaller difference in SBP than walking more than other people, and the between-person association needed adjustment for BMI to approach its true value. When a time-varying covariate is affected by treatment, adjusting for it changes the treatment estimand from a total to a direct effect, so trial primary analyses should not adjust for it. Time should be measured as actually elapsed, which also makes irregular designs such as KIDNEY straightforward to analyse. Curved trajectories can be described with polynomials, piecewise lines, natural splines or penalised smooths in a GAMM; the piecewise model gave interpretable rates for the early and late phases, the spline and GAMM followed the true curves closely, and the quadratic showed the artefacts typical of polynomials. None of these associations with steps can be read causally without further assumptions.

Curran and Bauer (2011) explain the separation of within-person and between-person effects in longitudinal models, including the contextual effect.
Enders and Tofighi (2007) discuss centring of predictors in multilevel models and what each choice estimates.
Wood (2017) is the reference text for generalized additive models and mgcv, including GAMMs.
Fitzmaurice et al. (2011) (chapters on modelling the mean and time-varying covariates) cover polynomial and spline trajectories and the problems of time-varying covariates.
Hernán and Robins (2020) introduce causal inference for time-varying treatments, the background for Module 13.

title: 10  Missing data and dropout
text:
Learning outcomes
Almost every longitudinal study loses data. Participants miss visits, leave the study early, or have covariates that were never recorded. Missing data reduce precision, but the more serious danger is bias: if the people who leave differ from those who stay in ways related to the outcome, an analysis of the people who remain can give the wrong answer, and no amount of sample size fixes it. This module shows how to describe missing data, explains the three mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and what each implies, shows why a likelihood-based mixed model of all observed data is valid under MAR while complete-case analysis and last observation carried forward are not, teaches multiple imputation that respects the longitudinal structure, and ends with sensitivity analysis for departures from MAR and with informative visit timing.
By the end of this module participants will be able to:

title: 10  Missing data and dropout
text:
10.1 Classify intermittent missingness, dropout and missing covariates, and describe the missingness pattern in a dataset.
10.2 Define MCAR, MAR and MNAR with practical examples, and explain what observed data can and cannot establish about the missingness mechanism.
10.3 State the conditions under which a likelihood-based mixed-model analysis of the observed data is valid under MAR.
10.4 Show by simulation why last observation carried forward is generally unsuitable.
10.5 Carry out multiple imputation that respects the longitudinal or multilevel structure, and combine the results with Rubin’s rules.
10.6 Conduct and report a delta-adjustment sensitivity analysis for departures from MAR.
10.7 Explain the consequences of informative visit timing.

title: 10  Missing data and dropout
text:
Prerequisites
Modules 4 and 6 (the WALK primary model and the difference in mean change at month 12), Module 2 (participant flow and missingness maps) and Module 5 (covariance structures). Module 7 introduced inverse-probability-weighted GEE, which is referred to briefly here.






WarningSimulated data



All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.

title: 10  Missing data and dropout
section: 10.1 Kinds of missing data and the WALK pattern
text:
10.1 Kinds of missing data and the WALK pattern
Three kinds of missing data occur in longitudinal studies.

Intermittent missingness: a participant misses a visit and returns later. In WALK, about 5% of scheduled visits were missed in this way.
Dropout (monotone missingness): a participant leaves and is not seen again. Every later visit is missing. Dropout is usually the more worrying kind, because the reasons for leaving are often related to how the participant is doing.
Missing covariates: a baseline or time-varying covariate is not recorded. In WALK all baseline covariates are complete; in many studies they are not.

A fourth situation is related but different: measurements that stop because of death or another terminal event (as with kidney failure in KIDNEY). After death, blood pressure is not “missing”, it does not exist, and the estimand must be defined with that in mind (International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) 2019).
The first step is always to describe the pattern. In long data, missed visits are simply absent rows; the complete grid of scheduled visits shows what is missing. walk_complete.csv holds every scheduled visit together with an observed flag. In a real study this file does not exist, but the grid of scheduled visits does, and the observed flag can be built from the visit schedule.

pattern <- walk_c |>
  arrange(id, visit) |>
  group_by(id, arm) |>
  summarise(pattern = paste(ifelse(observed, "O", "."), collapse = ""),
            n_obs = sum(observed), last = max(visit[observed])) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(type = case_when(
    n_obs == 6 ~ "Complete",
    n_obs == last ~ "Dropout only",
    last == 6 ~ "Intermittent only",
    TRUE ~ "Intermittent and dropout"))
count(pattern, pattern, sort = TRUE) |> head(8)

#> # A tibble: 8 × 2
#>   pattern     n
#>   <chr>   <int>
#> 1 OOOOOO    238
#> 2 OOOOO.     20
#> 3 O.....     15
#> 4 O.OOOO     15
#> 5 OO....     12
#> 6 OO.OOO     11
#> 7 OOO...     11
#> 8 OOO.OO     10

table(pattern$type, pattern$arm)

#>                           
#>                            UC SP EP
#>   Complete                 76 84 78
#>   Dropout only             23 19 24
#>   Intermittent and dropout  2  1  3
#>   Intermittent only        19 16 15


Each pattern is a string of six visits, with O for observed and . for missing. Of the 360 participants, 238 have complete data, 50 have only intermittent gaps and 72 drop out before month 12. Dropout ranges from 20 to 27 participants per arm.

plot_missing_map(walk_c, id, month_sched, observed,
                 order_by = as.numeric(observed) * visit) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, scales = "free_y", labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels))







Figure 10.1: Missingness map of WALK: each row is a participant and each column a scheduled visit. Dark cells are observed. Participants are sorted by their last attended visit, so dropout appears as a staircase and intermittent gaps as isolated light cells.





The next question is whether dropout is related to anything observed. A simple way is to model the probability of dropping out before each scheduled visit, among participants still in the study, as a function of the last observed SBP and the arm (a discrete-time dropout model):

risk <- walk_c |>
  arrange(id, visit) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(last_sbp = sapply(seq_along(visit), function(k) sbp[max(which(observed[1:k]))])) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(walk_b |> select(id, last_month_sched), by = "id") |>
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(prev_sbp = lag(last_sbp), prev_sched = lag(month_sched)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(visit > 1, prev_sched <= last_month_sched) |>
  mutate(drop_now = as.integer(prev_sched == last_month_sched),
         prev_sbp10 = (prev_sbp - 150) / 10)
m_drop <- glm(drop_now ~ prev_sbp10 + arm, family = binomial, data = risk)
fixef_table(m_drop, exponentiate = TRUE)

#>          term estimate      se   lower   upper         p
#> 1 (Intercept)  0.05286 0.20614 0.03529 0.07917 3.743e-46
#> 2  prev_sbp10  1.31720 0.09046 1.10319 1.57273 2.322e-03
#> 3       armSP  0.79466 0.30700 0.43537 1.45045 4.541e-01
#> 4       armEP  1.17643 0.28607 0.67153 2.06096 5.700e-01


Each row of risk is a participant who is still in the study at the previous scheduled visit; drop_now is 1 if that previous visit was their last. The odds of dropping out are 1.32 times higher (95% CI 1.10 to 1.57) for every 10 mmHg higher last observed SBP. Dropout is therefore related to observed blood pressure, and the data are not MCAR. The next section explains what this does and does not tell us.

title: 10  Missing data and dropout
section: 10.2 Missing-data mechanisms: MCAR, MAR and MNAR
text:
10.2 Missing-data mechanisms: MCAR, MAR and MNAR
Rubin (1976) classified missing data by how the probability of being missing relates to the data. Write \(\mathbf{y}_i\) for the complete vector of outcomes that participant \(i\) would have provided, split into the observed part \(\mathbf{y}_i^{o}\) and the missing part \(\mathbf{y}_i^{m}\), and let \(\mathbf{r}_i\) be the vector of indicators showing which values are observed. Covariates \(X_i\) are assumed fully observed.

Missing completely at random (MCAR): \(P(\mathbf{r}_i \mid \mathbf{y}_i, X_i) = P(\mathbf{r}_i \mid X_i)\). Missingness does not depend on any outcome values, observed or not (it may depend on covariates; some authors call this covariate-dependent MCAR). Example: a WALK participant misses a visit because the clinic’s blood pressure monitor broke, or moves away for a new job.
Missing at random (MAR): \(P(\mathbf{r}_i \mid \mathbf{y}_i, X_i) = P(\mathbf{r}_i \mid \mathbf{y}_i^{o}, X_i)\). Given the observed data, missingness does not depend on the unobserved values. Example: a participant whose SBP was high at their last visit is referred to their GP and leaves the study. The reason (the high reading) is recorded.
Missing not at random (MNAR): missingness depends on unobserved values even after conditioning on the observed data. Example: a participant whose blood pressure has risen since their last visit feels unwell, suspects the programme is not working and stops attending; the rise itself is never measured.

These definitions are about the relationship between missingness and the data, not about whether the reason for missing data is “random” in everyday language. The names are standard but confusing: MAR is not random in the everyday sense.
The mechanism matters because it determines which analyses give valid answers. Under MCAR, the observed participants are a random subsample, so nearly any analysis is unbiased (though not efficient). Under MAR, analyses that use all the observed data through a correctly specified likelihood are valid, but analyses of completers or of observed means are not. Under MNAR, no analysis of the observed data alone is guaranteed to be valid, and one must make untestable assumptions about the missing values.

10.2.1 Consequences of each mechanism: a simulation on the complete WALK data
Because WALK is simulated, we can do what is impossible in a real study: start from the complete data, delete values under each mechanism, and see what happens. The script scripts/10b_missing_data_simulations.R does this 200 times per mechanism. In each replicate it imposes monotone dropout on walk_complete.csv: before each post-baseline visit, a participant still in the study leaves with probability \(\text{logit}^{-1}(a + b\,x)\), where

MCAR: \(x = 0\) (leaving is unrelated to blood pressure);
MAR: \(x\) is the change in SBP from baseline at the last observed visit;
MNAR: \(x\) is the change in SBP from baseline at the visit about to be missed, which is never recorded.

The story is the same in both MAR and MNAR: participants whose blood pressure has risen become discouraged and leave. The difference is whether the rise that drives their decision was measured. It then estimates the difference in mean change at month 12 in four ways: observed means (mean SBP at month 12 among those seen, minus the baseline mean), last observation carried forward (LOCF), the primary mixed model fitted to completers only, and the primary mixed model fitted to all observed data. The benchmark is the same mixed model fitted to the complete data (no missingness), so the “bias” measures only the effect of missing data.

sim1 <- read_csv(here("outputs", "tables", "m10_sim_mechanisms.csv"),
                 show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(mechanism = factor(mechanism, levels = c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR")),
         method = factor(method, levels = c("Observed means", "LOCF",
                                            "Complete cases",
                                            "Mixed model, all data")))
sim1 |>
  select(mechanism, method, arm, bias, mcse_bias, emp_se, dropout) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 2))) |>
  arrange(mechanism, method, desc(arm))

#>    mechanism method                arm    bias mcse_bias emp_se dropout

ggplot(sim1, aes(bias, method, colour = arm)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = bias - 1.96 * mcse_bias, xmax = bias + 1.96 * mcse_bias),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~ mechanism) +
  scale_colour_arm(name = NULL, labels = c(SP = "SP vs UC", EP = "EP vs UC")) +
  labs(x = "Bias (mmHg)", y = NULL)







Figure 10.2: Bias in the difference in mean change at month 12 (programme versus usual care) under MCAR, MAR and MNAR dropout, for four analyses. 200 simulated dropout patterns imposed on the complete WALK data per mechanism; bars are ±1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors. Bias is measured against the same mixed model fitted to the complete data. Positive bias means the treatment effect is underestimated (pulled towards zero).





About 32% to 38% of participants drop out in each scenario. The pattern in Figure 10.2 is the central lesson of the module.

Under MCAR every method except LOCF is essentially unbiased. LOCF underestimates the EP effect by 1.43 mmHg even though the dropout is completely random (the reason is explained in the LOCF section).
Under MAR the mixed model using all observed data remains unbiased (-0.01 mmHg for EP), but complete-case analysis is biased by 1.65 mmHg and observed means by 0.70 mmHg. All the biased methods pull the effect towards zero here, because participants whose SBP rises, more common under usual care, leave and take their poor results with them.
Under MNAR every method is biased, including the mixed model (1.23 mmHg for EP). The mixed model is less biased than complete-case analysis and LOCF, but here no better than the observed means: once the mechanism is MNAR, using the observed data well no longer guarantees anything.

The column emp_se is the standard deviation of the estimates across the 200 dropout patterns. It measures only the variation caused by which values happen to be deleted (the complete data are fixed), so it is not the usual sampling standard error. It shows that the mixed model also uses the data more efficiently than complete-case analysis or observed means.


10.2.2 What the observed data can and cannot tell us
The observed data can show that data are not MCAR: if dropout is related to observed SBP, as in the WALK dropout model above, MCAR is untenable. They cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR. The reason is fundamental: MNAR means that missingness depends on values we did not observe, and we have no data on those values. For every MNAR model, there is an MAR model that fits the observed data exactly as well but implies different values for the missing data (Molenberghs and Kenward 2007). Any “test” of MAR against MNAR rests on assumptions (such as normality of the complete data) that are themselves untestable.
The simulation makes this concrete. Take one replicate under MAR and one under MNAR and fit the same dropout model to each, using only what an analyst would see:

impose_dropout <- function(d, mechanism, a = -2.3, b = 0.15) {
  d <- arrange(d, id, visit)
  sbp <- matrix(d$sbp, ncol = 6, byrow = TRUE)
  keep <- matrix(TRUE, nrow(sbp), 6)
  for (k in 2:6) {
    x <- switch(mechanism, MAR = sbp[, k - 1] - sbp[, 1], MNAR = sbp[, k] - sbp[, 1])
    keep[, k] <- keep[, k - 1] & !(runif(nrow(sbp)) < plogis(a + b * x))
  }
  d$obs_sim <- as.vector(t(keep)); d
}
observed_dropout_model <- function(d) {
  r <- d |> arrange(id, visit) |> group_by(id) |>
    mutate(last_change = lag(sbp) - sbp[1], at_risk = lag(obs_sim)) |>
    ungroup() |> filter(visit > 1, at_risk)
  coef(summary(glm(!obs_sim ~ last_change, family = binomial, data = r)))[2, ]
}
set.seed(11)
rbind(MAR  = observed_dropout_model(impose_dropout(walk_c, "MAR")),
      MNAR = observed_dropout_model(impose_dropout(walk_c, "MNAR")))

#>      Estimate Std. Error z value  Pr(>|z|)
#> MAR   0.14476    0.01603   9.028 1.744e-19
#> MNAR  0.09709    0.01531   6.340 2.298e-10


In both data sets, dropout is clearly related to the last observed change in SBP. Under MNAR the association arises because the last observed change is correlated with the unobserved current change that really drives dropout. An analyst who sees only the observed data cannot tell the two situations apart, yet the mixed model is unbiased in one and biased in the other. The choice between MAR and MNAR must therefore be justified by knowledge of the study (why do people leave? were reasons recorded?) and examined by sensitivity analysis, not by a statistical test.






NoteWhy this matters



Reports that “Little’s test showed the data were MCAR” or “missingness was tested and found to be MAR” misunderstand what data can show. At most, data can show evidence against MCAR. MAR is an assumption, chosen because it is plausible and analysable, and it should be accompanied by sensitivity analyses (National Research Council 2010; Carpenter and Kenward 2013).

title: 10  Missing data and dropout
section: 10.3 The mixed model of all observed data under MAR
text:
10.3 The mixed model of all observed data under MAR

10.3.1 The research question and estimand
The estimand is the WALK primary estimand: the difference in mean change in SBP from baseline to month 12 between each programme and usual care, in the population of randomised participants, as if all participants had been followed up under their assigned treatment. This is a treatment-policy-style estimand for a trial where dropout does not change the treatment received (an assumption of this simulation; real estimand frameworks require a decision on what happens after dropout (International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) 2019)). Because the data are simulated, its true values are −4.6 mmHg (SP) and −8.1 mmHg (EP).


10.3.2 Data structure and outcome types
Long-format data with one row per attended visit. Missed visits need no rows. Participants with only a baseline measurement still contribute. The outcome here is continuous; the same argument applies to GLMMs fitted by maximum likelihood (Module 8).


10.3.3 Intuition
A mixed model learns, from the participants who stayed, how SBP at later visits relates to SBP at earlier visits (through the random effects and the residual correlation). For a participant who left after month 3, the model uses their observed values at months 0, 1 and 3 to predict where they would have been, in effect filling in their trajectory from the information they did provide. If dropout depends only on the observed values (MAR), participants with the same observed history who stayed and who left have the same distribution of future SBP, so the stayers are a valid guide to the leavers. Complete-case analysis discards that information, and observed means compare different groups of people at different visits.


10.3.4 The model
The analysis model is the primary model,
\[
y_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_{ij}^\top\boldsymbol\beta + b_{0i} + b_{1i}t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \mathbf{y}_i \sim N(X_i\boldsymbol\beta,\; V_i), \quad V_i = Z_i G Z_i^\top + \sigma^2 I,
\]
with a mean for each arm at each scheduled visit in \(X_i\boldsymbol\beta\), random intercept and slope on actual time \(t_{ij}\) with covariance matrix \(G\), and residual variance \(\sigma^2\). Write \(\boldsymbol\theta = (\boldsymbol\beta, G, \sigma^2)\) for the parameters of the outcome model and \(\boldsymbol\psi\) for the parameters of the missingness model \(P(\mathbf{r}_i \mid \mathbf{y}_i, X_i, \boldsymbol\psi)\). The likelihood of what was actually seen, the observed outcomes and the missingness pattern, factorises under MAR:
\[
f(\mathbf{y}_i^{o}, \mathbf{r}_i \mid X_i, \boldsymbol\theta, \boldsymbol\psi) = \underbrace{f(\mathbf{y}_i^{o} \mid X_i, \boldsymbol\theta)}_{\text{outcome model}} \times \underbrace{P(\mathbf{r}_i \mid \mathbf{y}_i^{o}, X_i, \boldsymbol\psi)}_{\text{missingness model}} .
\]
Here \(f(\mathbf{y}_i^{o} \mid X_i, \boldsymbol\theta)\) is simply the multivariate normal density of the observed elements of \(\mathbf{y}_i\), with mean and covariance taken from the rows and columns of \(X_i\boldsymbol\beta\) and \(V_i\) that correspond to the attended visits. This is exactly what lmer() maximises. If, in addition, \(\boldsymbol\theta\) and \(\boldsymbol\psi\) are separable (distinct, with no shared parameters or constraints), the second factor does not involve \(\boldsymbol\theta\), and maximising the first factor alone gives valid likelihood-based inference about \(\boldsymbol\theta\). The missingness mechanism is then called ignorable for likelihood inference (Rubin 1976; Little and Rubin 2019; Molenberghs and Kenward 2007).


10.3.5 Assumptions and limitations
A likelihood-based mixed-model analysis of the observed data is valid under these conditions:

MAR: missingness depends only on observed data (observed outcomes and covariates in the model).
Separability: the parameters of the outcome model and of the missingness model are distinct. Together with MAR this makes the mechanism ignorable.
A correctly specified model for the joint distribution of the repeated outcomes, both mean and covariance. Under MAR the model’s implied conditional distribution of later values given earlier ones is what predicts the missing data. A misspecified covariance structure, harmless with complete data, can bias the mean under MAR (unlike GEE with complete data, where only the mean must be right).
The variables that drive dropout are in the model. MAR is relative to the variables included. In WALK dropout depends on the last observed SBP, which is the outcome itself and therefore automatically in the likelihood, and on arm, which is in the mean model. If dropout depended on a variable not in the model (for example, a side effect recorded at each visit), the analysis would be MNAR with respect to the model’s variables; such auxiliary variables can be added to the model if they are baseline covariates, or used through multiple imputation if they are post-baseline.
Inference uses the full likelihood, which lmer() does, with standard errors from the observed information. (GEE is not likelihood-based and needs MCAR, or weighting under MAR: Module 7.)

None of these conditions can be fully verified from the data. Condition 1 in particular is an assumption, to be assessed with sensitivity analyses.


10.3.6 Fitting the model in R
There is nothing special to do: fit the primary model to all observed rows.

m_lmm  <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk,
               control = lmer_ctrl)
completers <- walk_b$id[!walk_b$dropout]
m_cc   <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id),
               data = filter(walk, id %in% completers), control = lmer_ctrl)
m_full <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk_c,
               control = lmer_ctrl)              # simulation only
locf <- walk |>
  group_by(id, arm) |>
  summarise(base = sbp[visit == 1], last = sbp[which.max(visit)]) |>
  ungroup()
m_locf <- lm(I(last - base) ~ arm, data = locf)



10.3.7 Interpreting the output

diff_change <- function(m) {
  e  <- emmeans(m, ~ visit_f | arm, at = list(visit_f = c("0", "12")))
  ch <- contrast(e, list(change = c(-1, 1)), by = "arm")
  as.data.frame(summary(contrast(ch, "trt.vs.ctrl", by = NULL),
                        infer = TRUE, adjust = "none"))
}
lt <- fixef_table(m_locf) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)")
comp <- bind_rows(
  diff_change(m_full) |> mutate(analysis = "Complete data (simulation only)"),
  diff_change(m_lmm)  |> mutate(analysis = "Mixed model, all observed data"),
  diff_change(m_cc)   |> mutate(analysis = "Mixed model, completers only"),
  data.frame(contrast = c("change SP - change UC", "change EP - change UC"),
             estimate = lt$estimate, SE = lt$se, lower.CL = lt$lower,
             upper.CL = lt$upper, analysis = "LOCF"))
comp |> select(analysis, contrast, estimate, SE, lower.CL, upper.CL) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(., 2)))

#>                          analysis              contrast estimate   SE
#> 1 Complete data (simulation only) change SP - change UC    -5.67 1.32
#> 2 Complete data (simulation only) change EP - change UC    -8.40 1.32
#> 3  Mixed model, all observed data change SP - change UC    -5.38 1.42
#> 4  Mixed model, all observed data change EP - change UC    -8.97 1.44
#> 5    Mixed model, completers only change SP - change UC    -5.77 1.47
#> 6    Mixed model, completers only change EP - change UC    -9.20 1.50
#> 7                            LOCF change SP - change UC    -5.13 1.22
#> 8                            LOCF change EP - change UC    -8.69 1.22
#>   lower.CL upper.CL
